lessons.title: What Web Engineering Is: Clients, Servers and the Stack
lessons.content:
Imagine your aunt runs a small grocery shop in Mirpur called Bazar. Every morning people phone her: 'Do you have fresh lal shak today? How much is a kilo of potatoes? Can you send rice to Road 10?' She answers the same questions fifty times a day, writes orders on scraps of paper, and loses some of them. One day you say, 'Khala, let me build you a website.' Customers will open it on their phones, see today's prices, put items in a cart, log in, and place an order that lands neatly in a list. This course is about exactly that job: building such a web application properly, from the first line of HTML to the moment it runs on a real server for real customers. We will use Bazar as our running example in every lesson.

The Internet and the web are not the same thing: People mix these two words up all the time. The Internet is the global network of networks: cables, routers, Wi-Fi, mobile towers and the TCP/IP protocols that move packets between millions of computers. It carries many kinds of traffic: email, video calls, online games, file transfer. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on top of the Internet. It is a huge collection of documents and applications that are named by URLs, fetched with the HTTP protocol, and shown in a web browser. A simple way to remember it: the Internet is the road network of Bangladesh, and the web is one kind of vehicle, like buses, that runs on those roads. Email and online games are other vehicles on the same roads.

A very short history: In 1989 and 1990, Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, a physics laboratory in Switzerland, proposed and built the first web system. He combined three simple ideas: HTML to write pages with links, URLs to give every page an address, and HTTP to fetch a page from a server. The first pages were plain text with links. Then came images, then CSS for styling (first proposed in 1994), then JavaScript (created at Netscape in 1995) to make pages interactive. Today the same three building blocks, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, still run every website you visit, from Prothom Alo to Daraz to your university result portal.

Client and server: The web follows the client-server model. A client is the program that asks for something; a server is the program that answers. Your browser, Chrome or Firefox or Safari, is the client. When you type a web address, the browser sends a request across the Internet to a server, a computer that is always on and runs a program waiting for requests. The server sends back a response: an HTML page, an image, or some data. One server can serve thousands of clients. Think of a restaurant: you, the customer, are the client who orders; the kitchen is the server that prepares and sends food. You never walk into the kitchen; you only see what comes to your table.

The browser's job: A browser is far more than a window. It sends HTTP requests, receives responses, reads HTML and builds a tree of elements from it, applies CSS rules to decide colors and positions, runs JavaScript code, draws pixels on the screen, stores cookies, and keeps you safe by separating one website from another. Every browser contains a rendering engine (for example Blink in Chrome and Edge, Gecko in Firefox, WebKit in Safari) and a JavaScript engine (for example V8 in Chrome). As web developers we write code that the browser must understand, so we must know what the browser does with it.

The web server's job: On the other side, a web server program such as Nginx or Apache listens for requests, usually on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. For a simple file like logo.png it just reads the file from disk and sends it. For a smarter request like 'show me my orders', it passes the request to an application, code written by us in a language like JavaScript (Node.js), Python, PHP or Java. That application may ask a database for data, build a response, and hand it back. So the word 'server' can mean the physical or virtual machine, or the server program running on it; the meaning is usually clear from context.

Front end, back end and full stack: Everything that runs in the user's browser is called the front end, or client side: the HTML structure, the CSS look, and the JavaScript behavior. Everything that runs on the server is the back end, or server side: business rules, database access, login checks, payment handling. A developer who works on both is called a full-stack developer. In Bazar, the product cards, the cart icon that shows a number, and the 'Add to cart' button animation are front end. Checking that 2 kg of potatoes are really in stock, saving the order, and calculating the delivery charge are back end. A golden rule: anything about money, stock or permissions must be checked on the back end, because the user can change anything that runs in their own browser.

Static sites: A static website is a set of ready-made files: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. The server sends the same file to everyone. If Bazar only needed a page with the shop address, phone number and a photo, a static site would be perfect. Static sites are fast, cheap and hard to hack, because there is no program running on the server and no database. They can be hosted almost free on static hosting services. Their weakness: to change content, someone must edit the files and upload them again.

Dynamic sites: A dynamic website builds pages or data at the moment of the request. When Karim logs in and opens 'My orders', the server runs code, asks the database for Karim's orders, and creates an answer that is different from what Rahima sees. Facebook, Daraz, bKash's web pages and online banking are all dynamic. Dynamic sites can be personal and always up to date, but they need a server program, a database, more security care and more resources.

Website versus web application: The line is blurry, but here is a useful way to think. A website mostly shows information for people to read: a newspaper, a college notice board, a portfolio. A web application lets people do tasks: fill forms, log in, buy, chat, edit documents. Google Docs, an online exam system, and our Bazar shop with carts and orders are web applications. Web engineering in a university syllabus focuses on web applications, because they need all the skills: front end, back end, database, security and deployment.

The stack, layer by layer: A web app is built from layers, often called the stack. At the bottom is the network (Internet, DNS, TCP, HTTP), which you studied in Computer Networks. Then the server machine and its operating system, often Linux. Then the web server or runtime, such as Nginx or Node.js. Then our application code with its framework. Then the database, such as MySQL, PostgreSQL or MongoDB. On the client side we have the browser, running HTML for structure, CSS for presentation and JavaScript for behavior. Remember the classic trio: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the clothes and makeup, and JavaScript is the muscles that make things move.

A tiny trace through the stack: Let's follow one click in Bazar. Rahima taps 'Rice 5 kg, Add to cart'. JavaScript in her browser catches the tap and sends a small HTTP request, POST /api/cart with the body {product: 12, qty: 1}. The request travels through her mobile network to our server. Nginx receives it and passes it to the Node.js application. The application checks Rahima's login, asks the database whether product 12 has stock, saves the cart row, and replies with status 201 and the new cart total, say 3 items, 1,250 taka. JavaScript in the browser reads the reply and changes the cart badge from 2 to 3. Six layers worked together in a fraction of a second.

Why call it engineering: Anyone can make a single page in an afternoon. Engineering means building something that keeps working when there are 10,000 users instead of 10, when the developer who wrote it leaves, when a hacker attacks it, and when the shop wants a new feature next month. Web engineering applies software engineering ideas to the web: clear requirements, good design, version control, testing, security, performance measurement, accessibility for all users, and a repeatable way to deploy. The web also has special challenges: users on slow 3G and fast fiber, tiny phones and big monitors, many browsers, and everything exposed to the whole Internet.

Quality attributes of a good web app: Teachers often ask for the qualities a web application should have. The common list is: usability (easy to use), performance (fast to load and respond), reliability and availability (up when people need it), security (data and money safe), scalability (handles growth), maintainability (easy to change), accessibility (usable by people with disabilities), and compatibility (works across browsers and devices). Keep this list in mind; almost every later lesson improves one of these.

Standards and who makes them: The web works across companies because of open standards. HTML and the DOM are maintained as living standards by WHATWG, a group formed by browser makers. CSS is standardized by the W3C, the World Wide Web Consortium. JavaScript's official name in the standard is ECMAScript, maintained by Ecma International's TC39 committee. HTTP and many Internet protocols come from the IETF as RFC documents. As a developer, a reliable reference for all of these is MDN Web Docs, which explains each feature and shows which browsers support it.

The tools you need: Very little. A text editor such as VS Code, a modern browser, and its developer tools, opened with F12 or right-click and Inspect. DevTools lets you see the HTML tree, change CSS live, run JavaScript in the console, and watch every network request. Later we will add Node.js to run server code, a database, and Git for version control. You can start this course today with just a laptop.

Real-life example 1, a university result portal: On result day, thousands of students in Bangladesh open the same result site at once. The front end is a simple form: roll number and registration number. The back end receives the form, looks up the database, and returns a page with the grades. If the engineers did not plan for the crowd, the server is overloaded and students see errors or endless loading. Good web engineering here means caching the results, adding more servers, and keeping the page small so it loads even on weak mobile data.

Real-life example 2, a food delivery app's website: When you order biryani on a food delivery website, the front end shows restaurants, photos and a cart. The back end calculates the price with the discount code, checks that the restaurant is open, takes payment through a gateway, and sends the order to the restaurant and a rider. Live tracking uses JavaScript that asks the server for the rider's location every few seconds. Every part of this course, forms, APIs, sessions, security and performance, is visible in that one order.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often write that the Internet and the web are the same; they are not. Another mistake is thinking HTML is a programming language; it is a markup language that describes structure, with no loops or logic. JavaScript is not Java; the names are similar for historical marketing reasons only. And trusting the front end for security is a classic beginner bug. Typical exam questions: define web engineering; differentiate Internet and WWW; explain the client-server model with a diagram; compare static and dynamic websites; list the attributes of a quality web application; explain the role of HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

The course map: We start with how a page travels to you, from a developer's eye (lesson 2). Then HTML, its semantics and forms (3 to 5); CSS from selectors to flexbox, grid and responsive design (6 to 10); JavaScript, the DOM, async code and fetch (11 to 15). Then we cross to the server: Node and Express style back ends, MVC, REST APIs and databases (16 to 19). Then sessions, tokens, password security and web attacks (20 to 22). Then performance, accessibility, SPAs and SEO (23 to 25), and finally deployment and CI (26). By the end, you could build and launch Bazar yourself.

Recap: The Internet is the network; the web is a service on it made of pages and apps fetched with HTTP. Browsers are clients, servers answer. The front end runs in the browser with HTML, CSS and JavaScript; the back end runs on the server with application code and a database. Static sites send the same files to all; dynamic sites build answers per request. Web engineering means building web apps that are usable, fast, secure, scalable and maintainable, using open standards and good process.
key_points: The Internet is the global network; the World Wide Web is one service on it, using URLs, HTTP and browsers.
In the client-server model the browser (client) sends requests and the server sends responses.
Front end runs in the browser (HTML structure, CSS look, JavaScript behavior); back end runs on the server (logic, database, security).
Static sites send the same ready-made files to everyone; dynamic sites build responses per request, often from a database.
Money, stock and permission checks must always happen on the back end, because users control their own browser.
Web engineering applies software engineering to the web: usability, performance, security, scalability, maintainability, accessibility.
Open standards (WHATWG, W3C, ECMAScript/TC39, IETF RFCs) let every browser and server work together; MDN is the go-to reference.
lessons.tip: Keep your browser's DevTools open (F12) whenever you browse this semester. Seeing real pages from the inside is the fastest way to make every lesson of this course concrete.
lessons.task: Open any shopping website on your phone or laptop and make two lists: things you think run on the front end (in the browser) and things that must run on the back end (on the server). Then decide whether the site is static or dynamic and write one line explaining why.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Internet and the web is correct?
options: They are two names for the same thing
The web is a service that runs on top of the Internet
The Internet runs on top of the web
The web was invented before the Internet
quiz.explain: The Internet is the network of networks; the web is one service on it, using HTTP, URLs and browsers.

quiz.q: In the client-server model, what is the browser?
quiz.explain: The browser sends requests, so it is the client; the server answers.

quiz.q: Where must the check 'is this product really in stock' happen in Bazar?
quiz.explain: Users can change anything in their own browser, so stock, money and permission checks belong on the server.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a static and a dynamic website?
options: Static sites must use a database
A dynamic site builds its response per request, a static site sends the same files to everyone
quiz.explain: Static means ready-made files; dynamic means server code builds the answer, often from a database, for each request.

quiz.explain: HTML gives structure, CSS gives presentation, JavaScript gives behavior.

lessons.title: How a Page Reaches You: URLs, HTTP, Status Codes and Cookies from a Developer's View
lessons.content:
Think of sending a parcel through a courier in Dhaka. You write the full address on the box: the city, the area, the house number, the flat, and maybe a note like 'call before delivery'. The courier office reads it, finds the right place, and the receiver signs a slip saying 'received' or 'nobody home'. The web works the same way. The URL is the address, the HTTP request is the parcel with notes, and the HTTP response comes back with a status code that tells you exactly what happened. In Computer Networks you studied HTTP from the network's point of view, counting round-trip times. In this lesson we look at the same things through a web developer's eyes: what we must write, read and debug every day while building Bazar.

Anatomy of a URL: Take this address: https://bazar.com.bd:443/products/rice?sort=price&page=2#reviews. It has six parts. The scheme, https, says which protocol to use. The host, bazar.com.bd, names the server. The port, 443, says which door on that server; it is usually hidden because 443 is the default for https and 80 is the default for http. The path, /products/rice, says which resource on the server we want. The query string, sort=price&page=2, starts after the question mark and carries extra name=value pairs joined by the ampersand. The fragment, reviews, comes after the hash sign and points to a place inside the page.

Two URL details that bite beginners: First, the fragment is never sent to the server. The browser keeps it and uses it to scroll to the element whose id is reviews, or JavaScript can read it. So the server cannot know which section you wanted. Second, URLs can only contain a limited set of characters, so others are percent-encoded. A space becomes %20 (or a plus sign inside form data), and a Bangla word becomes its UTF-8 bytes written as %E0%A6... sequences. If Bazar lets users search for 'lal shak', the URL becomes /search?q=lal%20shak, and the server decodes it back. Also remember absolute vs relative: https://bazar.com.bd/cart is absolute; /cart is relative to the current host.

What happens before the request, in one breath: You studied this in Computer Networks, so here is just the recap. The browser asks DNS to turn bazar.com.bd into an IP address, opens a TCP connection to that IP on port 443, performs a TLS handshake so the connection is encrypted and the server's certificate is checked, and only then sends the HTTP request. With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 the browser can send many requests over one connection at once. As a developer you rarely touch these steps directly, but they explain why the first visit to a site is slower than later clicks: DNS answers and connections get reused.

The request as a developer sees it: A request has a method, a path, headers and an optional body. For example: GET /products/rice?page=2, with headers Host: bazar.com.bd, Accept: text/html, Accept-Language: bn,en, User-Agent describing the browser, and Cookie: sid=abc123. A login request might be POST /login with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded and a body phone=01711000000&password=.... When the front end talks to an API in JSON, the header is Content-Type: application/json and the body is a JSON text.

Opening DevTools Network tab: Press F12, choose the Network tab, and reload the page. Each row is one request: the HTML document, CSS files, JavaScript files, images, fonts and API calls. Columns show the name, the status code, the type, the size, and the time taken, plus a waterfall bar that shows when each request started and finished. Click a row and you see the request headers, the response headers, the payload you sent, and a preview of the response. When a Bazar button 'does nothing', the Network tab is the first place to look: did the request go out, and what status came back?

Methods and what they promise: GET reads a resource and should never change data on the server. POST creates something or triggers an action, like placing an order. PUT replaces a resource fully at a known URL, PATCH changes part of it, and DELETE removes it. HEAD is GET without the body, and OPTIONS asks what is allowed, which browsers use for CORS preflight, as we will see in lesson 15. A common bug is a 'delete' link done with GET: a search engine crawler or a prefetching browser may follow the link and delete data. Use the right method for the job.

Safe and idempotent: Two words exams love. A safe method does not change server state: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe. An idempotent method gives the same final server state whether you send it once or ten times: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. Deleting order 55 twice leaves it deleted; putting the same price twice leaves the same price. POST is neither: pressing 'Place order' twice may create two orders. That is why browsers warn you before resubmitting a POST form on refresh, and why careful apps redirect after a successful POST.

The response: A response carries a status code, headers and usually a body. Example: status 200, headers Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8, Content-Length: 5120, Cache-Control: max-age=60, and then the HTML. The Content-Type is crucial: if a server sends JSON but labels it text/html, or forgets charset=utf-8 so Bangla shows as broken symbols, the browser will misbehave. Many Bangla 'garbage text' bugs are just a missing or wrong charset.

Status codes a web developer meets daily: 200 OK is general success. 201 Created means a new resource was made, often with a Location header pointing to it. 204 No Content means success with no body, common after a delete. 301 Moved Permanently and 302 Found are redirects; the browser follows the Location header. 304 Not Modified tells the browser to use its cached copy. 400 Bad Request means the request was malformed. 401 Unauthorized actually means not authenticated, you need to log in. 403 Forbidden means you are known but not allowed. 404 Not Found means no such resource. 405 Method Not Allowed means right path, wrong method. 429 Too Many Requests means slow down. 500 Internal Server Error means our code crashed. 502 Bad Gateway and 503 Service Unavailable often mean the app behind Nginx is down or overloaded.

Reading status codes like a detective: The first digit tells you whose fault it is. A 4xx means look at what the client sent: wrong URL, missing field, no login. A 5xx means look at the server: read the server logs. Example: Bazar's checkout returns 500. The front end is probably fine; the server code threw an error, maybe because the database was unreachable. If it returns 422 or 400, the server is saying 'your data is invalid', so check the form values. Using correct codes in your own API, which we cover in lesson 18, makes life easier for everyone.

Important headers: Content-Type says what the body is. Content-Length says how many bytes. Location gives the target of a redirect or the URL of a newly created resource. Cache-Control tells browsers and CDNs how long they may keep a copy, for example max-age=3600 for one hour or no-store for private pages. Authorization carries credentials such as a token, written like Authorization: Bearer followed by the token. Accept says what formats the client wants. User-Agent identifies the browser. Set-Cookie and Cookie carry cookies. Header names are case-insensitive.

Why cookies exist: HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and the server does not remember you between requests. But Bazar must remember that Rahima is logged in and that she has rice in her cart. The cookie mechanism solves this. The server sends a response header like Set-Cookie: sid=abc123. The browser stores it, and on every later request to the same site it automatically adds the header Cookie: sid=abc123. The server looks up abc123 in its session store and knows who it is. Lesson 20 goes deep into sessions and tokens; here we learn the cookie itself.

Cookie attributes, one by one: A full cookie looks like Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax. Expires gives a date, or Max-Age gives seconds, after which the cookie is deleted; without either, it is a session cookie removed when the browser session ends. Domain decides which hosts receive it; if omitted, only the exact host that set it gets it back. Path limits it to URLs under a path. Secure means send it only over HTTPS. HttpOnly means JavaScript in the page cannot read it through document.cookie, which protects session cookies if an attacker manages to run script on the page. SameSite controls whether the cookie is sent with requests coming from other sites.

SameSite in simple words: SameSite=Strict sends the cookie only when the request starts from your own site. SameSite=Lax also sends it when the user clicks a normal link from another site to yours, but not on cross-site form posts or background requests. SameSite=None sends it everywhere, and browsers require Secure with it. Lax is a sensible default for login cookies, and many modern browsers treat a cookie without a SameSite attribute as Lax. This attribute is a strong defence against CSRF attacks, covered in lesson 22.

Cookie limits and privacy: Each cookie is small, about 4 KB at most, and every cookie is sent with every matching request, so stuffing large data into cookies slows the site. Never put secrets like passwords or a user's balance directly in a cookie value; store only a random id and keep the real data on the server. Cookies set by the site you are visiting are first-party; cookies set by another domain embedded in the page, like an ad network, are third-party and are used for tracking, which is why browsers are restricting them and many sites show cookie consent banners.

Real-life example 1, logging in to Bazar: Rahima opens bazar.com.bd/login with GET and receives 200 and the login form. She submits it: POST /login with her phone and password. The server checks them and replies 302 Found with Location: /account and Set-Cookie: sid=7f3k9; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. The browser follows the redirect: GET /account, now automatically carrying Cookie: sid=7f3k9. The server finds the session and replies 200 with 'Welcome, Rahima'. This POST then redirect then GET pattern is called Post/Redirect/Get, and it means refreshing the page will not resubmit the password form.

Real-life example 2, a broken mobile recharge page: A student reports that a recharge site shows a blank white page. Opening DevTools Network, you see the HTML loaded with 200, but app.js shows 404. Someone renamed the JavaScript file during deployment and forgot to update the script tag. Another day the same page shows 503 for every request: the server behind the load balancer was overloaded during an Eid offer. Two different problems, and the status codes pointed to each one in seconds.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Confusing 401 and 403 is very common: 401 means 'who are you? log in', 403 means 'I know you, but no'. Thinking the fragment reaches the server is another. Using GET to change data, or putting passwords in a query string where they get saved in history and server logs, is dangerous. Forgetting HttpOnly and Secure on session cookies is a security bug. Exams ask: label the parts of a URL; list HTTP methods and say which are safe and idempotent; explain status code classes with examples; explain how cookies maintain state over stateless HTTP; explain cookie attributes such as HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.

Recap: A URL has scheme, host, port, path, query string and fragment, and the fragment stays in the browser. After DNS, TCP and TLS, the browser sends a request with a method, path, headers and body, and gets a response with a status code, headers and body. GET is safe; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither. Status code classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client problem, 5xx server problem. Cookies add memory to stateless HTTP, and attributes like Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite make them safer. The Network tab in DevTools shows all of it live.
key_points: URL parts: scheme, host, port (default 80/443), path, query string (?a=1&b=2) and fragment (#id), and the fragment is never sent to the server.
Special characters in URLs are percent-encoded, for example a space becomes %20.
A request has method, path, headers and optional body; a response has status code, headers and body.
Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change data; idempotent ones (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE) give the same result when repeated; POST is neither.
Status classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found), 5xx server error.
Key headers: Content-Type (with charset), Location, Cache-Control, Authorization, Cookie and Set-Cookie.
Cookies add state to stateless HTTP; use Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on session cookies and store only an id, not secrets.
The DevTools Network tab shows every request, status, header and timing, and is your first debugging tool.
lessons.tip: When something on a page fails, do not guess. Open the Network tab, find the request, and read its status code and response. The first digit alone usually tells you whether to look at the front end or the server.
lessons.task: Open DevTools (F12), go to the Network tab and load any news site. Find the main HTML request and write down its status code, Content-Type and two other response headers. Then find any Set-Cookie header and note which attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Max-Age) it uses.

quiz.q: In https://bazar.com.bd/products?page=2#reviews, which part is NOT sent to the server?
quiz.explain: The fragment after # stays in the browser; it is used to jump within the page.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is neither safe nor idempotent?
quiz.explain: Sending POST twice can create two orders, so it is not idempotent, and it changes data, so it is not safe.

quiz.q: A logged-in customer opens the admin page and is refused. Which status code fits best?
quiz.explain: The server knows who the user is but does not allow access: that is 403. 401 means not authenticated.

quiz.q: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute do?
options: Sends the cookie only over HTTP, not HTTPS
Deletes the cookie when the tab closes
Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie
Sends the cookie to all domains
quiz.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, protecting session ids if a script is injected.

quiz.q: Bazar's checkout API returns 503 for every user. Where should you look first?
options: The server side: the app or service behind the web server
quiz.explain: 5xx codes are server-side problems; 503 often means the app is down or overloaded.

lessons.title: HTML Basics: Elements, Attributes, Links, Images and the DOM
lessons.content:
Imagine you hand a typed letter to a printing press in Nilkhet and say, 'Make the shop name big and bold, put the price list in a table, and make the phone number something people can tap.' The printer cannot guess which words are a heading and which are a price; you must mark them. HTML does exactly this marking for the browser. HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. Hypertext means text with links to other text, and markup means notes we put around content to say what each piece is. In this lesson we build the first real page of Bazar, the grocery shop website, and learn how the browser turns our text into a living tree. HTML is not a programming language: It has no variables, no loops, no if statements. It only describes structure and meaning: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link, this is an image. That is why we write HTML, not 'program' it. The behavior comes later from JavaScript and the look from CSS. Because HTML is so simple, browsers are also very forgiving: if you forget to close a tag, the browser usually guesses and still shows something. Forgiving is nice for beginners but dangerous for engineers, because different guesses can give different results, so we aim to write clean, valid HTML. Elements and tags: An element is one piece of the page. Most elements are written with an opening tag, content, and a closing tag. For example,

Fresh vegetables every morning

is a paragraph element:

opens it,

closes it with a slash, and the text in between is the content. Tag names are not case-sensitive, but lowercase is the convention. Some elements are void elements and have no content and no closing tag, such as
for a line break, for an image, for a form field, and for page information. Attributes: Extra information about an element goes in attributes inside the opening tag, written as name='value'. In Today's offers, href is an attribute telling the link where to go. In , src and alt are attributes. Some attributes can go on any element: id gives a unique name (only one element per page should have a given id), class gives a group name that many elements can share, title gives a tooltip, and lang gives the language. Quotes around values can be single or double; be consistent. Nesting: Elements go inside other elements, like boxes inside boxes.

Price: 60 taka per kg

puts a strong element inside a paragraph. The rule is: close the inner one before the outer one.

wrong

crosses the boxes and is invalid. Think of plates stacked on a tray: the last plate you put on must be the first you take off. Indenting nested elements by two or four spaces makes the structure easy to see. The skeleton of every page: Every HTML document starts the same way. First , which tells the browser to use modern standards mode instead of an old 'quirks' mode. Then the root element , telling search engines and screen readers that the page is in Bangla. Inside it come exactly two children: and . The head holds information about the page that is not shown directly: its title, character set, links to CSS files. The body holds everything the user sees. A minimal Bazar page is: , , with , and Bazar, fresh groceries in Mirpur, then with the content, then the closing tags. The two meta tags you must never forget: tells the browser that the bytes of the file are UTF-8 encoded. UTF-8 can represent every character in Unicode, including Bangla letters like ক and conjuncts. Without it, a browser may guess a wrong encoding and show Bangla as rubbish. The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to use the real screen width instead of pretending to be a 980-pixel-wide desktop and shrinking the page. Without it, your Bazar page will look tiny on a phone. We will return to it in the responsive design lesson. The text appears in the browser tab, in bookmarks, and as the blue headline in search results. Headings and paragraphs: HTML has six heading levels, <h1> to <h6>. <h1> is the main title of the page, <h2> marks big sections, <h3> sub-sections, and so on. Use them for structure, not for size: if you want small text, use CSS, not <h5>. A good page usually has one <h1>, and levels should not jump, for example from <h2> straight to <h4>. Paragraphs use <p>. Inside text, <strong> marks strong importance (shown bold), <em> marks stress emphasis (shown italic), <br> forces a line break, and <hr> shows a thematic break line. Remember: browsers collapse multiple spaces and line breaks in your source into a single space, so pressing Enter in the code does not create a new line on screen. Links: The anchor element <a> creates hyperlinks, the heart of the web. Its href can be several kinds of URL. An absolute URL includes the scheme and host: <a href='https://www.bangladesh.gov.bd'>Government portal</a>. A root-relative URL starts with a slash and is relative to the site's root: href='/products'. A document-relative URL has no leading slash and is relative to the current file's folder: if you are at /shop/index.html, href='rice.html' means /shop/rice.html, and href='../about.html' goes up one folder to /about.html. A fragment link jumps within a page: href='#contact' goes to the element with id='contact'. Special schemes work too: href='tel:+8801711000000' opens the phone dialer, and href='mailto:hello@bazar.com.bd' opens email. Link attributes worth knowing: target='_blank' opens the link in a new tab. When you do that for external sites, add rel='noopener' so the new page cannot control your page through window.opener; modern browsers now apply this behavior by default for target='_blank', but writing it is harmless and clear. The download attribute asks the browser to download the file instead of opening it. Link text should describe the destination: 'Download price list (PDF)' is better than 'click here', both for screen reader users and for search engines. Images: <img src='images/potato.jpg' alt='Fresh potatoes in a basket' width='400' height='300'> shows an image. src is the path to the file. alt is alternative text: it is read by screen readers for blind users, shown if the image fails to load, and used by search engines. For purely decorative images, use alt='' (empty) so screen readers skip it. Giving width and height lets the browser reserve the space before the image arrives, so the page does not jump around while loading. Common formats are JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics with sharp edges or transparency, SVG for logos and icons that must scale, and WebP or AVIF for smaller modern files. Lists: Unordered lists use <ul> with <li> items and show bullets: perfect for a list of categories like vegetables, fish, rice and lentils. Ordered lists use <ol> with <li> and show numbers: perfect for steps such as 'Choose items, Add to cart, Pay, Receive delivery'. Description lists use <dl>, with <dt> for a term and <dd> for its description, for example a term 'Delivery charge' and the description '50 taka inside Mirpur'. Lists can be nested: an <li> can contain another <ul>. Navigation menus are almost always built as lists of links. Tables: Tables are for tabular data, information with rows and columns, like a price list. <table> holds everything, <tr> is a table row, <th> is a header cell and <td> is a data cell. A Bazar price table could have a header row with Item, Unit, Price, then rows like Potato, 1 kg, 40 taka, and Onion, 1 kg, 90 taka. For better structure use <thead>, <tbody> and <caption>, which names the table. colspan='2' makes a cell stretch across two columns, and rowspan='2' across two rows. Long ago people used tables to lay out whole pages; today that is a mistake, and CSS flexbox and grid do layout. Comments and whitespace: A comment is written as <!-- this is a note for developers -->. Browsers ignore it, but it is still sent to every visitor and visible with View Source, so never put passwords or private notes in HTML comments. Special characters that HTML uses for itself must be written as character references: < for <, > for >, and & for &. So to show 'Rice & Lentils' safely you write Rice & Lentils, and   gives a non-breaking space. How the browser builds the DOM: When the HTML arrives, the browser does not keep it as text. It parses it, reading tokens like 'start tag p', 'text', 'end tag p', and builds a tree of objects called the DOM, the Document Object Model. The document is the root; under it is html; under html are head and body; under body are h1, p, ul and so on; text inside elements becomes text nodes. For <ul><li>Fish</li><li>Rice</li></ul>, the tree has a ul node with two li children, each holding a text node. CSS styles these nodes and JavaScript can read and change them, which is lesson 13. DevTools' Elements panel shows you this live tree, not your original file, so if the browser fixed a missing tag, you will see its fixed version there. Validation: Because browsers forgive mistakes, you need a tool that does not. The W3C Markup Validation Service, at validator.w3.org, checks your HTML against the standard and lists errors like a missing closing tag, a duplicate id, or an image without alt. Many editors, such as VS Code with extensions, show these problems as you type. Valid HTML gives more predictable results across browsers, better accessibility, and fewer strange CSS bugs. File naming and structure: A website is a folder. The home page is usually named index.html, because most web servers send index.html when someone asks for a folder like /. Keep names lowercase without spaces, for example fresh-fish.html, because spaces become %20 in URLs and some servers treat Rice.jpg and rice.jpg as different files. A typical small project has index.html at the top, and folders such as css/, js/ and images/. Real-life example 1, Bazar's first page: The body starts with <h1>Bazar</h1> and a <p> saying 'Fresh groceries delivered in Mirpur within 2 hours.' Then <h2>Today's prices</h2> with a table of five items. Then <h2>Categories</h2> with a <ul> of links to /vegetables, /fish and /rice. Then <h2>Contact</h2> with <a href='tel:+8801711000000'>Call us</a>. Without any CSS it looks plain, but it is complete, readable on any phone, understandable to a screen reader, and indexable by search engines. That is the power of good HTML. Real-life example 2, a college notice board: Many college websites in Bangladesh post notices as scanned images only. A student using a screen reader, or someone on slow data, cannot read them, and search engines cannot find 'Admission test date' inside a picture. If the notice were written as HTML text, with an <h1> title, a <p> body, a <time> date and a link to the PDF, everyone could read and search it. Simple HTML choices decide who can use your site. Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the doctype or meta charset, using headings for font size, using <br> again and again instead of paragraphs or CSS margins, missing alt text, wrong nesting, duplicate ids, and writing ../ paths wrongly are the classics. Exams ask: what is HTML and why is it called a markup language; write the basic structure of an HTML5 document; difference between element, tag and attribute; difference between absolute and relative URLs; write HTML for a given table with colspan or rowspan; explain ordered and unordered lists; what is the DOM. Recap: HTML marks up content so the browser knows its structure. Elements have opening and closing tags (or are void), attributes add details, and elements nest like boxes. Every page has the doctype, html, head and body, plus meta charset utf-8 and the viewport meta. Headings show structure, links connect pages with absolute, relative or special URLs, images need alt text, lists and tables organize content. The browser parses HTML into a DOM tree that CSS and JavaScript work on, and validators keep your HTML clean.
key_points: HTML is a markup language that describes structure and meaning; it has no logic like loops or conditions.
An element usually has an opening tag, content and closing tag; void elements like img, br, input and meta have no closing tag.
Attributes add details as name='value'; id must be unique per page, class can be shared by many elements.
Every page needs <!DOCTYPE html>, html with lang, head (meta charset utf-8, viewport meta, title) and body.
Links use absolute URLs, root-relative (/path), document-relative (file.html, ../file.html), fragments (#id) or special schemes (tel:, mailto:).
Images need alt text (empty alt for decorative ones) and width/height to avoid layout jumps.
Use ul/ol/li for lists and table/tr/th/td for tabular data, never tables for page layout.
The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree; validators like validator.w3.org catch errors browsers silently fix.
lessons.tip: Type every small HTML page by hand at first instead of copying. Your fingers learn opening and closing tags, and you will spot nesting errors instantly later.
lessons.task: Using any text editor (even Notepad), make a file index.html with the full HTML5 skeleton and build a mini price list for a shop near you: one h1, one paragraph, a table with at least 4 items and prices, an unordered list of 3 categories, and a tel: link. Open it in your browser and then check it at validator.w3.org by direct input.

quiz.q: Why do we call HTML a markup language and not a programming language?
options: It can only be written by browsers
It describes structure and meaning but has no logic like loops or conditions
It is compiled into machine code
quiz.explain: HTML marks what each piece of content is; behavior comes from JavaScript.

quiz.q: What does <meta charset='utf-8'> mainly prevent?
options: Bangla and other characters showing as garbled symbols
The page being too small on mobile
quiz.explain: It tells the browser the file is UTF-8 encoded, so characters like Bangla display correctly.

quiz.q: You are on /shop/index.html. Where does href='../about.html' point?
quiz.explain: ../ goes up one folder from /shop/ to the root, so the link is /about.html.

quiz.q: What alt value should a purely decorative image have?
quiz.explain: Empty alt tells screen readers to skip decorative images; missing alt may make them read the file name.

quiz.q: What does the browser build from the HTML it receives?
options: A tree of objects called the DOM
quiz.explain: The HTML parser builds the Document Object Model, a tree that CSS and JavaScript work with.

lessons.title: HTML5 Semantics and Media: Meaningful Structure, Audio, Video and Graphics
lessons.content:
Walk into a well-organized hospital in Dhaka. Above each door there is a sign: Reception, Emergency, Pharmacy, Exit. A newcomer, a blind visitor with a helper, or a delivery person can all find their way because each area announces what it is. Now imagine the same building where every door just says 'Room'. You could still walk around, but you would waste time and get lost. Old web pages were like that second building: everything was a
. HTML5 gave us signs for the doors: elements like
,
,
and
that say what each part of the page is for. This is called semantic HTML, and in this lesson we rebuild the Bazar page with proper signs, then add audio, video and graphics. What semantic means: Semantic means 'about meaning'. A semantic element tells the browser, search engines and assistive technology what its content is, not just how it looks.

says 'main heading',
says 'navigation links',
says 'a complete piece of content'. A non-semantic element like
says nothing: it is a plain box. Both can be styled to look the same, so a sighted user might not notice the difference, but machines do. Semantics is about telling the truth about your content. The div and span era: Before HTML5, developers wrote
,
,
. The names were in ids and classes that only humans understood. Every site invented its own names: one used 'top', another 'masthead', another 'hdr'. A screen reader could not know which div was the menu. HTML5, finalized as a W3C recommendation in 2014 and now maintained by WHATWG as a living standard, added a set of sectioning and landmark elements based on the names developers were using most often. The header element:
holds introductory content for the page or for a section: usually the logo, the site name and sometimes a search box. A page can have more than one header, because an
can have its own header with its title and date. For Bazar, the top header holds the Bazar logo, the tagline 'Fresh groceries in Mirpur', and a search form. The nav element:
wraps a block of major navigation links, such as the main menu or a table of contents. Not every group of links needs
; a few links in a footer can live without it. Bazar's nav contains a list of links: Home, Vegetables, Fish, Rice and Lentils, My Orders. Screen reader users can jump straight to the navigation landmark instead of listening to the whole page. The main element:
holds the dominant, unique content of the page, the part that changes from page to page, not the repeated header, menu or footer. There should be only one visible
per page. On Bazar's home page, main holds today's offers and the product grid. Screen readers offer 'skip to main content', and some browser reading modes use
to find what to show. Article versus section: These two confuse everyone, so let's be precise. An
is a self-contained composition that would make sense on its own if you took it out of the page: a blog post, a news story, a product card, a user comment. A
is a thematic grouping of content inside a document, normally with its own heading, like 'Today's offers' or 'Customer reviews'. A simple test: could this piece be shared or syndicated alone, for example in a feed? Then article. Is it just a chapter of this page? Then section. And if you only need a box for styling, with no meaning, use
. Sections can contain articles (a 'Reviews' section full of review articles) and articles can contain sections (a long blog post with chapters). Aside and footer:
holds content that is related but secondary to the main content around it: a sidebar with 'Popular items', a pull quote, or a box of tips.
holds information about its section or page: copyright, contact links, address, social links. Like header, footer can appear in the page and inside articles; an article footer may show the author and tags. More meaningful elements:
key_points: Semantic elements describe what content is, not how it looks; div and span are meaningless generic boxes.
Page landmarks: header, nav, main (one visible per page), aside and footer; screen readers let users jump between them.
Article is self-contained and could stand alone; section is a themed group of a page, usually with a heading.
figure/figcaption, time with datetime, address, mark and abbr add more precise meaning.
Semantics improves accessibility, helps search engines understand pages and makes code easier to maintain.
Block elements start on a new line and fill the width; inline elements flow within text; CSS display decides the final behavior.
video and audio play natively: controls, poster, multiple source formats, muted autoplay, preload, and track for WebVTT captions.
Canvas is a JavaScript-drawn pixel bitmap; SVG shapes are DOM elements that scale crisply and can be styled and clicked.
lessons.tip: Before writing any page, sketch it on paper and label each block with a semantic name: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer. If you cannot name a block, it is probably just a div.
lessons.task: Pick the home page of any Bangladeshi news or shopping site. On paper, draw its layout as boxes and label each box with the HTML5 element you would use. Then open DevTools Elements panel and check: does the site actually use header, nav, main and footer, or just divs?

quiz.q: What does a semantic element mainly add to a page?
options: Information about what the content is
quiz.explain: Semantic elements describe meaning, which helps screen readers, search engines and developers.

quiz.q: A customer review card on Bazar that could be shown on its own elsewhere is best marked as:
quiz.explain: A self-contained piece that makes sense independently is an article.

quiz.q: How many visible <main> elements should a page have?
quiz.explain: main holds the page's unique primary content, so only one visible main per page.

quiz.q: Which is true about canvas and SVG?
options: Canvas shapes are DOM elements you can click individually
SVG is a bitmap that blurs when zoomed
Both need a plugin like Flash
SVG shapes live in the DOM and stay sharp when scaled
quiz.explain: SVG is vector shapes as DOM elements; canvas is pixels drawn by JavaScript.

quiz.q: Which element adds subtitle or caption files to a video?
quiz.explain: track points to a WebVTT file with kind='captions' or 'subtitles'; caption is for tables, figcaption for figures.

lessons.title: HTML Forms: Inputs, Labels, GET vs POST and Built-in Validation
lessons.content:
Think of the admission form you filled in for college: boxes for your name, father's name, date of birth, a tick box for your group, a space to paste a photo, and a signature at the bottom. The office collects thousands of these, and a clerk checks each one: is the roll number filled in, is the date sensible? A web form is the same paper form, made digital. It is how almost every useful thing on the web begins: searching, logging in, signing up, placing a Bazar order, paying a bill. In this lesson we learn how HTML forms are built, how their data travels to the server, and how the browser can check inputs before sending them.

The form element: Everything starts with <form action='/order' method='post'>. The action attribute is the URL that will receive the data; if you leave it out, the form submits to the current page's URL. The method attribute is the HTTP method, either get or post; if you leave it out, the default is get. Inside the form go the controls: inputs, select boxes, text areas and buttons. When the user presses a submit button, the browser collects the controls' values, encodes them, and sends an HTTP request to the action URL, then shows whatever page the server returns.

Name and value, the most important rule: Each control sends one or more name=value pairs. The name comes from the control's name attribute, and the value is what the user typed or chose. <input name='phone'> with 01711000000 typed into it sends phone=01711000000. A control without a name attribute is not submitted at all, no matter what the user typed. This is the number one beginner bug: the form looks perfect, but the server receives nothing because the inputs have only ids, no names. The id is for labels, CSS and JavaScript; the name is for the server.

GET forms: With method='get', the pairs are added to the URL as a query string. A Bazar search form with one input name='q' sends the user to /search?q=potato. This is perfect for searches and filters: the URL can be bookmarked, shared on Messenger, and the back button works naturally. But everything is visible in the address bar, saved in browser history and in server logs, and URLs have practical length limits. So GET forms are for reading, never for passwords or for actions that change data.

POST forms: With method='post', the pairs travel in the request body, not the URL. Login, sign-up, placing an order, uploading a file and posting a comment use POST. The data is not shown in the address bar or history, and the body can be large. But careful: POST does not mean encrypted. Anyone who can see the traffic can read a POST body just as easily as a URL, unless the site uses HTTPS. Privacy comes from HTTPS; POST only keeps the data out of the URL.

URL encoding in action: By default the body uses the format application/x-www-form-urlencoded, which looks exactly like a query string: name=Rahima+Akter&area=Mirpur+10&qty=2. Spaces become plus signs, and characters like & and = inside values are percent-encoded so they do not break the pairs. Bangla text becomes percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes. The server's framework decodes all of this automatically, so you get back the original strings.

Text-like inputs: The input element changes behavior with its type attribute. type='text' is a single line. type='password' hides the characters as dots, but only on screen. type='email' expects an address with an @ and shows an email keyboard on phones. type='tel' shows a number pad on phones but does not check the format, since phone formats differ by country. type='number' allows only numbers, with min, max and step. type='url' expects a web address. type='search' is a text box styled for searching. Choosing the right type costs nothing and makes mobile typing much easier for Bazar customers.

Choice inputs: type='checkbox' is a tick box for yes/no or multiple choices; an unchecked checkbox sends nothing at all, and a checked one sends its value, or 'on' if no value is set. type='radio' lets the user pick exactly one from a group; radios belong to the same group when they share the same name. For Bazar delivery time, three radios named slot with values morning, afternoon and evening send slot=evening if the third is chosen. Add the checked attribute to pre-select one. <select name='area'> with <option value='mirpur'>Mirpur</option> children gives a drop-down list; add multiple to allow several choices, and selected to pre-select.

Other useful controls: type='date' and type='time' show the browser's own date and time pickers, and the value is sent in a standard format like 2025-04-14 regardless of how it is displayed. type='range' is a slider, type='color' a color picker, type='file' lets users choose files, with accept='image/*' to suggest images and multiple for several files. type='hidden' sends a value the user does not see, such as an order id, but remember the user can still see and change it in DevTools. <textarea name='note' rows='4'></textarea> is a multi-line box for a delivery note like 'Gate is on the left side'. <datalist> offers suggestions for a text input while still allowing free typing.

Labels: Every control needs a visible label. The best way: <label for='phone'>Mobile number</label> followed by <input id='phone' name='phone' type='tel'>. The for attribute matches the input's id. You can also wrap the input inside the label. This does two things. A screen reader announces 'Mobile number, edit text' when focus lands on the input, so blind users know what to type. And clicking the label text focuses the input or toggles the checkbox, which gives a bigger tap target on small phones. A placeholder, the grey hint text inside the box, is not a label: it disappears when typing begins and is often low contrast.

Grouping with fieldset: <fieldset> groups related controls and <legend> gives the group a title. A group of radios for 'Payment method: Cash on delivery, bKash, Card' should sit inside a fieldset with that legend, so screen readers read the question along with each option. Fieldsets can also be disabled as a whole.

Buttons: <button type='submit'>Place order</button> submits the form. <button type='reset'> clears all fields back to their initial values, which users rarely want, so it is seldom used. <button type='button'> does nothing by itself and is used for JavaScript actions like 'add one more item'. Important trap: a <button> inside a form with no type attribute defaults to submit. Many beginners put a 'Show password' button in a login form and are surprised when clicking it submits the form. Always write the type. Pressing Enter in a text field also submits the form.

Built-in validation: HTML can check inputs before sending, with no JavaScript. required means the field must not be empty. minlength and maxlength limit text length. min and max limit numbers and dates; step sets allowed increments. type='email' and type='url' check the format. pattern takes a regular expression that the whole value must match. For a Bangladeshi mobile number: pattern='01[3-9][0-9]{8}' means 0, 1, one digit from 3 to 9, then exactly eight more digits, 11 digits total. If a rule fails, the browser blocks submission and shows a message near the field. CSS can style fields with :invalid and :valid. Adding novalidate to the form turns these checks off, for example when you want custom JavaScript messages.

A worked validation example: Bazar's order form has quantity <input type='number' name='qty' min='1' max='20' required>. The user types 0: blocked, value too small. Types 25: blocked, too large. Leaves it empty: blocked, required. Types 3: allowed. For the phone field with the pattern above, 01711000000 passes, 0171100000 (10 digits) fails, and 01211000000 fails because the third digit 2 is not in 3 to 9. The user gets instant feedback without waiting for the server.

Client validation is not security: This is the most important sentence of the lesson. Browser validation is for convenience only. Anyone can open DevTools and delete the required attribute, change max='20' to max='9999', or skip the form entirely and send a request with a tool like curl or Postman. The server must check every value again: is qty a positive integer within stock, is the phone format right, does the product exist, is the price taken from the database and never from a hidden field. Never trust the client.

File uploads and enctype: To upload files, the form needs method='post' and enctype='multipart/form-data'. In that format the body is split into parts separated by a boundary string, each part with its own headers, so binary file bytes can travel alongside text fields. Without the right enctype, only the file name is sent, not the file. On the server you must check the file type and size and store it safely, never trusting the file name. If Bazar lets shops upload product photos, limiting accept to images in the browser is just a hint; the server must verify.

Autocomplete and usability: The autocomplete attribute tells the browser what a field is, such as autocomplete='name', 'tel', 'street-address', 'email', 'current-password' or 'new-password', so it can fill saved data and password managers work correctly. Keep forms short, ask only what you need, put labels above fields on mobile, show errors next to the field in plain words, and keep the user's typed data when the server returns an error. Every extra field loses some customers.

Real-life example 1, Bazar checkout: The form has action='/orders' and method='post'. A fieldset 'Delivery details' has name (required, autocomplete='name'), mobile (type='tel', pattern as above, required), area (a select of Mirpur sections), address (textarea, required), and delivery slot radios. A fieldset 'Payment' has radios for Cash on delivery and bKash. The submit button says 'Place order, 1,250 taka'. The browser sends name=...&mobile=...&area=mirpur-10&slot=evening&payment=cod. The server re-validates everything, recalculates the price from its database, saves the order, and redirects to /orders/57 with Post/Redirect/Get.

Real-life example 2, a search on an e-commerce site: The search bar is a GET form: <form action='/search'> with <input type='search' name='q'> and filters like price range and brand as more inputs. Searching 'saree' with brand filters gives a URL like /search?q=saree&brand=aarong&max=5000. Customers can copy that URL and send it to a friend, who sees the same results. This is why search and filter forms use GET.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Missing name attributes, using GET for login, believing POST is secure without HTTPS, labels not linked to inputs, placeholder as the only label, buttons without type submitting by accident, forgetting enctype for uploads, and trusting hidden fields or client validation. Exams ask: explain the form tag and its action and method attributes; compare GET and POST for form submission; list HTML5 input types; write a registration form with validation; what is the purpose of the label element; why is server-side validation still needed.

Recap: A form collects name=value pairs from its controls and sends them to the action URL using the method. GET puts data in the URL and suits searches; POST puts data in the body and suits changes, and only HTTPS makes it private. Input types give better keyboards and checks; labels, fieldsets and legends make forms accessible. Buttons default to submit inside forms. required, min, max, pattern and friends validate in the browser, but the server must validate again. File uploads need POST and multipart/form-data.
key_points: A form sends name=value pairs to its action URL with its method; the default method is GET, and controls without a name are not sent.
GET puts data in the URL (good for search, bookmarkable); POST puts it in the body (good for changes); only HTTPS makes either private.
Input types (email, tel, number, date, checkbox, radio, file, hidden) give suitable keyboards and checks; unchecked checkboxes send nothing.
Radios with the same name form one group where only one can be chosen.
Link labels with for and id; placeholders are not labels; group related controls with fieldset and legend.
A button inside a form defaults to type submit, so always write type='button' for non-submitting buttons.
Built-in validation: required, minlength, maxlength, min, max, step, pattern; but the server must validate everything again.
File uploads need method='post' and enctype='multipart/form-data'.
lessons.tip: After building any form, open DevTools Network, submit it, and look at the payload. If a field is missing there, it has no name attribute. This one habit saves hours of confusion.
lessons.task: Write an HTML sign-up form for Bazar with: full name (required), a Bangladeshi mobile number with pattern 01[3-9][0-9]{8}, email, password (minlength 8), area as a select, and a terms checkbox (required). Use proper labels. Test it in your browser by entering wrong values, then remove one required attribute in DevTools and notice how easily client validation is bypassed.

quiz.q: A Bazar form has inputs with ids but no name attributes. What will the server receive from them?
quiz.explain: Only controls with a name attribute are submitted; ids are for labels, CSS and JavaScript.

quiz.q: Which method is best for a product search form, and why?
options: POST, because it hides the data
GET, because the result URL can be bookmarked and shared
DELETE, because it removes old results
quiz.explain: Search only reads data, and GET puts the query in the URL so it can be shared and bookmarked.

quiz.q: What happens when you click a <button> with no type attribute inside a form?
quiz.explain: The default type of a button inside a form is submit.

quiz.q: Why must the server validate data even if the HTML has required and pattern?
options: Because users can bypass client-side checks with DevTools or direct requests
Because pattern only works on GET forms
quiz.explain: Client validation is only a convenience; attackers can edit the page or send requests directly.

quiz.q: Which enctype is needed to upload a product photo through a form?
quiz.explain: multipart/form-data splits the body into parts so file bytes can be sent; it needs method post.

lessons.title: CSS Fundamentals: Selectors, the Cascade and Specificity
lessons.content:
Imagine you have built the walls, doors and rooms of a new flat in Mirpur. Everything stands, but it is bare grey cement. Now you call the painter and the interior designer: this wall light green, these curtains blue, the sofa near the window. They do not move any walls; they only decide how things look and where they sit. On a web page, HTML is the walls and rooms, and CSS is the painter and the interior designer. In this lesson we learn how to tell the browser 'make this text green' in a way that is precise, predictable and easy to change later. What CSS is: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It is a language for describing the presentation of a document: colors, fonts, spacing, sizes, borders, backgrounds, layout and even simple animations. HTML says what something is (a heading, a list, a button); CSS says how it looks. Keeping these two apart is called separation of concerns. The same HTML can look completely different with a different style sheet, and one style sheet can style hundreds of pages at once. If Bazar, our Dhaka grocery shop, wants a new brand color for Eid, the developer changes one line in one CSS file instead of editing 200 HTML pages. Why CSS was invented: In the early web, people styled pages with HTML tags like font and attributes like bgcolor written inside every element. Changing the look of a site meant editing every tag on every page, and the HTML became messy and hard to read. CSS was proposed by Hakon Wium Lie in 1994 and became a W3C recommendation in 1996. Today CSS is developed as separate modules (selectors, flexbox, grid and so on), and browsers add features as each module matures. You do not need to remember version numbers; you need to know which features browsers support, and the website caniuse.com answers exactly that. Three ways to add CSS: First, inline styles, written in a style attribute directly on an element:

Sold out

. Second, an internal style sheet, written inside a
key_points: CSS describes presentation (colors, fonts, spacing, layout); HTML describes structure.
External style sheets are preferred: shared by all pages, cacheable, clean HTML; inline styles are hard to override and reuse.
A rule is a selector plus declarations (property: value;); invalid declarations are silently ignored.
Selectors: type, .class, #id, [attribute], combinators (space, >, +, ~), :pseudo-class, ::pseudo-element.
Cascade order: origin and !important, then specificity, then source order (later wins).
Specificity is (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements), compared left to right; one id beats any number of classes.
Text properties like color and font inherit; box properties like margin and border do not.
rem is relative to the root font size (usually 16px), em to font size, % to the parent, vw/vh to the viewport; custom properties (--name, var()) make themes easy.
lessons.tip: Whenever a style refuses to work, do not guess. Right-click the element, choose Inspect, and read the Styles panel: the winning rule is on top and the losers are crossed out. Five minutes of this daily teaches specificity faster than any book.
lessons.task: Write the specificity (a,b,c) of these selectors on paper and rank them: #menu a, .nav .item a:hover, ul li a, .card > .title, a[href^='https']. Then create a tiny HTML file with a paragraph matched by two of them, open it in your browser and confirm the winner in DevTools.

quiz.q: Which selector has the highest specificity?
quiz.explain: #cart p is (1,0,1); one id beats any number of classes or types.

quiz.q: What happens if you write colr: green; in a CSS rule?
options: The whole style sheet stops working
The browser shows an error dialog
The browser ignores that declaration and continues
quiz.explain: CSS is forgiving: unknown properties or invalid values are skipped, the rest of the rule still applies.

quiz.q: With the root font size at 16px, what is 1.5rem?
quiz.explain: rem multiplies the root font size: 1.5 x 16 = 24px.

quiz.q: Which property is NOT inherited by child elements by default?
quiz.explain: Box properties such as margin, padding and border do not inherit; text properties do.

quiz.q: Two rules have equal specificity and importance and set the same property. Which wins?
options: The one written later in the source
Neither; the browser default is used
quiz.explain: When origin, importance and specificity tie, source order decides and the later rule wins.

lessons.title: The Box Model and Positioning
lessons.content:
Imagine packing a gift of mangoes from Rajshahi to send to a cousin in Dhaka. The mangoes sit in the middle. Around them you stuff newspaper so they do not bruise. Around that is the cardboard box itself. And when the courier stacks boxes in the van, they leave a little gap between boxes. Mangoes, newspaper, cardboard, gap: four layers. A browser thinks about every single element on a web page in exactly this way. Every heading, paragraph, image and button is a rectangular box with four layers, and once you see the boxes, CSS layout stops being magic.

What the box model is: The CSS box model says that each element generates a rectangle made of four areas, from inside out. The content area holds the text or image. The padding is the space between content and border, filled with the element's background. The border is a line around the padding, which can have a width, style and color. The margin is transparent space outside the border that pushes other boxes away. In our gift: mangoes are content, newspaper is padding, cardboard is border, the gap in the van is margin.

Setting the four layers: You write padding: 20px; for all four sides, or padding: 10px 20px; meaning 10px top and bottom, 20px left and right, or four values in clockwise order starting from the top: padding: 5px 10px 15px 20px; means top 5, right 10, bottom 15, left 20. A handy memory trick is TRouBLe: Top, Right, Bottom, Left. The same pattern works for margin. Borders are written as border: 2px solid #2e7d32; with width, style (solid, dashed, dotted, none) and color, or per side like border-bottom. border-radius rounds the corners, and border-radius: 50% on a square image makes a circle.

Width with content-box, worked: By default, box-sizing is content-box, which means the width property sets only the content width. Suppose .card { width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; margin: 10px; }. The visible box is 300 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 5 = 350px wide. Add the margins and it occupies 350 + 10 + 10 = 370px of horizontal space. Beginners write width: 300px and are surprised the card is wider than 300 and breaks their layout. Two cards side by side in a 600px row would need 740px and wrap to the next line.

Width with border-box, worked: With box-sizing: border-box, the width includes padding and border. The same card now has a visible width of exactly 300px, and the browser shrinks the content area to 300 - 40 - 10 = 250px. Margins are still outside, so it occupies 320px. This is far easier to reason about, which is why most modern projects start with a small reset: *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }. You decide the outer size; padding grows inward.

Margin collapsing: Here is a famous surprise. When two block elements sit one above the other, their vertical margins do not add up; they collapse into one margin equal to the larger. If a heading has margin-bottom: 20px and the paragraph below has margin-top: 30px, the gap is 30px, not 50px. Collapsing happens only with vertical margins of block boxes in normal flow; horizontal margins never collapse, and margins of flex or grid items do not collapse. A parent's top margin can also collapse with its first child's top margin when there is no padding or border between them, which is why a child's margin sometimes seems to push the parent down instead. Adding a little padding or a border to the parent stops it.

The display property: display decides what kind of box an element makes. block boxes start on a new line and stretch to fill the parent's width by default; div, p, h1 and section are block. inline boxes flow inside a line of text like words; span, a, strong and img are inline, and width and height do not apply to inline text elements; vertical padding and margin on them do not push surrounding lines apart. inline-block flows like a word but accepts width, height and vertical spacing, useful for badges and buttons in a row. display: none removes the element completely: it takes no space, is not shown and is generally hidden from screen readers too. Two more values, flex and grid, turn an element into a layout container and get their own lessons next.

visibility versus display none: visibility: hidden makes an element invisible but it still occupies its space, like an empty chair kept for a guest. display: none removes the chair too. opacity: 0 makes it transparent but it can still be clicked. Choose based on whether the layout should change. For example, a 'Loading' message that disappears should usually use display: none so the content below moves up.

Normal flow: Without any positioning, boxes are laid out in normal flow: block boxes stack top to bottom, inline content runs left to right and wraps, like writing in a notebook. The position property lets you take an element out of or shift it within this flow. It has five values: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky, used with the offsets top, right, bottom and left.

static and relative: static is the default; the element sits in normal flow and offsets have no effect. relative keeps the element in normal flow, but then shifts it visually by the offsets. position: relative; top: 10px; left: 20px; moves it 10px down and 20px right, while its original space stays reserved, so nothing else moves. The most common use of relative is not moving anything at all; it is making the element a reference point for absolutely positioned children.

absolute: An absolutely positioned element is removed from normal flow, so other elements behave as if it does not exist. It is placed using offsets relative to its containing block, which is the nearest ancestor whose position is not static. If there is none, it uses the initial containing block, which is basically the page. Worked example: Bazar's product card has position: relative, and inside it a '20% OFF' badge has position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px;. The badge sits 8px from the card's top-right corner. Forget position: relative on the card, and the badge flies to the top-right of the whole page. That bug happens to almost everyone once.

fixed: A fixed element is also removed from flow, but positioned relative to the viewport, the visible window. It stays in place when you scroll. Chat buttons in a bottom corner, such as a 'Message us on WhatsApp' bubble, often use position: fixed; bottom: 16px; right: 16px;. Because it covers content, give the page enough padding at the bottom so the last line is not hidden behind it.

sticky: sticky is a hybrid. The element behaves like relative in normal flow until the page scrolls to a threshold you set, like top: 0, then it sticks there like fixed, but only while its parent container is still on screen. A table header that stays visible while you scroll through 300 rows of exam results is a classic use: th { position: sticky; top: 0; background: white; }. If sticky seems not to work, usually no threshold like top was set, or an ancestor has overflow: hidden, which creates a different scroll container.

z-index and stacking: When positioned boxes overlap, which one is on top? By default, later elements in the HTML paint on top of earlier ones. z-index changes this for positioned elements (and for flex and grid items): a higher number is drawn above a lower one, so a dropdown menu with z-index: 10 appears above content with z-index: 1. One subtlety: certain properties such as a z-index on a positioned element or opacity below 1 create a stacking context, a group whose children are stacked only among themselves. A child with z-index: 9999 cannot escape its parent's group. When a modal refuses to come on top, check the parents' stacking contexts.

overflow: What if content is bigger than its box, like a long product description in a fixed-height card? overflow: visible (the default) lets it spill outside. hidden clips the extra. scroll always shows scrollbars. auto shows scrollbars only when needed, usually the best choice. You can control directions separately with overflow-x and overflow-y; a wide table on a phone often gets a wrapper with overflow-x: auto so it scrolls sideways instead of breaking the page.

Centering tricks: For text and inline content, text-align: center on the parent. For a block with a known width, margin: 0 auto; splits the leftover horizontal space equally, so the box sits in the middle. Vertical centering used to be painful; today the cleanest way is the parent with display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;, which you will learn properly in the flexbox lesson. With absolute positioning, top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%); places the element's centre at the centre of its containing block.

outline versus border: An outline is drawn outside the border and does not take up space, so it never shifts the layout. Browsers use outlines to show keyboard focus. Removing them with outline: none and giving nothing in return makes a site unusable for keyboard users, so if you dislike the default, replace it with your own clear focus style rather than deleting it.

Real-life example 1, Bazar's product grid bug: Three cards should fit in a 960px container, each width: 320px. They wrap into two rows. Why? Each card has padding: 16px and border: 1px, so under content-box each is 320 + 32 + 2 = 354px, and three need 1,062px. Switching to box-sizing: border-box makes each exactly 320px and they fit. Then the developer adds the absolute discount badge, remembers position: relative on .card, and adds overflow: hidden with border-radius so product images do not poke out of the rounded corners.

Real-life example 2, a news site header: A Bangla news portal wants its red menu bar to stay visible while readers scroll a long article about the budget. The header gets position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 100; so it stays above article images. A 'Back to top' button uses position: fixed at the bottom right. A breaking-news ticker uses overflow: hidden so the scrolling text never escapes its strip. Each problem maps to one property you learned today.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that width excludes padding and border under content-box. Expecting two vertical margins to add up. Setting width on an inline span and wondering why nothing happens.
