Using absolute without a positioned parent. Fighting z-index wars with ever bigger numbers instead of checking stacking contexts. Using display: none when visibility: hidden was intended, or the reverse. Removing focus outlines. In DevTools, the Computed tab shows a diagram of the box model with exact pixel values for content, padding, border and margin, which settles most arguments.

What exams ask: Draw and label the box model. Calculate the total rendered width and occupied space for given width, padding, border and margin, under both content-box and border-box. Explain margin collapsing with an example. Compare the five position values, and explain what the containing block of an absolute element is. Differentiate block, inline and inline-block, and display: none versus visibility: hidden.

Recap: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width mean the outer size, which is why it is the usual reset. Vertical margins of stacked blocks collapse to the larger one. display chooses block, inline, inline-block or none. position chooses static, relative, absolute (relative to the nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to the viewport) or sticky (relative until a threshold). z-index stacks positioned boxes within stacking contexts, and overflow handles content that does not fit. Next lesson, flexbox makes arranging boxes in a row or column almost effortless.
key_points: Each element is a box: content, padding, border, margin (inside to outside).
content-box: width is content only; rendered width = width + left/right padding + left/right border.
border-box: width includes padding and border, so the content shrinks; the usual reset is box-sizing: border-box on everything.
Vertical margins of stacked block boxes collapse to the larger value; horizontal margins never collapse.
display: block (new line, full width), inline (no width/height), inline-block, none (removed); visibility: hidden keeps the space.
position: static (default), relative (shift, space kept), absolute (relative to nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (viewport), sticky (sticks at a threshold).
z-index stacks positioned elements within stacking contexts; overflow (visible, hidden, scroll, auto) handles content that does not fit.
Never remove focus outlines without giving a visible replacement.
lessons.tip: Open DevTools, select any element and look at the box model diagram in the Computed tab. Hover each layer and the page highlights padding in green and margin in orange. Do this on five sites and box model questions become easy.
lessons.task: On paper: a box has width 250px, padding 15px, border 3px and margin 12px. Calculate its visible width and the horizontal space it occupies with content-box, then with border-box (and its content width). Then build a card in an HTML file with a corner badge using position: relative and absolute, and check your numbers in DevTools.

quiz.q: With box-sizing: content-box, width 200px, padding 10px and border 2px, what is the visible width?
quiz.explain: 200 + 10 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 224px; content-box adds padding and border to the width.

quiz.q: A heading has margin-bottom 24px and the next paragraph has margin-top 16px. What is the vertical gap?
quiz.explain: Vertical margins of adjacent blocks collapse to the larger value, 24px.

quiz.q: An element with position: absolute is placed relative to what?
options: Its nearest positioned (non-static) ancestor, or the initial containing block if none
quiz.explain: The containing block of an absolute element is the nearest ancestor with position other than static.

quiz.q: Which hides an element but keeps its space in the layout?
quiz.explain: visibility: hidden keeps the box's space; display: none removes it entirely.

quiz.q: Which position value keeps an element in normal flow until a scroll threshold, then holds it there?
quiz.explain: sticky acts like relative until the threshold (for example top: 0) is reached, then sticks while its container is visible.

lessons.title: Flexbox: Laying Out Things in a Row or a Column
lessons.content:
Imagine a school assembly in Chattogram. The teacher shouts: 'Class Six, stand in one line! Leave equal gaps! Tallest in the middle! The line should be centered on the field!' The students do not need individual instructions about where each one stands; they follow rules for the whole line. Flexbox is exactly that for a web page. You tell a parent element how its children should line up, spread out, shrink and grow, and the browser works out every position. Before flexbox, developers built rows with floats and odd hacks; even centering one thing vertically was a classic headache. Flexbox made it a few lines.

What flexbox is: The Flexible Box Layout, flexbox for short, is a CSS layout mode for arranging items in one dimension: either a row or a column at a time. You turn it on by setting display: flex on a parent. That parent becomes a flex container, and its direct children automatically become flex items. Only direct children are affected; grandchildren lay out normally unless their own parent is also a flex container. There is also display: inline-flex, which makes the container itself behave like an inline box while its children still flex.

Why one dimension matters: Flexbox thinks about a single line of items, like beads on a thread. It is perfect for navigation bars, toolbars, a row of buttons, a card's internal layout, a form row with a label and an input, or centering one thing. When you need rows and columns aligned together at the same time, like a full page grid or a photo gallery whose columns must line up, CSS Grid, the next lesson, is the better tool. Many real pages use both: grid for the big page regions, flexbox inside each region.

The two axes: Every flex container has a main axis and a cross axis. The main axis is the direction items are placed in; the cross axis is perpendicular to it. With the default flex-direction: row, the main axis runs left to right and the cross axis runs top to bottom. With flex-direction: column, the main axis runs top to bottom and the cross axis runs left to right. This is the single most important idea: justify-content always works along the main axis and align-items always works along the cross axis, so when you change direction, their visual effect swaps.

flex-direction: The four values are row (default, left to right in English and Bangla text), row-reverse (right to left), column (top to bottom) and column-reverse (bottom to top). A navbar is usually row; a mobile sidebar menu or a card's internal stack of image, title, price and button is usually column. Reversing only changes the visual order, not the order in the HTML.

Start and end, not left and right: Notice that values are named flex-start and flex-end, not left and right. That is deliberate. Flexbox follows the writing direction of the page, so on an Arabic or Urdu page written right to left, a row starts on the right. If Bazar ever adds an Urdu version, the same CSS keeps working without changes. Thinking in start and end instead of left and right is a good habit across modern CSS.

justify-content: This distributes items and leftover space along the main axis. flex-start packs items at the start (the default). flex-end packs them at the end. center puts them in the middle. space-between puts the first item at the start, the last at the end, and equal gaps between items. space-around gives each item equal space on both sides, so the edges get half the gap of the middle. space-evenly makes every gap, including the edges, equal. Worked example: a 600px row with three 100px items has 300px of free space. With space-between, the two gaps are 150px each. With space-evenly, there are four gaps of 75px each. With space-around, each item gets 50px on each side, so edges are 50px and middle gaps 100px.

align-items and align-self: align-items aligns items along the cross axis inside their line. stretch (the default) makes items fill the cross size, which is why flex children in a row often become equal height, very handy for cards. flex-start, flex-end and center align them to the top, bottom or middle in a row. baseline lines up the first lines of text, useful when items have different font sizes. align-self on a single item overrides align-items just for that item, for example one button aligned to the bottom while others stay at the top.

Perfect centering: The famous three lines: .box { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; } center the child both horizontally and vertically. Give the container a height, such as min-height: 100vh for a full-screen splash page, and the child sits exactly in the middle. Years of tricks were replaced by this.

flex-wrap and gap: By default, flex-wrap: nowrap forces all items onto one line, and they shrink to fit, even if they get squashed. flex-wrap: wrap lets items move to a new line when there is not enough room, just like words in a paragraph. When items wrap, align-content controls how the lines themselves are spaced along the cross axis, similar to justify-content but for lines. The gap property sets space between items, for example gap: 16px, without adding margin to the outer edges. gap is cleaner than margins because you no longer need to remove the margin from the last item.

order: Each flex item has order: 0 by default, and items are placed in ascending order. Setting order: -1 on one item moves it first visually. Use this carefully: screen readers and keyboard Tab order still follow the HTML source order, so if the visual order and the source order disagree, keyboard users jump around in confusing ways. Prefer changing the HTML order when the meaning changes.

flex-grow: Now the flexible part. flex-grow says how an item shares leftover positive space. The default is 0, meaning do not grow. Worked example: a 600px container holds three items, each with flex-basis 100px, so 300px is used and 300px is free. If their flex-grow values are 1, 2 and 1, the total is 4 shares, so each share is 300 / 4 = 75px. The items become 100 + 75 = 175px, 100 + 150 = 250px and 100 + 75 = 175px. Total 600px. If all three have flex-grow: 1, each gets 100 extra and they are 200px each.

flex-shrink: flex-shrink decides how items give up space when they do not fit. The default is 1, so items can shrink. Worked example: a 500px container holds three items with flex-basis 200px, needing 600px, so there is 100px of overflow. With equal shrink values of 1, each loses 100 / 3, about 33.3px, ending near 166.7px. With shrink values 1, 1 and 2 and equal bases, the weights are 1 : 1 : 2, so they lose 25px, 25px and 50px, ending at 175px, 175px and 150px. To be precise, the browser weights shrinking by flex-shrink multiplied by flex-basis, so bigger items shrink more; with equal bases it reduces to the simple ratio. flex-shrink: 0 means never shrink, useful for a logo or an avatar that must keep its size.

flex-basis and the flex shorthand: flex-basis is the starting size along the main axis before growing or shrinking, like a width in a row. Its default is auto, meaning use the item's width or its content size. Most people write the shorthand flex: grow shrink basis. flex: 1 is common and means flex: 1 1 0%, so items start from zero and share all space equally, giving equal-width columns no matter their content. flex: none means 0 0 auto, a rigid item. flex: 0 0 250px fixes an item at 250px, like a sidebar.

The min-width surprise: Flex items have a default minimum size of auto, which roughly means they refuse to shrink smaller than their content. A long unbroken word or URL, or a wide image, can stop an item from shrinking and push the layout wider than the screen. The fix is often min-width: 0 on the item (or overflow: hidden), which allows it to shrink, together with overflow-wrap: anywhere for long text. Knowing this saves hours of confused debugging.

auto margins: In a flex container, margin: auto on an item soaks up all free space on that side. A classic navbar: logo, links, and a 'Login' button that should sit at the far right. Put display: flex on the nav and margin-left: auto on the login button, and the button is pushed to the right edge while the others stay left. No extra wrapper needed.

Real-life example 1, Bazar's navbar: The HTML is a nav containing a logo image, three links (Rice and Dal, Vegetables, Fish) and a cart button. CSS: nav { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 24px; padding: 12px 16px; } and .cart { margin-left: auto; }. align-items: center lines up the tall logo and the short text links on the same middle line. On phones, the developer adds flex-wrap: wrap so links drop to a second line instead of overflowing. The logo has flex-shrink: 0 so it never squashes.

Real-life example 2, Bazar's product cards: The product list is .cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 16px; } and each card is .card { flex: 1 1 220px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; }. On a 1000px laptop screen, four cards fit per row (4 x 220 plus 3 gaps of 16 = 928px; the leftover 72px is shared, so each grows to 238px). On a 360px phone only one fits, and it grows to the full width. Inside each card, the column direction stacks image, name and price, and the 'Add to cart' button gets margin-top: auto, which pushes it to the bottom so all buttons line up even when one product name is two lines long, like 'Radhuni Turmeric Powder 200 g'.

Another everyday pattern, the sticky footer: On short pages, the footer floats in the middle of the screen. Fix it with body { display: flex; flex-direction: column; min-height: 100vh; } and main { flex: 1; }. The main area grows to fill the free space, pushing the footer to the bottom of the screen when content is short, and normally below the content when it is long.

Common mistakes: Putting display: flex on the items instead of their parent. Expecting justify-content to center vertically in a row; in a row, vertical is the cross axis, so you need align-items. Forgetting the container height when trying to center vertically, so there is no space to center within. Using order and breaking keyboard order. Expecting nowrap items to stay their width, when they actually shrink. Forgetting the min-width: auto behaviour with long words. DevTools shows a small 'flex' badge next to flex containers; clicking it overlays the items, gaps and free space on the page.

What exams ask: Define flex container and flex item, main axis and cross axis. Explain justify-content values with a diagram or numbers, like the space-between and space-evenly calculation. Compute final item sizes from flex-grow or flex-shrink values. Write CSS for a navbar or a centered box. Compare flexbox and grid and say when to use each.

Recap: display: flex turns a parent into a one-dimensional layout container whose direct children are flex items. flex-direction sets the main axis; justify-content distributes along it and align-items aligns across it. flex-wrap and gap handle multiple lines and spacing. flex-grow shares leftover space by ratio, flex-shrink removes overflow by weighted ratio, and flex-basis is the starting size; flex: 1 gives equal columns. Auto margins push items apart, and order changes only the visual order. Next lesson, CSS Grid takes us to two dimensions.
key_points: display: flex makes a flex container; only its direct children become flex items.
Flexbox is one-dimensional: a row or a column; grid is for rows and columns together.
flex-direction sets the main axis; justify-content works on the main axis, align-items on the cross axis.
justify-content: flex-start, flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly; align-items default is stretch.
flex-wrap: wrap allows new lines; gap adds space between items only.
flex-grow shares free space by ratio; flex-shrink removes overflow (weighted by flex-shrink x basis); flex-basis is the starting size.
flex: 1 means 1 1 0%, giving equal-width items; margin-left: auto pushes an item to the far end.
order changes only visual order, not keyboard or screen reader order; min-width: 0 lets items with long content shrink.
lessons.tip: Learn flexbox by playing, not reading. Make one HTML file with a container and five colored divs, then change one property at a time in DevTools and watch. Free games like Flexbox Froggy also turn the property names into muscle memory.
lessons.task: Calculate on paper: a 900px flex container has three items with flex-basis 200px and flex-grow 1, 1 and 2. What is each item's final width? Then build a navbar with a logo on the left and a cart button pushed to the right using margin-left: auto, and resize the window to see how wrap behaves.

quiz.q: In a container with flex-direction: row, which property centers items vertically?
quiz.explain: In a row the cross axis is vertical, and align-items works on the cross axis.

quiz.q: A 600px row holds three 100px items with justify-content: space-evenly. How big is each gap?
quiz.explain: Free space 300px is split into four equal gaps (both edges and two middles): 300 / 4 = 75px.

quiz.q: Which children become flex items when display: flex is set on a div?
options: Only elements with the class flex-item
quiz.explain: Flex layout applies to the container's direct children only.

quiz.q: A 500px container has two items, flex-basis 100px, flex-grow 1 and 3. What are their final widths?
quiz.explain: Free space 300px in 4 shares of 75px: 100 + 75 = 175px and 100 + 225 = 325px.

quiz.q: What does flex: 1 expand to?
quiz.explain: flex: 1 is shorthand for 1 1 0%, so items share all space equally.

lessons.title: CSS Grid: Two-Dimensional Layout
lessons.content:
Think of an exam hall at Dhaka University. Before students arrive, the invigilator has already decided the layout: 8 rows of benches, 6 columns, an aisle between columns, roll numbers taped on each seat. Some long benches take two seats; the invigilator's desk spans the whole front row. Students do not push each other around to find places; the grid is planned first and everyone drops into a cell. CSS Grid works the same way. You draw rows and columns on a container, then place items into cells or across several cells. Flexbox lines things up in one direction; Grid controls both directions at the same time.

What CSS Grid is: CSS Grid Layout is a layout mode for two-dimensional layouts: rows and columns together. You set display: grid on a container, and its direct children become grid items. You then define tracks: columns with grid-template-columns and rows with grid-template-rows. The lines between tracks are called grid lines, a single box formed by one row and one column is a grid cell, and any rectangle of cells is a grid area. With these few words you can describe almost any page layout, from a simple gallery to a full dashboard.

Why grid was needed: Before grid, whole page layouts were built with floats, tables used for layout, or later flexbox with many nested wrappers. Each had problems. Floats were meant for wrapping text around images, not for columns. Layout tables mixed presentation into HTML and confused screen readers. Flexbox handles one line well but cannot make items in different rows line up into the same columns without tricks. Grid was designed specifically for layout, so the HTML can stay simple and meaningful while CSS decides the arrangement.

Defining columns and rows: grid-template-columns: 200px 300px 200px; creates three columns of fixed width. grid-template-rows: 80px auto 60px; creates three rows: 80px tall, sized by content, and 60px. Items are placed automatically, one per cell, left to right, top to bottom, in source order. A fourth item would start the second row. Fixed pixel columns do not adapt to screen size, which is why grid introduced a new flexible unit.

The fr unit, worked: fr means a fraction of the free space in the grid container. The browser first subtracts fixed-size tracks and gaps, then divides what remains among the fr tracks by ratio. Example: a 1000px container with grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 2fr; and column-gap: 20px. There are two gaps, 40px total. Free space is 1000 - 200 - 40 = 760px. There are 3 fr in total, so 1fr = 760 / 3, about 253.3px, and 2fr is about 506.7px. Unlike percentages, fr never causes overflow because gaps are already subtracted. grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr gives three equal columns.

repeat(): Writing 1fr twelve times is tiring, so repeat(12, 1fr) does it for you. You can repeat patterns too: repeat(2, 100px 1fr) expands to 100px 1fr 100px 1fr. A common 12-column page system is grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr); and then items span as many columns as they need.

minmax(): minmax(min, max) defines a track that is never smaller than min and never larger than max. grid-template-columns: 250px minmax(400px, 1fr); means a fixed sidebar and a main column that takes the rest but never goes below 400px. For rows, grid-auto-rows: minmax(120px, auto) means every row is at least 120px tall but grows if its content needs more, so text is never cut off.

auto-fill and auto-fit, worked: The most famous grid line is grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));. It means: fit as many columns as possible, each at least 200px, and stretch them to share leftover space. On a 1000px container with no gap, that is 5 columns of 200px. On 900px it is 4 columns of 225px. On a 360px phone it is 1 column of 360px. No media query needed. The difference between auto-fill and auto-fit shows when there are few items. Suppose 1000px and only 2 items. auto-fill still creates 5 tracks, so the 2 items are 200px each and 3 empty tracks remain. auto-fit creates them too but collapses the empty ones to zero, so the 2 items stretch to 500px each. Use auto-fill when you want items to keep a steady size; auto-fit when you want them to fill the row.

Gaps: column-gap and row-gap, or the shorthand gap: 16px 24px (row gap then column gap), put space between tracks. Gaps never appear on the outside edges, so you do not need negative margins or special rules for the last item. The same gap property works in flexbox, as you saw last lesson.

Grid lines and placing items: Lines are numbered starting at 1 from the start edge. Three columns have four vertical lines: 1, 2, 3 and 4. Negative numbers count from the end, so -1 is always the last line. To place an item, give its start and end lines: grid-column: 1 / 3; makes it cover columns one and two. grid-column: 1 / -1; spans the full width whatever the number of columns. grid-row: 2 / 4; covers rows two and three. Instead of an end line you can say span: grid-column: span 2; means take two columns from wherever I am placed. Items can even overlap if you place them into the same cells, and z-index decides which is on top.

A worked placement: Take a grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr) and six items, A to F. Give only A the rule grid-column: 2 / 4; grid-row: 1 / 3;. A now covers columns two and three in rows one and two, a block of four cells. The other items are auto-placed in source order into the free cells: B goes to row 1, column 1; C to row 1, column 4; D to row 2, column 1; E to row 2, column 4; and F starts row 3 at column 1. Drawing this on squared paper is the fastest way to check exam answers about placement, because you can see exactly which cells are taken before the auto-placement algorithm fills the rest.

grid-template-areas: This is the most readable feature of grid. You name regions with strings that look like a map of the page: grid-template-areas: 'header header' 'sidebar main' 'footer footer'; together with grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr;. Each string is a row, each word a cell. Then each item says where it belongs: header { grid-area: header; }, aside { grid-area: sidebar; }, main { grid-area: main; }, footer { grid-area: footer; }. Repeating a name across cells makes that area span them. A dot means an empty cell. Every named area must form a rectangle; an L-shape is invalid. The beauty is that changing the layout for phones is just rewriting the map: 'header' 'main' 'sidebar' 'footer' with one column.

The implicit grid: What if you define 3 rows but have 20 items? Grid creates extra rows automatically. The tracks you define are the explicit grid; the extra ones are the implicit grid. Their size is set by grid-auto-rows (and grid-auto-columns), which defaults to auto, meaning sized by content. grid-auto-flow controls the auto-placement direction: row (the default) fills row by row, column fills column by column, and adding dense lets the browser backfill holes left by big items, which can change visual order, so use it for galleries rather than content whose order matters.

Aligning inside cells: Within each cell, justify-items aligns items along the row (inline) direction and align-items along the column (block) direction. Both default to stretch, so items fill their cells. place-items: center is a shorthand for both and centers every item in its cell. justify-self and align-self do the same for one item. If the tracks together are smaller than the container, justify-content and align-content move the whole grid, for example justify-content: center centers a fixed-width grid on a wide screen.

Grid or flexbox?: A good rule: flexbox is content-out, grid is layout-in. With flexbox, the items' sizes drive where things wrap, which is great for a row of tags or buttons whose widths vary. With grid, you decide the tracks first and items fit into them, which is great when columns must line up across rows, such as a product gallery, a calendar or the main page skeleton. They combine naturally: a grid for the page and the gallery, flexbox inside each card. Neither is old or new-fashioned; both are standard tools supported by all modern browsers.

Real-life example 1, Bazar's page skeleton: The body becomes a grid: grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; and grid-template-areas: 'header header' 'filters products' 'footer footer';. The header with the logo and search box spans both columns. The left column holds filters (price range, category: rice, dal, oil, fish). The right holds products. On phones, a media query switches to one column and the map 'header' 'products' 'footer', and the filters move into a pop-up drawer. The HTML did not change at all.

Real-life example 2, the product gallery and a class routine: Inside the products area, .grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(180px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; } creates a gallery that shows six cards on a big monitor and two on a phone, all in perfectly aligned columns. A featured item, like a mango season offer, gets grid-column: span 2 to be twice as wide. A university class routine page is another natural grid: columns for Sunday to Thursday, rows for time slots, and a two-hour lab placed with grid-row: span 2. A table also works for routine data, but grid helps when the visual layout must change on small screens.

Accessibility note: Grid can place items anywhere visually, regardless of source order. Screen readers and keyboard focus follow the HTML order. If you move the footer to the top visually, keyboard users still reach it last, which confuses everyone. Keep the HTML in a logical reading order and use grid placement for arrangement, not for changing meaning.

Grid is not a replacement for tables: Because grid looks like a table, beginners sometimes rebuild real data tables, such as a bKash transaction history or an exam result sheet, with divs and grid. That throws away meaning. An HTML table tells screen readers which cell belongs to which column header, so a blind user hears 'Amount, 500 taka' instead of a stream of numbers. Rule of thumb: if the data has rows and columns by nature, use table elements and style them with CSS; if you are arranging page regions or cards, use grid.

Common mistakes: Forgetting display: grid on the parent. Counting columns instead of lines, so grid-column: 1 / 3 is expected to cover three columns when it covers two. Using percentages plus gaps and getting overflow, where fr would have worked. Writing a non-rectangular template area or leaving out a name used by grid-area. Mixing up auto-fill and auto-fit. Expecting grid to replace flexbox completely. In DevTools, clicking the 'grid' badge next to the container overlays line numbers, area names and gaps on the page, which makes placement mistakes obvious.

What exams ask: Define grid container, item, line, track, cell and area. Compute column widths from a template with fr units, fixed tracks and gaps. Write a grid-template-areas layout for header, sidebar, main and footer. Explain auto-fill versus auto-fit, explicit versus implicit grid, and compare grid with flexbox. Place an item spanning given rows and columns using line numbers.

Recap: display: grid creates a two-dimensional container. grid-template-columns and rows define tracks; fr shares free space after fixed tracks and gaps; repeat and minmax make templates short and flexible, and repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...)) gives responsive galleries without media queries. Items are placed automatically or by line numbers, spans and named areas. Extra rows form the implicit grid sized by grid-auto-rows. Use grid for layout-in structure and flexbox for content-out rows. Next lesson we make all of this responsive for phones, tablets and big screens.
key_points: display: grid creates a two-dimensional layout container; its direct children are grid items.
Tracks are rows and columns; lines separate tracks and are numbered from 1, with -1 as the last line.
fr divides free space after fixed tracks and gaps are subtracted (1000px, 200px 1fr 2fr, two 20px gaps: 1fr is about 253px).
repeat() shortens templates; minmax(min, max) bounds a track; repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) is responsive without media queries.
auto-fill keeps empty tracks; auto-fit collapses them so items stretch.
Place items with grid-column: 1 / 3, span 2, or named grid-template-areas that must be rectangles.
Extra items create the implicit grid, sized by grid-auto-rows; grid-auto-flow sets the placement direction.
Grid is layout-in (two dimensions), flexbox content-out (one dimension); keep HTML in logical order for accessibility.
lessons.tip: Before writing grid CSS, draw your layout on paper as boxes, number the lines along the top and side, and write the area names inside. Your grid-template-areas strings then become a copy of the drawing.
lessons.task: On paper: a 1200px container has grid-template-columns: 300px 1fr 1fr 2fr and gap 24px. Compute each column width. Then build a page with grid-template-areas for header, sidebar, main and footer, and add a media query that turns it into one column below 700px.

quiz.q: Container 800px, grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr, no gap. How wide is each 1fr column?
quiz.explain: Free space 800 - 200 = 600px shared by 2fr, so 1fr = 300px.

quiz.q: With four columns, which grid-column value makes an item span the full width?
quiz.explain: Lines run 1 to 5, and -1 is always the last line, so 1 / -1 covers all columns.

quiz.q: What is the difference between auto-fill and auto-fit in repeat()?
options: auto-fit collapses empty tracks so items stretch; auto-fill keeps empty tracks
quiz.explain: Both create as many tracks as fit, but auto-fit collapses unused tracks to zero, letting items grow.

quiz.q: Items beyond the rows you defined are placed in:
options: The implicit grid, sized by grid-auto-rows
quiz.explain: Grid adds implicit tracks for extra items; grid-auto-rows sets their size.

quiz.q: Which is the best fit for CSS Grid rather than flexbox?
options: A single row of tags with different widths
A product gallery whose columns must line up across rows
Centering one icon in a button
quiz.explain: When both rows and columns must align, two-dimensional grid is the natural tool.

lessons.title: Responsive Design: One Site for Every Screen
lessons.content: Think of water poured into different containers: a glass, a jug, a bucket. The water does not need a different recipe for each; it takes the shape of whatever holds it. A good website should behave like that water. The same Bazar shop is opened by a rickshaw puller's son on a cheap 5-inch Android phone in Sylhet, by an office worker on a 14-inch laptop in Motijheel, and by a shopkeeper on a tablet behind the counter. Building one site that reshapes itself sensibly for every screen is called responsive web design, and in a country where most people reach the internet through phones, it is not optional. What responsive design is: Responsive web design means one HTML document, one URL, and CSS that adapts the layout to the screen size and capabilities of the device. The term was coined by Ethan Marcotte in 2010, and he described three ingredients: fluid grids that use relative widths instead of fixed pixels, flexible images that scale inside their containers, and media queries that apply different CSS rules at different screen widths. Flexbox and grid, from the last two lessons, have made the first ingredient much easier than it was in 2010. Why not separate mobile sites: Years ago many companies built a second site, often at an m. address, just for phones. That meant two codebases, two sets of bugs, content that went out of sync, and confusing links when someone shared a mobile URL to a desktop user. Search engines also prefer one URL per piece of content. A responsive site is cheaper to maintain and gives everyone the same content. Google now uses the mobile version of a page for indexing and ranking, so a site that is broken on phones is effectively broken for search too. CSS pixels and device pixels: A phone may have a screen 1080 physical pixels wide, but CSS treats it as about 360 CSS pixels wide. The ratio, here 3, is the device pixel ratio. Browsers do this so that 16px text is readable on every device instead of microscopic on sharp screens. When you write a media query or a width in CSS, you are always talking about CSS pixels, not physical ones. That is why a phone that is 'Full HD' still triggers your small-screen layout. The viewport meta tag: Without help, mobile browsers assume a page was designed for desktop. They render it on a virtual canvas around 980 CSS pixels wide and then shrink everything to fit, so text becomes tiny and users must pinch and zoom. The fix is one line in the head: . It tells the browser to make the layout viewport equal to the device's width in CSS pixels and start at normal zoom. Forget it, and none of your media queries will behave as expected on phones. Do not disable zoom with maximum-scale or user-scalable=no; people with weak eyesight need to zoom. Fluid layouts: Instead of width: 960px, use widths that follow the container: percentages, fr units in grid, flex-grow in flexbox. A useful pattern for the main content is .container { width: 100%; max-width: 1100px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 0 16px; }. On a phone it fills the screen with 16px breathing space on each side; on a big monitor it stops at 1100px and stays centered so lines of text do not stretch across the whole screen. For reading comfort, long text is often limited to about 60 to 75 characters per line, and the ch unit makes that easy: max-width: 65ch. Media queries: A media query applies a block of CSS only when a condition is true. Syntax: @media (min-width: 768px) { .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); } }. The condition is checked continuously, so resizing a browser window or rotating a tablet switches styles instantly. Common features you can test are min-width and max-width, orientation: portrait or landscape, hover: hover (does the main input device support hover, true for a mouse, usually false for touch), prefers-color-scheme: dark for dark mode, and prefers-reduced-motion: reduce for people who get dizzy from animations. You can combine conditions with and, for example @media (min-width: 768px) and (orientation: landscape). Newer browsers also accept a range syntax like @media (width >= 768px), but min-width remains the most widely used form. Mobile-first: There are two ways to write media queries. Desktop-first writes the full desktop layout as the default and uses max-width queries to undo things for smaller screens. Mobile-first writes the simple one-column phone layout as the default, then uses min-width queries to add columns and extras as space grows. Mobile-first is the common recommendation because the phone styles are simpler, phones do not download and then override desktop rules, and it forces you to decide what content truly matters. Worked example: .cards { display: grid; gap: 12px; } gives one column by default; @media (min-width: 600px) { .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } } and @media (min-width: 1000px) { .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); } }. A 360px phone sees 1 column, a 768px tablet 2, a 1280px laptop 4. Choosing breakpoints: A breakpoint is a width where the layout changes. Do not choose breakpoints from a list of popular phone models; models change every year. Instead, start narrow, widen the window slowly, and add a breakpoint where the design starts to look bad, such as lines getting too long or cards stretching too wide. Frameworks give convenient defaults; Bootstrap's are around 576, 768, 992 and 1200 pixels, but they are a starting point, not a law. Often grid's repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) removes the need for a breakpoint entirely. Flexible images: An image with its natural width of 1600px will burst out of a 360px phone screen. The classic fix is img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }: the image never gets wider than its container and keeps its proportions. Also write width and height attributes on img tags, like width='800' height='600'. Browsers use them to reserve the right amount of space before the image downloads, so the text does not jump down when the picture arrives, which is part of good performance. srcset and sizes: Sending a 1600px, 400 KB photo to a phone that shows it at 360px wastes data, and data costs money for many users in Bangladesh. The srcset attribute lists several versions: srcset='hilsha-400.jpg 400w, hilsha-800.jpg 800w, hilsha-1600.jpg 1600w', where w gives each file's real width. The sizes attribute tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed, for example sizes='(min-width: 1000px) 25vw, 100vw', meaning a quarter of the viewport on large screens and full width otherwise. The browser then picks the smallest file that is sharp enough, considering the device pixel ratio. On a 360px phone with ratio 2, it needs about 720 pixels, so it picks the 800w file, not the 1600w one. The picture element: picture lets you control which image appears. For art direction, a wide banner of a busy Dhaka market might be cropped to a close-up of the stall on phones: . A source can also offer modern formats with type='image/avif' or type='image/webp', and browsers that do not support them fall back to the img. The img inside is required; it holds the alt text and the fallback. Responsive typography: Text can scale with the screen using clamp(min, preferred, max). h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw, 3rem); } means 4% of the viewport width, but never smaller than 1.75rem or larger than 3rem. On a 360px phone, 4vw is 14.4px, so the minimum 28px applies; on a 1000px laptop, 4vw is 40px, which is within range. Using rem for the min and max keeps user font settings working. Bangla text often needs a slightly larger size and line height than English to keep conjunct letters readable, so test with real Bangla content, not just English placeholder text. Touch and interaction: Fingers are less precise than a mouse pointer. Buttons and links on phones should be comfortably large; a common guideline is around 44 to 48 pixels for touch targets, with space between them so users do not tap the wrong one. Hover effects do not exist on touch screens, so never hide essential information behind hover only. The hover media feature lets you add hover-only extras just for mouse users. Container queries: Media queries look at the whole viewport, but a component like a product card may sit in a narrow sidebar on a wide screen. Container queries, supported by current major browsers, let a component react to the width of its own container: mark the parent with container-type: inline-size, then write @container (min-width: 400px) { ... }. The card can then switch from a stacked layout to a side-by-side layout wherever it is placed. Media queries are still the main tool for page-level layout. Testing: Every desktop browser's DevTools has a device mode (a phone and tablet icon) that resizes the viewport to common sizes and simulates touch and device pixel ratio. It is fast, but not perfect, so also test on at least one real low-cost Android phone, since that is what many of your users hold. Throttle the network to a slow 3G or 4G profile in DevTools to feel how the site behaves on a weak connection in a village. CSS frameworks and preprocessors: Bootstrap is a CSS framework with a ready 12-column responsive grid and components such as navbars, cards and modals; you write classes like col-md-6 meaning half width from the medium breakpoint upward. Tailwind CSS is a utility-first framework: you compose small single-purpose classes in the HTML, such as flex, p-4 and md:grid-cols-3, where the md: prefix applies from a minimum width, so it is mobile-first too. Sass is a preprocessor: you write .scss files with nesting, variables and mixins, and a tool compiles them into plain CSS, because browsers only understand CSS. All of these produce ordinary CSS in the end, so the fundamentals you learned still decide whether the result works. Real-life example 1, Bazar on three screens: The base CSS is mobile-first: one column of product cards, a big search box at the top, a sticky bottom bar with the cart total and a 'Checkout' button large enough for a thumb. At 600px, cards become two columns. At 1000px, a grid layout appears with the filter sidebar on the left, products in four columns and the cart moved to the header. Product photos use srcset, so phone users download 400px versions of about 30 KB instead of 300 KB originals. On a slow connection, the page becomes usable much sooner. Real-life example 2, a board exam result page: On result day, lakhs of students check results on phones. A responsive result page keeps the form simple (board, year, roll), uses full-width inputs with type='number' to bring up the numeric keypad, and shows the grade table so that on narrow screens it scrolls sideways inside a wrapper with overflow-x: auto instead of breaking the page. The print stylesheet, @media print, hides the menu and ads so the printed mark sheet is clean. Common mistakes: Forgetting the viewport meta tag. Using fixed widths like width: 1000px on containers. Choosing breakpoints by device names. Hiding important content on mobile with display: none instead of rethinking the layout. Images without max-width that overflow. Disabling zoom. Testing only in desktop DevTools and never on a real phone. Writing desktop-first and then fighting with many max-width overrides. What exams ask: Define responsive web design and its three ingredients. Explain the viewport meta tag and why it is needed. Write media queries for a given set of layouts, and explain mobile-first versus desktop-first. Explain srcset and sizes, and the picture element. Compare px, %, em, rem and vw for responsive work. Recap: Responsive design means one site that adapts to every screen through fluid layouts, flexible images and media queries. The viewport meta tag makes phones use their real width. Mobile-first CSS starts simple and adds with min-width queries, with breakpoints chosen by content. srcset, sizes and picture send the right image to each device, saving data. clamp scales text, touch targets must be big, and container queries let components adapt to their own space. Next we leave styling and start making pages behave, with JavaScript.
key_points: Responsive design: one site and URL whose layout adapts using fluid grids, flexible images and media queries (term coined by Ethan Marcotte, 2010).
The viewport meta tag (width=device-width, initial-scale=1) stops phones from rendering a zoomed-out desktop page; never disable zoom.
CSS pixels differ from physical pixels; the ratio is the device pixel ratio.
Mobile-first: phone layout by default, then min-width media queries add columns as space grows.
Choose breakpoints where the content breaks, not from device lists.
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } plus srcset/sizes and picture send suitable images and save data.
clamp() scales type within limits; make touch targets large and do not hide essentials behind hover.
Test in DevTools device mode and on a real low-cost phone with a throttled network; frameworks like Bootstrap and Tailwind still compile to plain CSS.
lessons.tip: Build every page at 360px wide first. If it works for a thumb on a small screen, widening it is easy; shrinking a desktop design later is always painful.
lessons.task: Make a page with six product cards. Write mobile-first CSS: one column by default, two columns from 600px, three from 900px. Add the viewport meta tag, then remove it and open the page in DevTools device mode to see the difference. Finally, work out which image a 360px phone with device pixel ratio 2 should pick from srcset widths 400w, 800w and 1600w when the image is shown full width.

quiz.q: Who coined the term responsive web design, and when?
quiz.explain: Ethan Marcotte introduced the term in 2010 with fluid grids, flexible images and media queries.

quiz.q: What happens on a phone if the viewport meta tag is missing?
options: The browser renders a wide virtual page (around 980px) and shrinks it, making text tiny
quiz.explain: Without it, mobile browsers assume a desktop design and zoom out to fit.

quiz.q: Mobile-first CSS mainly uses which kind of media query?
quiz.explain: Default styles target small screens, and min-width queries add layout as screens get wider.

quiz.q: What does the w in srcset='photo-800.jpg 800w' tell the browser?
options: The real pixel width of that image file
quiz.explain: The w descriptor gives the image file's intrinsic width; sizes tells the browser the display width.

quiz.q: On a 360px wide viewport, what font size does clamp(1.75rem, 4vw, 3rem) give (root 16px)?
quiz.explain: 4vw = 14.4px, which is below the minimum 1.75rem = 28px, so 28px is used.

lessons.title: JavaScript Basics: Types, Variables and Control Flow
lessons.content:
Think of a shop page as a house. HTML is the bricks and rooms, CSS is the paint and furniture, and JavaScript is the electricity. Without electricity the house still stands and looks nice, but nothing moves: the fan does not spin, the bell does not ring. In our Bazar shop, HTML shows the list of rice, dal and oil, CSS makes it pretty, and JavaScript is what makes the 'Add to cart' button actually add something, update the little cart number and warn you when you type a wrong phone number. This lesson builds JavaScript from zero: where it runs, how to store values, what types exist, and how to make decisions and repeat work.

What JavaScript is: JavaScript (JS) is a programming language created in 1995 by Brendan Eich at Netscape, written in about ten days for the first version. Despite the name it has almost nothing to do with Java; the name was a marketing choice. The language is standardized as ECMAScript by the group Ecma TC39, and new features are added through yearly editions, such as ES2015 (also called ES6), which brought let, const, arrow functions, classes and modules. When people say 'modern JavaScript' they usually mean ES2015 and later.

Where it runs: JS code needs an engine, a program that reads the code and runs it. Chrome and Edge use V8, Firefox uses SpiderMonkey, Safari uses JavaScriptCore. Inside the browser, the engine is joined by browser features such as the DOM (the page as objects), timers and fetch for network calls. Outside the browser, Node.js takes the V8 engine and adds file, network and process features, so the same language can run a web server. That is why JS is the only language that runs natively in every browser and also on servers, which makes full-stack JS possible.

The script tag: You attach JS to a page with the script element. You can write code inside it directly, but the clean way is an external file: script src='app.js'. A plain script in the head blocks the HTML parser: the browser stops building the page, downloads the file, runs it, then continues. Two attributes fix this. defer downloads the file in parallel and runs it after the HTML is fully parsed, keeping the order of deferred scripts. async also downloads in parallel but runs as soon as it arrives, in any order, which suits independent scripts like analytics. For your own app code, defer is usually the right choice. Older tutorials put scripts at the end of the body for the same reason.

The console: Every browser has developer tools (press F12) with a Console tab. Writing console.log('hello') prints a message there. It is your best friend for learning: you can type expressions directly into the console and see the result immediately, for example 2 + 3 gives 5. In Node.js, console.log prints to the terminal.

Variables with let, const and var: A variable is a named box that holds a value. Modern JS gives three keywords. const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned: const shopName = 'Bazar'. let creates a variable you can change later: let cartCount = 0; then cartCount = cartCount + 1. var is the old keyword from before 2015; it is function-scoped rather than block-scoped and has surprising behaviour, so new code avoids it. A good habit: use const by default, and switch to let only when you really need to reassign. Note that const does not freeze an object; const cart = [] still lets you push items into the array, you just cannot point cart at a different array.

Naming rules: Names can contain letters, digits, underscore and dollar sign, but cannot start with a digit, and cannot be reserved words like if or class. JS is case-sensitive, so price and Price are two different variables. The common style is camelCase: totalPrice, isLoggedIn, deliveryCharge.

Primitive types: JS values come in types. There are seven primitive types. number holds both integers and decimals in one 64-bit floating point format, so 7 and 7.5 are both numbers; this is why 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, a classic surprise. It also has special values Infinity and NaN (Not a Number, for example from 'abc' * 2). bigint holds arbitrarily large integers, written with an n at the end like 9007199254740993n. string holds text in single quotes, double quotes or backticks. boolean is true or false. undefined means a variable exists but has no value yet. null means 'intentionally empty', set by the programmer. symbol creates unique identifiers, mostly used in advanced code.

Objects: Everything that is not a primitive is an object: plain objects like { name: 'Miniket rice', price: 75 }, arrays like [10, 20, 30], functions, dates and more. Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared by reference. If you write const a = { qty: 1 }; const b = a; b.qty = 5; then a.qty is also 5, because a and b point at the same object. We go deeper into objects and arrays in the next lesson.

The typeof operator: typeof tells you the type of a value as a string. typeof 42 is 'number', typeof 'dal' is 'string', typeof true is 'boolean', typeof undefined is 'undefined', typeof {} is 'object', and typeof function(){} is 'function'. Two famous oddities: typeof null is 'object', a bug kept from the first version for compatibility, and typeof [] is also 'object'; to test for an array use Array.isArray(value).

null versus undefined: Both mean 'no value', but who decides is different. undefined is what JS gives you automatically: a declared variable without a value, a missing object property, a function that returns nothing. null is what you put there on purpose, for example let selectedProduct = null until the user picks one. In Bazar, if the customer has not chosen a delivery slot, the code might store null to say 'nothing chosen yet', while reading order.coupon when no coupon property exists gives undefined.

Type coercion and == versus ===: JS often converts types automatically, which is called coercion. The + operator with a string joins text: '5' + 2 gives '52', but '5' - 2 gives 3 because minus only works on numbers. This matters for forms: values read from an input box are always strings, so if a user types 2 in the quantity box and you write qty + 1, you get '21', not 3. Convert first with Number(qty) or parseInt(qty, 10). Equality has two forms. Loose equality == converts types before comparing, so 0 == '0' is true, '' == 0 is true and null == undefined is true. Strict equality === compares without conversion, so 0 === '0' is false. Rule: always use === and !==, unless you have a specific reason.

Truthy and falsy: When a value is used in a condition, JS turns it into a boolean. Exactly these values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '' (empty string), null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including '0', 'false', [] and {}. So if (cartItems.length) works because 0 is falsy, but be careful: if (price) treats a valid free item with price 0 as 'no price'. Two helpful operators build on this: a || b returns the first truthy value, and a ?? b (nullish coalescing) returns b only when a is null or undefined, so a discount of 0 survives with discount ?? 10 but not with discount || 10.

Operators: Arithmetic operators are +, -, *, /, % (remainder) and ** (power), so 2 ** 10 is 1024 and 17 % 5 is 2. Comparison operators are <, >, <=, >=, ===, !==. Logical operators are && (and), || (or) and ! (not). Assignment shortcuts include += and ++, so total += 75 adds 75 to total. Optional chaining ?. safely reads deep properties: user?.address?.city gives undefined instead of an error when user or address is missing.

Making decisions with if and switch: An if statement runs code only when a condition is true. Bazar charges delivery like this: if (total >= 1000) { delivery = 0; } else if (insideDhaka) { delivery = 60; } else { delivery = 120; }. The ternary operator is a short form for simple choices: const label = stock > 0 ? 'In stock' : 'Sold out'. switch compares one value against many cases using strict equality: switch (paymentMethod) { case 'bkash': ...; break; case 'nagad': ...; break; default: ... }. Forgetting break makes execution fall through into the next case, a common bug.

Repeating work with loops: A for loop has three parts, start, condition and step: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { console.log(i); } prints 0 to 4. A while loop repeats while a condition holds, useful when you do not know the count in advance. for...of walks over the values of an array or string: for (const item of cart) { total += item.price * item.qty; }. for...in walks over the keys of an object, and is not recommended for arrays. break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next round.

A worked loop: Suppose the cart holds rice 2 kg at 75 taka, dal 1 kg at 140 taka and oil 2 litres at 190 taka. Start total = 0. First round adds 2 x 75 = 150, total 150. Second adds 140, total 290. Third adds 2 x 190 = 380, total 670. Since 670 is under 1000 and the customer is in Dhaka, delivery is 60 and the bill is 730 taka. Tracing a loop on paper like this, writing the variable values after each round, is the single best way to find bugs.

Template literals: Strings written with backticks can span several lines and insert values with dollar-brace: `Total: ${total} taka, delivery ${delivery} taka` builds the message without messy + joins. This is the normal way to build text in modern JS.

Strict mode: Adding 'use strict'; at the top of a file or function turns on a safer version of JS. For example, assigning to an undeclared variable becomes an error instead of silently creating a global variable. ES modules and class bodies are automatically in strict mode, so in modern projects you often get it for free.

Real-life example 1, the Bazar quantity box: A customer in Mirpur types 3 in the quantity field for eggs priced at 12 taka each. The code reads input.value, which is the string '3'. A beginner writes const cost = input.value * 12 and gets 36, which looks right because * converts to number. Then they write const newQty = input.value + 1 to add one more and get '31'. The fix is const qty = Number(input.value), then check Number.isNaN(qty) or qty < 1 to reject bad input before doing any maths.

Real-life example 2, a bKash-style payment label: A payment page shows a status message. With const status = response.status ?? 'pending', a missing status shows 'pending'. A switch then turns 'success', 'failed' and 'pending' into Bangla or English messages, and the default case catches anything unexpected so the user never sees a blank screen. Small, careful handling of types and conditions like this is most of everyday front-end work.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Students mix up == and ===, forget that input values are strings, think const makes objects unchangeable, and confuse null with undefined. Exams ask you to list primitive types, predict the output of expressions like '5' + 2, '5' - 2, typeof null, 0 == '' and [] ? 'yes' : 'no', explain the difference between let, const and var, and explain defer versus async. Practise by predicting first, then checking in the console.

Recap: JavaScript is the behaviour layer of the web, standardized as ECMAScript and run by engines like V8 in browsers and in Node.js. Load it with defer, store values with const and let, know the seven primitives plus objects, prefer === to avoid coercion surprises, remember the eight falsy values, and control flow with if, switch and loops. Next lesson we package logic into functions and work with objects and arrays.
key_points: JavaScript adds behaviour to pages; it is standardized as ECMAScript and runs in engines like V8, in browsers and in Node.js.
Use script with defer for app code; async suits independent scripts; a plain script in the head blocks parsing.
Prefer const, use let when reassigning, avoid var; const does not freeze objects.
Seven primitives: number, bigint, string, boolean, undefined, null, symbol; everything else is an object.
typeof null is 'object' (historic bug); use Array.isArray for arrays.
Use === and !== to avoid coercion; '5' + 2 is '52' but '5' - 2 is 3; input values are strings.
Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, empty string, null, undefined, NaN; ?? only replaces null or undefined.
Control flow: if/else, ternary, switch with break, for, while, for...of for arrays.
lessons.tip: Keep the browser console open while you learn. Before running any expression, say your prediction out loud, then check. The surprises are exactly what exams ask.
lessons.task: Open the browser console (F12) and type: '5' + 2, '5' - 2, 0 == '', 0 === '', typeof null, typeof [], 0.1 + 0.2, null ?? 'x', 0 || 'x', 0 ?? 'x'. Write your prediction for each on paper first, then compare and explain each surprise in one line.

quiz.q: Which keyword should you use by default for a variable that will not be reassigned?
quiz.explain: const is the default choice; use let only when you need to reassign, and avoid var in new code.

quiz.q: What is the result of '5' + 2 in JavaScript?
quiz.explain: With a string operand, + joins text, so the number 2 is converted to '2' and the result is the string '52'.

quiz.q: What does typeof null return?
quiz.explain: It returns 'object', a bug from the first version of JavaScript kept for compatibility.

quiz.q: Which script attribute downloads in parallel and runs the script after the HTML is fully parsed, keeping order?
quiz.explain: defer waits until parsing finishes and keeps the order of deferred scripts; async runs as soon as the file arrives.

quiz.q: Which value is truthy?
quiz.explain: The string '0' is not empty, so it is truthy. 0, empty string and null are all falsy.

lessons.title: Functions, Objects and Arrays in JavaScript
lessons.content:
Think of a pressure cooker in a Bangladeshi kitchen. You put in rice, water and a pinch of salt, close the lid, wait for the whistles, and out comes cooked rice. You do not need to know the physics each time; you just use the cooker again and again. A function is the pressure cooker of programming: you give it inputs, it does a fixed job, and it gives back a result. Objects and arrays are the shelves and containers of the kitchen: objects hold related facts together, arrays hold lists. Almost every line of a real web app uses these three ideas, so this lesson builds them carefully, with the Bazar shop as our running example.

Why functions exist: Without functions you would copy the same lines everywhere. If the delivery rule changes from 60 to 70 taka, you would have to find and fix every copy, and you would miss one. A function gives a block of code a name so you can reuse it, test it alone and change it in one place. It also lets you think at a higher level: calculateTotal(cart) reads like plain English, and a teammate can use it without reading its insides.

Function declarations: The classic form is function add(a, b) { return a + b; }. Here add is the name, a and b are parameters (the input slots), and return sends a value back. Calling add(2, 3) passes arguments 2 and 3 into those slots and the call evaluates to 5. If a function reaches its end without return, it returns undefined. A declaration is hoisted, which means you can call it even above the line where it is written, because the engine sets it up before running the code.

Function expressions and arrow functions: In JS a function is a value, just like a number. So you can store one in a variable: const add = function (a, b) { return a + b; };. Since ES2015 there is a shorter arrow syntax: const add = (a, b) => a + b;. With one expression after the arrow, its value is returned automatically. With a block body you write return yourself: const vat = (price) => { const rate = 0.05; return price * rate; };. Expressions stored in const are not usable before their line. Arrow functions also differ in how they treat this, which we touch on below.

Parameters, defaults and rest: If you call a function with fewer arguments than parameters, the missing ones are undefined. Default values fix this: function deliveryFee(total, area = 'dhaka') { ... }. Calling deliveryFee(500) uses 'dhaka'. A rest parameter collects extra arguments into an array: function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((s, n) => s + n, 0); } so sum(1, 2, 3) gives 6.

Functions as values: Because functions are values, you can pass them to other functions and return them from functions. A function that takes or returns a function is called a higher-order function. You have already seen one: setTimeout(showOffer, 2000) passes the function showOffer to be called later. Passing a function to be called later is called a callback, and it is the base of event handling and asynchronous code in the next two lessons.

Scope: Scope is the region of code where a name is visible. Global scope is the whole program. Function scope is everything inside a function. Block scope is everything inside curly braces such as an if or a for body. let and const are block-scoped; var is only function-scoped. Inner code can see outer names, but outer code cannot see inner ones. Example: function f() { const secret = 1; } then reading secret outside f gives a ReferenceError. When two scopes use the same name, the inner one shadows the outer one.

Hoisting in brief: Before running a scope, the engine registers all declarations in it. Function declarations are fully ready. var variables exist but hold undefined, so reading one early gives undefined, not an error. let and const are registered but cannot be touched before their line; the gap is called the temporal dead zone, and touching them early throws an error. This is one more reason to prefer let and const: mistakes show up loudly.

Closures, worked: A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished. Example: function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return () => { count = count + 1; return count; }; }. Now const next = makeCounter(); then next() gives 1, next() gives 2, next() gives 3. makeCounter finished long ago, but the returned arrow function still holds on to its own count. Calling makeCounter() again creates a fresh, separate count starting from 0. Closures give private state: nobody outside can change count directly. Bazar could use this to generate order numbers in a demo, or to remember a user's last search.

Objects: An object is a collection of key-value pairs, called properties. const product = { id: 7, name: 'Miniket rice', price: 75, unit: 'kg', inStock: true };. Read with dot notation, product.price, or bracket notation, product['price']; brackets are needed when the key is in a variable, product[field]. You can add properties (product.brand = 'Local'), change them, and remove them with delete product.brand. Reading a missing key gives undefined. Object.keys(product) gives an array of keys, and Object.entries gives key-value pairs, handy for looping.

Methods and this: A property whose value is a function is called a method: const cart = { items: [], add(item) { this.items.push(item); } };. Inside a regular method, this refers to the object the method was called on, so cart.add(x) makes this equal to cart. The value of this depends on how the function is called, not where it was written, which confuses many learners. Arrow functions do not have their own this; they use the this of the surrounding code. Rule of thumb: use regular method syntax for object methods, and arrow functions for small callbacks inside them.

Arrays: An array is an ordered list, indexed from 0. const prices = [75, 140, 190];. prices[0] is 75, prices.length is 3, and prices[3] is undefined. push adds at the end, pop removes from the end, unshift and shift work at the front. includes checks membership, indexOf finds a position, and slice copies a part without changing the original, while splice changes the array in place. Arrays can hold objects, which is the normal shape of data from an API: a list of products, each an object.

map, filter, reduce worked: These three methods replace most hand-written loops. Take const cart = [{ name: 'rice', price: 75, qty: 2 }, { name: 'dal', price: 140, qty: 1 }, { name: 'oil', price: 190, qty: 2 }];. map transforms each item and returns a new array of the same length: cart.map(i => i.price * i.qty) gives [150, 140, 380]. filter keeps the items that pass a test: cart.filter(i => i.price > 100) gives the dal and oil objects. reduce folds the array into one value using an accumulator: cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0). Trace it: sum starts at 0, after rice 150, after dal 290, after oil 670. None of the three change the original cart. Others worth knowing: find returns the first match, some and every return booleans, sort sorts in place (pass a compare function for numbers: (a, b) => a - b, otherwise numbers are compared as strings and 10 comes before 9).

Destructuring: Destructuring pulls values out into variables in one line. From objects: const { name, price } = product; creates name and price. From arrays: const [first, second] = prices; gives 75 and 140. It works in parameters too: function showProduct({ name, price }) { ... }, which makes it clear what the function needs.

Spread and copies: The spread syntax ... expands an array or object. [...prices, 60] makes a new array with 60 added. { ...product, price: 80 } makes a new object with the same properties but price 80. This is a shallow copy: nested objects inside are still shared. Making new copies instead of changing the original is called immutability, and front-end frameworks rely on it to notice changes.

Modules: Real apps split code into files. ES modules use export and import. In cart.js: export function calculateTotal(cart) { ... }. In app.js: import { calculateTotal } from './cart.js';. A file can also have one default export. In the browser you load the entry file with script type='module' src='app.js'; module scripts are deferred automatically and run in strict mode, and each module has its own scope, so names do not leak into the global scope. Node.js supports ES modules too, and also has an older system called CommonJS with require and module.exports, which you will still see in many projects.

Classes as syntax: JS has had objects and prototypes from the start; the class keyword (ES2015) is a cleaner way to write them. class Product { constructor(name, price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; } withVat() { return this.price * 1.05; } } then new Product('Sugar', 130).withVat() gives 136.5. Under the hood methods live on a shared prototype object. You already know OOP ideas from your OOP course; in JS, plain objects and functions are used more often than deep class trees.

Real-life example 1, Bazar search: A customer types 'dal' in the search box. The app has an array of 300 product objects. const results = products.filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())); keeps matching items. Then results.map(p => p.name + ' - ' + p.price + ' taka') builds display lines. Two short lines replace a whole page of loops, and each step is easy to test alone.

Real-life example 2, a mess bill in a Dhaka hostel: Six students share a monthly bazar. Store expenses as objects { who: 'Rafi', amount: 1200 }. reduce gives the total spent, say 9,000 taka, so each share is 1,500. A second reduce groups the expenses per person into an object, like { Rafi: 2700, Tania: 900 }. Then a map over Object.entries turns each pair into a line: Rafi paid 2,700, so he gets back 2,700 - 1,500 = 1,200; Tania paid 900, so she owes 600. A final filter keeps only the people who owe money, so the hostel manager gets a short list to collect from. Notice the pattern: data as an array of objects, then a chain of small functions, each doing one clear job. The same functions power real expense-splitting apps.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Forgetting return in a block-bodied arrow function, so the result is undefined. Using map when you want filter. Sorting numbers without a compare function. Expecting const to freeze an object. Losing this when passing a method as a callback. Exams ask you to define closure and trace a counter, compare declarations, expressions and arrow functions, explain scope and hoisting, and write map, filter and reduce for a given array with the output.

Recap: Functions package reusable logic with parameters and return values, and because they are values they can be passed around as callbacks. Scope decides visibility; closures let a function keep private state. Objects group named properties and methods; arrays hold ordered lists and are processed with map, filter and reduce. Destructuring, spread, modules and classes make code shorter and better organised. Next, we use all of this to change the page itself through the DOM.
key_points: A function names reusable logic: parameters in, return value out; with no return it gives undefined.
Declarations are hoisted; function expressions and arrow functions in const are not usable before their line.
let and const are block-scoped, var is function-scoped; inner scopes see outer names, not the reverse.
A closure is a function that remembers variables from where it was created, giving private state like a counter.
Objects hold key-value properties; methods use this, which depends on how the function is called; arrows have no own this.
map transforms, filter selects, reduce combines into one value; none of them change the original array.
Destructuring and spread copy and unpack data; spread makes shallow copies.
ES modules use export/import and script type='module'; classes are cleaner syntax over prototypes.
lessons.tip: Whenever you meet a map, filter or reduce, write a tiny 3-item array on paper and trace it step by step. After five such traces you will read them as fast as a for loop.
lessons.task: Write on paper (or in the console) an array of 5 Bazar products with name, price and qty. Use map to get line totals, filter to keep items over 100 taka, and reduce to get the grand total. Then write makeCounter and call it three times, predicting each output before you run it.

quiz.q: What does const next = makeCounter(); next(); next(); return on the second call, if makeCounter returns a function that increments a private count starting at 0?
quiz.explain: The closure keeps the same count between calls: first call gives 1, second gives 2.

quiz.q: Which array method returns a new array containing only items that pass a test?
quiz.explain: filter keeps items whose callback returns a truthy value; map transforms each item; reduce combines into one value.

quiz.q: What is the scope of a variable declared with let inside an if block?
quiz.explain: let and const are block-scoped, so the variable exists only inside the curly braces of the if.

quiz.q: What does [10, 9, 1].sort() give, with no compare function?
quiz.explain: Without a compare function, sort compares values as strings, so '10' comes before '9'. Use (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

quiz.q: Which statement about arrow functions is correct?
options: They do not have their own this
They are hoisted like function declarations
They must always use the return keyword
quiz.explain: Arrow functions take this from the surrounding code. They are not hoisted when stored in const, and with a single expression they return it automatically.

lessons.title: The DOM and Events: Making Pages React
lessons.content:
Imagine a family tree painted on the wall of your grandparents' house in Barishal. At the top is the great-grandfather, below him his children, below them the grandchildren. If you want to talk about your cousin Mitu, you can say 'the second daughter of the eldest son'. The browser keeps every web page as a tree just like that, and JavaScript can walk the tree, find any member, change them, add new members or remove some. That tree is the DOM, and listening to clicks and key presses on it is called event handling. Together they turn a static page into an app.

What the DOM is: DOM stands for Document Object Model. When the browser receives HTML, the parser reads the tags and builds a tree of objects in memory. Each element becomes an element node, the text inside becomes text nodes, and comments become comment nodes. The root of everything is the document object. JavaScript never edits the HTML file on the server; it edits this live tree in memory, and the browser redraws the screen to match. That is why after a page is modified by JS, View Source still shows the original HTML, while the Elements tab in DevTools shows the current DOM.

A small tree, worked: Take this HTML: body, inside it h1 with text 'Bazar', and a ul with id 'cart' containing two li items 'Rice' and 'Dal'. The tree is: document, then html, then body; body has two element children, h1 and ul; h1 has one text child 'Bazar'; ul has two li children, each with a text child. Note that whitespace and line breaks between tags also become text nodes, which is why childNodes often contains more items than you expect, while children contains element nodes only.

Selecting elements: To change something you first need a reference to it. document.querySelector(selector) returns the first element matching a CSS selector, or null if none matches: document.querySelector('#cart'), document.querySelector('.price'), document.querySelector('nav a'). document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns a static NodeList of all matches, which you can loop with for...of or forEach. Older methods still work: getElementById('cart') and getElementsByClassName('price'); the latter returns a live collection that updates when the DOM changes. Because querySelector accepts any CSS selector you already know from the CSS lessons, it is the usual choice.

Reading and changing text: element.textContent gets or sets the plain text inside an element. document.querySelector('#count').textContent = 3 shows 3 in the cart badge. element.innerHTML gets or sets the HTML markup inside, so the browser parses whatever string you give it and builds new nodes. That is powerful but dangerous with user data.

Why innerHTML with user data is dangerous: Suppose Bazar shows reviews by doing reviewBox.innerHTML = review.text, and an attacker submits a review whose text is an img tag with a broken src and an onerror attribute containing JavaScript. The browser parses it as real HTML, the image fails, and the attacker's script runs in every visitor's browser, maybe sending their session data away. This is cross-site scripting (XSS), covered fully in the web security lesson. The rule: for anything a user typed, use textContent, which treats the string only as text, or create elements with createElement. Use innerHTML only with markup you fully control.

Attributes and properties: getAttribute('href') and setAttribute('href', '/offers') read and write HTML attributes. Many attributes are also available as properties: img.src, a.href, input.value, input.checked, button.disabled. Custom data can live in data-* attributes: a button with data-product-id='7' is read with button.dataset.productId, which gives the string '7'. This is a neat way to connect a button to the product it belongs to.

Classes and styles: element.classList is the clean way to change appearance. classList.add('active'), classList.remove('active'), classList.toggle('open') and classList.contains('open'). You can also set inline styles: element.style.color = 'red' or element.style.display = 'none'; CSS property names become camelCase in JS, so background-color becomes backgroundColor. Best practice: keep looks in the CSS file and only toggle classes from JS, so designers and developers do not fight over the same code.

Creating, inserting and removing elements: const li = document.createElement('li'); li.textContent = 'Oil 2 L'; cartList.append(li); creates a new list item and adds it at the end. prepend adds at the start, before and after insert as siblings, and element.remove() deletes an element. replaceChildren() with no arguments clears all children. Each change can make the browser recalculate layout, so when adding many items, build them first (for example in a DocumentFragment) and insert once.

Walking the tree: From any element you can move to its relatives, just like in the family tree. element.parentElement goes one level up, element.children gives the element children, firstElementChild and lastElementChild give the first and last, and nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling move sideways. element.closest(selector) climbs up through the ancestors, starting with the element itself, until it finds one that matches, and returns null if none does. element.matches(selector) simply answers true or false. Example: when a customer clicks the 'Remove' button inside a cart row, button.closest('li') finds that row so you can call remove() on it. Walking the tree is often cheaper and clearer than running a fresh querySelector over the whole document.

Input versus change, worked: Put both listeners on a quantity box that shows 1. The customer deletes the 1 and types 12. The input event fires three times, once when the box becomes empty and once for each typed digit, so your handler sees '' and then '1' and then '12'. The change event fires only once, with '12', when the customer presses Enter or clicks elsewhere.
