Use input for live feedback, such as updating a price preview, and change when you only care about the final value, such as saving to the cart.

Events: An event is a signal that something happened: a click, a key press, a form submit, the mouse moving, the page finishing loading, an input value changing. The browser creates an event object and delivers it to listeners. Common types are click, input (fires on every change of an input's value), change (fires when the value is committed, for example after leaving the box or picking an option), submit, keydown, mouseover, focus, blur and DOMContentLoaded (the HTML is parsed and the DOM is ready).

addEventListener: The modern way to react is element.addEventListener(type, handler). Example: addButton.addEventListener('click', () => { count++; badge.textContent = count; });. You can attach several listeners to the same event, and remove one later with removeEventListener, passing the same function reference. The old way, writing onclick='...' inside HTML, mixes behaviour into markup and allows only one handler per event on that property, so modern code avoids it.

The event object: The handler receives an event object, usually named e or event. e.type is the event name, e.target is the element where the event started (for example the exact button clicked), e.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running, e.key tells which key was pressed in keydown, and mouse events carry coordinates like clientX and clientY.

preventDefault: Some events have a default browser action: clicking a link navigates, submitting a form reloads the page with a new request, pressing space scrolls. e.preventDefault() cancels that action so your JS can take over. Bazar's checkout form uses form.addEventListener('submit', e => { e.preventDefault(); validate and send with fetch; }); so the page does not reload. Do not confuse it with e.stopPropagation(), which stops the event from travelling further through the tree.

Bubbling and capturing: When you click a button inside a card inside a list, which elements get the event? All of them. The event travels in three phases. Capturing phase: from window down through document, html, body, list, card to the button. Target phase: at the button itself. Bubbling phase: back up from the button to the card, list, body and document. By default addEventListener listens in the bubbling phase; passing { capture: true } listens during capturing. So if both the card and the button have click listeners, a click on the button runs the button's handler first, then the card's. A few events, such as focus and blur, do not bubble.

Event delegation: Because events bubble, you can put one listener on a parent instead of one on each child. Bazar shows 200 products, each with an 'Add' button. Instead of 200 listeners, attach one to the product list: list.addEventListener('click', e => { const btn = e.target.closest('button[data-product-id]'); if (!btn) return; addToCart(btn.dataset.productId); });. closest walks up from the clicked element to find the nearest matching ancestor, which handles clicks on an icon inside the button. Delegation uses less memory and, best of all, works for products added later, because the listener lives on the parent that never changes.

Running code at the right time: If your script runs before the elements exist, querySelector returns null and you get 'Cannot read properties of null'. Fixes: load scripts with defer or as modules, which run after parsing, or wrap startup code in document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init). The load event on window waits further, until images and stylesheets have finished too.

Worked example, a Bazar cart counter: HTML has a span with id 'count' showing 0, and a product list where each product has a button with class 'add' and a data-product-id. JS: let count = 0; const badge = document.querySelector('#count'); document.querySelector('#products').addEventListener('click', e => { const btn = e.target.closest('.add'); if (!btn) return; count++; badge.textContent = count; btn.textContent = 'Added'; btn.disabled = true; });. Trace: the customer clicks 'Add' on rice, the event bubbles to the list, closest finds the button, count becomes 1, the badge shows 1, and the button turns into a disabled 'Added'. Clicking empty space in the list finds no button and the handler simply returns.

Real-life example 1, a live search on a Daraz-style shop: An input event listener on the search box runs on every keystroke, filters the product array as in the last lesson, clears the results list with replaceChildren(), then creates one li per match with textContent. To avoid running a heavy filter on every single key, real sites often debounce: wait until the user stops typing for about 300 milliseconds, using setTimeout, which leads into the next lesson.

Real-life example 2, a show-password button on a bank login page: A small eye icon has a click listener that toggles input.type between 'password' and 'text' and toggles a class on the icon. A keydown listener could also warn when Caps Lock is on by checking e.getModifierState('CapsLock'). These tiny DOM tricks make forms friendlier without any page reload.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Running scripts before the DOM is ready, forgetting that querySelectorAll returns a list rather than one element, using innerHTML with user input, writing addEventListener('click', handler()) with parentheses, which calls the function immediately instead of passing it, and confusing target with currentTarget. Exams ask you to draw the DOM tree for a small HTML snippet, explain bubbling and capturing with the order of handlers, explain event delegation and its benefits, compare textContent and innerHTML, and write a short script that changes text when a button is clicked.

Recap: The DOM is the browser's live object tree of the page. Select nodes with querySelector, change them with textContent, attributes, classList and style, and build or remove nodes with createElement, append and remove. Events are signals delivered to listeners added with addEventListener; the event object tells you what happened, preventDefault cancels default actions, events capture down and bubble up, and delegation uses bubbling to handle many children with one listener. Next we deal with work that takes time, like waiting for the server.
key_points: The DOM is the browser's live tree of nodes built from HTML; JS edits this tree, not the HTML file.
querySelector returns the first match or null; querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList.
textContent treats strings as plain text; innerHTML parses HTML and is an XSS risk with user data.
Use classList to toggle classes, dataset for data-* attributes, and createElement/append/remove to change structure.
addEventListener(type, handler) attaches listeners; the event object gives type, target, currentTarget, key and more.
preventDefault cancels the default action (like form submit reload); stopPropagation stops travel through the tree.
Events capture from window down to the target, then bubble back up; listeners default to the bubbling phase.
Event delegation: one listener on a parent with e.target.closest handles many and future children.
lessons.tip: Open DevTools on any page, select an element in the Elements tab, then type $0 in the Console: it refers to that element. Try $0.textContent = 'Hi' and $0.classList.add('x') to feel the DOM come alive.
lessons.task: Draw on paper the DOM tree for a small HTML page with a header, a ul of three products and a footer. Then, in the console of any page, add a click listener to document.body that logs e.target, click around, and write down which element is reported each time and why.

quiz.q: What does document.querySelector('.price') return when no element matches?
quiz.explain: querySelector returns the first matching element, or null when nothing matches.

quiz.q: Why is element.innerHTML = userComment risky?
options: It only works in old browsers
The browser parses the string as HTML, so injected scripts can run (XSS)
quiz.explain: innerHTML builds real nodes from the string, so attacker markup with event handlers can execute. Use textContent for user data.

quiz.q: A button is inside a card; both have click listeners in the default phase. You click the button. Which runs first?
options: Both at exactly the same time
quiz.explain: Listeners default to the bubbling phase, so the event is handled at the target first, then bubbles up to the card.

quiz.q: What does e.preventDefault() do in a form's submit handler?
options: Cancels the browser's default page reload so JS can handle the submit
quiz.explain: preventDefault cancels the default action; stopping travel through the tree is stopPropagation.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of event delegation?
options: It makes events capture instead of bubble
One parent listener handles many children, including ones added later
quiz.explain: Because events bubble, a single listener on a stable parent can handle clicks on any current or future child.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: Event Loop, Callbacks, Promises and async/await
lessons.content:
Picture a busy tea stall near the Dhaka University campus. There is only one tea maker, Karim bhai. A customer orders a singara, which needs five minutes in the oil. Karim bhai does not stand staring at the pan for five minutes; he drops the singara in, pours three cups of tea for other customers, and when the singara is ready a helper shouts and he serves it. One worker, many jobs, no one stuck waiting. JavaScript in the browser works exactly like Karim bhai. It has one thread, yet it can wait for the network, timers and user clicks without freezing the page. This lesson explains how, and the three styles of writing such code: callbacks, promises and async/await.

Synchronous versus asynchronous: Synchronous code runs line by line; each line finishes before the next begins. That is fine for adding numbers. But some jobs take a long, unknown time: fetching products from a server might take 50 milliseconds on fibre in Dhaka or 3 seconds on a weak mobile signal in a village. If JS simply waited, the whole page would freeze: no scrolling, no clicks, nothing. Asynchronous code starts a slow job, carries on with other work, and handles the result later when it arrives.

One thread: The JS engine runs your code on a single main thread. Only one piece of JS runs at any instant. This keeps things simple, because two functions never change the same variable at the same moment, but it also means a long loop blocks everything. Try while (true) {} in a page's console and the tab stops responding. So the rule of web performance is: never do long work on the main thread; hand slow work to the browser and get called back.

The call stack: The engine tracks which function is running using a call stack. When you call a function, a frame is pushed on top; when it returns, the frame is popped. If main calls total, which calls price, the stack is main, total, price, and it unwinds in reverse. When the stack becomes empty, the current piece of JS has finished. An error message's stack trace is simply a printout of this stack at the moment of the error.

Web APIs do the waiting: Timers, network requests and event listening are not done by the JS engine itself but by the browser's own machinery, often called Web APIs (in Node.js, by its runtime and the libuv library). When you call setTimeout(fn, 2000), JS asks the browser to start a timer and immediately moves on. When the timer ends, the browser does not interrupt running JS; it puts fn in a queue to be run later.

Task queue, microtask queue and the event loop: There are two important queues. The task queue (also called the macrotask or callback queue) holds callbacks from timers, user events and similar sources. The microtask queue holds promise reactions (the functions given to then, catch, finally, and the continuation after await) and queueMicrotask callbacks. The event loop is a simple rule repeated forever: when the call stack is empty, first run all microtasks until the microtask queue is empty, then take one task from the task queue and run it, then check microtasks again, and between tasks the browser may update the screen. Microtasks always go before the next task.

Worked order puzzle: What does this print? console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');. Step by step: A is printed immediately. setTimeout hands its callback to the timer; after 0 milliseconds it goes into the task queue. Promise.resolve().then puts the C callback in the microtask queue. D is printed. Now the stack is empty, so the event loop runs microtasks first: C. Then it takes the task: B. Output: A, D, C, B. The lesson: setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean 'now', it means 'after the current code and all pending microtasks, at the earliest'. The delay is a minimum, not a promise of exact timing.

Callbacks: The oldest async style is passing a function to be called when the job ends. setTimeout(() => showOffer(), 3000) is a callback. In older Node.js code you will see the error-first convention: fs.readFile('menu.txt', (err, data) => { if (err) { handle; return; } use data; });. The first argument is an error or null, the second is the result.

Callback hell: Callbacks become painful when steps depend on each other. Bazar checkout: get the user, then their cart, then check stock, then create the order, then charge payment. With callbacks: getUser(id, (err, user) => { getCart(user, (err, cart) => { checkStock(cart, (err, ok) => { createOrder(cart, (err, order) => { ... }); }); }); });. The code drifts right in a 'pyramid of doom', every level needs its own error check, and it is easy to forget one or to call a callback twice. Promises were introduced into the language in ES2015 to fix this.

Promises: A promise is an object that stands for a value that will be available later, like a token from the singara stall. It is always in one of three states: pending (still working), fulfilled (finished with a value) or rejected (failed with a reason, usually an Error). Once fulfilled or rejected it is settled and never changes again. You create one with new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }), calling resolve(value) on success or reject(error) on failure. Most of the time, though, you use promises returned by APIs such as fetch.

then, catch and finally: promise.then(onFulfilled) registers what to do with the value. promise.catch(onRejected) handles errors. promise.finally(fn) runs either way, good for hiding a loading spinner. Each then returns a new promise, which is what makes chaining possible.

Chaining, worked: The checkout becomes flat: getUser(id).then(user => getCart(user)).then(cart => checkStock(cart)).then(cart => createOrder(cart)).then(order => showReceipt(order)).catch(err => showError(err)).finally(() => hideSpinner());. Rule: whatever a then callback returns becomes the value for the next then; if it returns a promise, the chain waits for that promise. If any step throws or rejects, control jumps straight to the nearest catch, skipping the remaining thens, like an exception. One catch at the end handles errors from every step.

async and await: ES2017 added syntax that lets async code look synchronous. Marking a function async makes it always return a promise. Inside it, await promise pauses that function until the promise settles, then gives the fulfilled value, or throws the rejection reason. The rest of the page keeps running while the function is paused; only this function waits. Checkout again: async function checkout(id) { const user = await getUser(id); const cart = await getCart(user); await checkStock(cart); const order = await createOrder(cart); showReceipt(order); }. It reads top to bottom like a recipe. Normally await is allowed only inside async functions; the one exception is the top level of an ES module, where top-level await is allowed. Under the hood this is still promises: async/await is a nicer way to write the same chain, not a different mechanism.

Errors with try/catch: Because a rejected await throws, you handle it with ordinary try/catch: try { showSpinner(); const order = await createOrder(cart); showReceipt(order); } catch (err) { showError('Order failed, please try again'); } finally { hideSpinner(); }. A common mistake is calling an async function without await or catch; if it fails, you get an 'unhandled promise rejection' warning and the user sees nothing.

Sequential versus parallel, worked: Suppose Bazar's home page needs products (300 ms), offers (200 ms) and the user's cart (100 ms), all independent. Writing const p = await getProducts(); const o = await getOffers(); const c = await getCart(); takes about 300 + 200 + 100 = 600 ms, because each waits for the previous. Start them together instead: const [p, o, c] = await Promise.all([getProducts(), getOffers(), getCart()]); now the total is about the slowest one, 300 ms. Only await one after another when a step truly needs the previous result.

Promise combinators: Promise.all(list) fulfills with an array of all values in the same order, but rejects as soon as any one rejects. Promise.allSettled(list) waits for every promise and gives an array of objects with status 'fulfilled' and value, or status 'rejected' and reason, so one failed widget does not kill the page. Promise.race(list) settles as soon as the first one settles, fulfilled or rejected, useful for timeouts. Promise.any(list) fulfills with the first fulfilled value and rejects only if all reject.

Turning a callback into a promise, worked: Old callback APIs can be wrapped once and then used with await. setTimeout has no promise version in the browser, so write const delay = (ms) => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));. Now await delay(1000) pauses an async function for one second. The pattern is always the same: create a promise, start the callback-style job inside it, call resolve with the result when it succeeds and reject with the error when it fails. Node.js even ships a helper, util.promisify, that does this for error-first callback functions, and most modern Node modules already offer promise versions, such as fs/promises.

Debouncing a search box, worked: The last lesson's live search should not hit the server on every key. A debounce keeps one timer: let timer; input.addEventListener('input', () => { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => search(input.value), 300); });. Trace typing 'dal' quickly: after 'd' a timer is set; 100 ms later 'a' clears it and sets a new one; 'l' does the same; then the user pauses, 300 ms pass with no new key, and search runs once with 'dal'. Three key presses, one request. This uses a closure (timer), the task queue (the timer callback) and the event loop together.

Real-life example 1, a timeout for slow networks: On a slow connection a request may hang. Build a timeout promise: const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Too slow')), 8000)); then await Promise.race([getProducts(), timeout]); shows a friendly 'network is slow, retry?' message after 8 seconds instead of a spinner forever. (The fetch API also supports cancelling with an AbortController, mentioned in the next lesson.)

Real-life example 2, a mobile recharge flow: A recharge page validates the number, calls a payment API, waits for confirmation, then shows the new balance. Each step depends on the previous, so it is a sequence of awaits inside one try/catch. Meanwhile, the loading of promotional banners runs in parallel with Promise.allSettled, so a failed banner never blocks the recharge. Mixing sequential and parallel this way is the everyday skill of async programming.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Believing setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately, forgetting that async functions return promises (so const x = getData() gives a promise, not data), using await inside a forEach and expecting it to wait (use for...of or Promise.all), awaiting independent calls one by one, and missing error handling. Exams ask you to explain the event loop with call stack and queues, predict the output order of a mix of logs, setTimeout and promises, list the three promise states, convert callback code to promises or async/await, and explain Promise.all versus allSettled.

Recap: JS runs on one thread with a call stack; slow work is done by the browser and its result comes back through queues. The event loop runs all microtasks (promise reactions) before the next task (timers, events). Callbacks came first but nest badly; promises represent future values with three states and chain with then and catch; async/await writes the same thing in a readable top-down style with try/catch. Start independent jobs together with Promise.all. Next lesson we use all this with fetch to talk to real servers.
key_points: JavaScript runs on one main thread with a call stack; long synchronous work freezes the page.
Browser Web APIs (timers, network, events) do the waiting and queue callbacks when done.
Event loop: when the stack is empty, run all microtasks (promise reactions) first, then one task (timers, events).
setTimeout(fn, 0) means 'as soon as possible after current code and microtasks', not immediately.
A promise is pending, fulfilled or rejected; then chains values, catch handles any earlier error, finally always runs.
async functions always return promises; await pauses only that function; handle failures with try/catch.
Run independent jobs in parallel with Promise.all; allSettled tolerates failures; race suits timeouts; any wants the first success.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see async code, draw three boxes on paper: call stack, microtask queue, task queue. Move each callback between the boxes by hand. Output-order questions become easy.
lessons.task: In the browser console, run: console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4); Predict the order first. Then write a small async function that awaits two setTimeout-based delays of 1 and 2 seconds, once one after another and once with Promise.all, and measure both with Date.now().

quiz.q: What does console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D'); print?
quiz.explain: Synchronous logs A and D run first; then microtasks (C); then the timer task (B).

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three states of a promise?
quiz.explain: A promise is pending, fulfilled or rejected. Once settled, it never changes.

quiz.q: What does an async function always return?
quiz.explain: An async function always returns a promise, which fulfills with the returned value or rejects with the thrown error.

quiz.q: Three independent requests take 300 ms, 200 ms and 100 ms. About how long does await Promise.all([...]) take?
quiz.explain: They run at the same time, so the total is roughly the slowest one, about 300 ms.

quiz.q: Which combinator waits for all promises and reports each result, even if some fail?
quiz.explain: allSettled gives every outcome with status fulfilled or rejected; Promise.all rejects on the first failure.

lessons.title: JSON, fetch and CORS: Talking to Servers from the Browser
lessons.content:
Think about ordering from a wholesale shop in Chawkbazar over the phone. You and the shopkeeper speak different home dialects, one from Chattogram and one from Sylhet, but you both switch to a plain, shared Bangla so nothing is misunderstood: 'Item: rice, quantity: 50 kg, price: 70 per kg.' Browsers and servers need the same thing: a plain shared format for data, and a polite way to ask for it. The format is JSON, the asking is done with fetch, and the rule about who is allowed to ask whom is the same-origin policy with its exception system, CORS. This lesson connects the front end you have been building to a real back end.

Why data, not pages: In the classic web, every click asked the server for a whole new HTML page. Modern apps often load the page once and afterwards exchange only data: 'give me the products in the Oil category', 'add item 7 to my cart'. The server sends back just the data, and JavaScript updates the DOM. This is faster, uses less mobile data, and lets the same server feed a website, an Android app and an iPhone app.

What JSON is: JSON, JavaScript Object Notation, is a text format for structured data, based on JavaScript object syntax, popularized by Douglas Crockford in the early 2000s and now standardized (ECMA-404 and RFC 8259). Despite the name, every major language reads and writes it: Python, Java, PHP, Dart, Go. A Bazar product looks like this: {"id": 7, "name": "Miniket rice", "price": 75, "inStock": true, "tags": ["rice", "staple"], "discount": null}. Its media type in HTTP is application/json.

JSON syntax rules: JSON is stricter than JavaScript. Keys must be strings in double quotes. Strings must use double quotes, never single quotes. Allowed values are only six kinds: string, number, boolean (true or false), null, object and array. There is no undefined, no functions, no dates, no comments and no trailing commas. Numbers cannot have leading zeros like 007 or be NaN or Infinity. So {name: 'rice',} is valid JavaScript but invalid JSON on three counts: unquoted key, single quotes, trailing comma. Most JSON bugs in exams and in real life are exactly these.

JSON versus XML: Before JSON, the common data format was XML, which wraps every value in named tags, like a product tag containing a name tag with Miniket rice inside and a price tag with 75 inside. XML is powerful: it supports attributes, namespaces, schemas for strict validation, and mixed text, which is why it is still used in documents, configuration files, RSS feeds, SOAP web services and many banking and government systems. But for app data it is longer, because every closing tag repeats the name, and the browser has to walk a document tree to get values out. JSON maps straight onto the objects and arrays programs already use, so the same product in JSON is noticeably shorter and needs just one JSON.parse call. That is why almost every modern web API, from payment gateways to map services, speaks JSON.

JSON.stringify and JSON.parse: To send data, turn a JS value into a JSON string with JSON.stringify(value). To read data, turn a JSON string into a JS value with JSON.parse(text). Example: const text = JSON.stringify({ id: 7, qty: 2 }); gives the string {"id":7,"qty":2}. JSON.parse(text).qty gives 2. A few details: stringify skips object properties whose values are undefined or functions; Date objects become ISO date strings, and parse does not turn them back into Dates automatically; JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) adds indentation for pretty printing. JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid text, so wrap it in try/catch when the text comes from outside. A common trick is saving a cart in the browser with localStorage.setItem('cart', JSON.stringify(cart)) and restoring it with JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('cart')).

AJAX and its history: Requesting data in the background without reloading the page is called AJAX, short for Asynchronous JavaScript and XML, a name coined in 2005, when Gmail and Google Maps made the idea famous. The tool was XMLHttpRequest (XHR), which Microsoft first shipped around 1999 and other browsers later copied. Despite 'XML' in both names, JSON soon replaced XML as the usual data format because it is shorter and maps directly to JS objects. XHR uses events and callbacks and is clumsy to write, so modern code uses fetch, which returns promises. You will still meet XHR in old code, and some libraries such as Axios use it under the hood in browsers.

fetch GET: fetch(url) starts an HTTP request and returns a promise for a Response object. Reading the body is a second asynchronous step, because the body may still be streaming in: response.json() returns a promise for the parsed data; response.text() gives raw text. So: async function loadProducts() { const res = await fetch('/api/products?category=oil'); const products = await res.json(); render(products); }. A relative URL like /api/products goes to the same server that served the page.

fetch does not reject on HTTP errors: This surprises almost everyone. The promise from fetch rejects only when the request could not complete at all: no network, DNS failure, the request was aborted, or the browser blocked it (for example, by CORS). If the server answers 404 or 500, fetch fulfills normally; it got a response, after all. You must check yourself: response.ok is true for status 200 to 299, and response.status holds the number. Pattern: const res = await fetch(url); if (!res.ok) { throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status); } const data = await res.json();.

fetch POST with headers and body: To send data, pass an options object. const res = await fetch('/api/cart', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ productId: 7, qty: 2 }) });. The Content-Type header tells the server the body is JSON so it can parse it. Without JSON.stringify you would send the useless text [object Object]. Other methods work the same way: method: 'PUT' to update, method: 'DELETE' to remove. For an HTML form with a file, pass a FormData object as the body and let the browser set the multipart Content-Type itself.

Loading and error states: A good UI shows three states for every request. Loading: show a spinner or skeleton and disable the button so the user does not click Buy twice. Success: show the data. Error: show a clear message and a Retry button. In code: button.disabled = true; try { ... } catch (err) { showError('Could not load products. Check your connection.'); } finally { button.disabled = false; }. An empty result is a fourth state worth designing: 'No products in this category yet' is better than a blank area. To cancel a request, for example when the user leaves the page or types a new search, pass the signal of an AbortController to fetch and call controller.abort().

A worked request, end to end: The customer opens the Oil category. JS calls fetch('/api/products?category=oil'). The browser sends GET with headers such as Accept. The server queries the database and replies 200 OK with Content-Type: application/json and a body like [{"id":12,"name":"Soybean oil 1L","price":190}]. fetch fulfills with the Response; res.ok is true; res.json() parses the array; JS builds one card per product with createElement and textContent. Total visible time might be 150 milliseconds, with no page reload.

The same-origin policy: Browsers protect users with a rule: a script from one origin may not freely read responses from another origin. An origin is the triple scheme, host and port. https://bazar.com.bd and https://bazar.com.bd/api share an origin. These all differ from it: http://bazar.com.bd (different scheme), https://api.bazar.com.bd (different host), https://bazar.com.bd:8443 (different port). Why? If you are logged in to your bank in one tab, a random site in another tab must not be able to use your cookies to read your bank balance with fetch. The policy blocks reading the response; it does not stop the browser from loading images, styles or scripts from other origins, which are allowed by older rules.

CORS: Real apps often need cross-origin calls: the Bazar front end at https://bazar.com.bd calls an API at https://api.bazar.com.bd. CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, lets the server opt in. The browser adds an Origin header to the request. If the server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://bazar.com.bd (or * for public data), the browser lets the script read the response; otherwise the script gets an error, and the console shows a CORS message, even though the server may have processed the request and the network tab shows a reply.

Preflight requests: For requests that could have side effects beyond what a plain HTML form could already do, the browser first asks permission. Examples are methods like PUT or DELETE, custom headers like Authorization, or Content-Type: application/json. The browser automatically sends an OPTIONS request with headers Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers that include them; only then does the browser send the real request. The server can add Access-Control-Max-Age so the browser caches the permission for a while. To send cookies cross-origin, fetch needs credentials: 'include', and the server must reply Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with an exact origin, not *.

What CORS is not: CORS is enforced by browsers to protect users; it is not server security. A tool like curl or a script on a server ignores CORS completely and can call your API directly. So your API still needs proper authentication and authorization, covered in later lessons. Also, a CORS error is fixed on the server by sending the right headers, not in front-end code. During development, a dev-server proxy that makes the API appear same-origin is a common workaround.

Real-life example 1, a cart that survives a weak connection: A customer in Rajshahi adds items while her mobile data keeps dropping. Bazar saves the cart in localStorage as JSON after every change, sends a POST with fetch, and on failure shows 'Saved on this phone, will sync when online' instead of losing the cart. When the connection returns, it retries. JSON, fetch, error states and storage work together here.

Real-life example 2, a public weather or prayer-time widget: A college website wants today's Dhaka weather or prayer times from a public API on another domain. Because the API sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, a simple fetch GET works directly from the browser. If the API did not send that header, the college would call it from its own server and pass the data on, because server-to-server calls are not subject to CORS.

Common mistakes and what exams ask: Writing JSON with single quotes or trailing commas, forgetting JSON.stringify for the body or the Content-Type header, forgetting that res.json() is itself a promise, assuming fetch rejects on 404, and trying to fix CORS in the front end. Exams ask you to spot errors in a JSON snippet, compare JSON and XML, explain AJAX, write a fetch GET and POST with error checking, define origin and the same-origin policy, and explain CORS and preflight with the headers involved.

Recap: JSON is the shared text format for web data, with strict rules: double quotes, six value types, no comments or trailing commas. JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert between JSON text and JS values. fetch returns a promise for a Response; check res.ok yourself, then read the body with res.json(). Send data with method, headers and a stringified body, and always design loading, success, empty and error states. Browsers allow cross-origin reads only when the server opts in through CORS headers, sometimes after an OPTIONS preflight. Next we move to the server side and build the API that answers these requests.
key_points: JSON is a text data format: double-quoted keys and strings, six value types, no comments, undefined or trailing commas.
JSON.stringify turns JS values into JSON text; JSON.parse turns JSON text into values and throws on invalid input.
AJAX means updating pages with background requests; XMLHttpRequest started it, fetch is the modern promise-based API.
fetch rejects only on network-level failure; check response.ok (200-299) and response.status yourself.
POST with fetch: method, Content-Type: application/json header, and body: JSON.stringify(data).
Design loading, success, empty and error states; AbortController can cancel a request.
Origin = scheme + host + port; the same-origin policy blocks scripts from reading other origins' responses.
CORS lets a server opt in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin; non-simple requests get an OPTIONS preflight; CORS is not server-side security.
lessons.tip: Keep the Network tab open while you write fetch code. Click the request, look at Headers, Payload and Response. Most bugs, including CORS errors, become obvious there in seconds.
lessons.task: Write this on paper and mark every JSON error: {name: 'Rice', 'price': 075, inStock: True, tags: ['a','b',],}. Then rewrite it as valid JSON. If you have a computer, open the console on any site and run JSON.parse on your fixed version to prove it is valid.

quiz.q: Which is valid JSON?
quiz.explain: JSON requires double-quoted keys and strings and forbids trailing commas.

quiz.q: The server answers a fetch with 404 Not Found. What happens to the fetch promise?
options: It rejects with a network error
It fulfills, and response.ok is false
quiz.explain: fetch rejects only on network-level failure; HTTP errors still fulfill, so check response.ok or response.status.

quiz.q: Which pair is the SAME origin?
quiz.explain: Origin is scheme, host and port; paths do not matter. The other pairs differ in scheme, host or port.

quiz.q: What is needed to send a JS object as JSON in a fetch POST?
options: Put the object directly in the URL
body: JSON.stringify(obj) with header Content-Type: application/json
quiz.explain: The body must be a JSON string, and the Content-Type header tells the server how to parse it.

quiz.q: Which statement about CORS is correct?
options: It protects the server from curl and bots
It is fixed by changing front-end code
It stops browsers from loading any image from other sites
The browser enforces it, and the server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin
quiz.explain: CORS is a browser rule to protect users; servers allow cross-origin reads through response headers. Non-browser clients ignore it.

lessons.title: Server-Side Basics: What the Back End Does
lessons.content:
Think of a busy restaurant in Old Dhaka. You sit at a table and see the menu, the plates and the waiter. That is the front end. But the real work happens in the kitchen you never see: the cook checks what is in stock, cooks your kacchi, writes the bill and keeps a record of every order. A website works the same way. The browser shows you the page, but behind it a program on another computer receives your request, checks things, talks to a database and decides what to send back. That hidden kitchen is the back end, or server side, and this lesson is your first walk through it.

What the back end is: The back end is the code that runs on a server, not in the user's browser. In the earlier lessons everything ran in the browser: HTML gave structure, CSS gave style and JavaScript reacted to clicks. But the browser cannot be trusted with everything. A user can open DevTools and change any JavaScript or HTML on their own machine. So anything that must be correct and secure, such as checking a password, calculating the real price, reducing stock or saving an order, must happen on a machine the shop controls. That machine runs the back end.

Why we need it, from first principles: Ask yourself three questions about our running example, the Bazar online grocery. Where does the list of products live so that every customer sees the same list? Who decides that an order of 3 kg rice costs 3 x 75 = 225 taka, so that a clever user cannot change it to 2 taka? Who remembers that Rahim placed an order yesterday? The answer to all three is the server. Shared data, trusted rules and memory over time are the three big jobs of the back end.

Static versus dynamic responses: A static response is a file sent exactly as it is stored, like logo.png or about.html. Any web server can do that with no custom code. A dynamic response is built at the moment of the request. When Rahim opens /orders, the server finds his orders in the database and builds a page or JSON just for him. Most real sites mix both: images, CSS and JavaScript files are static, while product lists, carts and accounts are dynamic.

The request lifecycle on a server: Let us follow one request step by step. First, the browser sends GET /products?category=rice to bazar.com.bd. Second, the server program, which has been waiting and listening on a port such as 443, accepts the connection and reads the HTTP request. Third, it parses the method, path, query string, headers and body into an object your code can read. Fourth, it decides which piece of your code should handle this path; this is called routing. Fifth, your handler runs: it may check who the user is, read from the database and do calculations. Sixth, it builds a response with a status code, headers and a body, such as 200 with a JSON list of rice products. Seventh, the response goes back and the connection is either kept alive for more requests or closed.

Web server versus application server: These words are often mixed up. A web server like Nginx or Apache is very good at the network side: accepting thousands of connections, serving static files fast, handling HTTPS and passing requests along. An application server, or app, is your own program with your business logic, for example a Node.js, Python or PHP program. In many real setups Nginx sits in front, serves the images directly and forwards dynamic requests to the app running behind it. This front role is called a reverse proxy, and we will meet it again in the deployment lesson.

Server-side languages: Almost any general-purpose language can run a back end, because all it needs is the ability to listen on a network port and read and write text. PHP was built for the web and still powers a huge number of sites, including WordPress. Python has Django and Flask. Java has Spring. C# has ASP.NET Core. Go is popular for fast network services. JavaScript runs on the server through Node.js. Routes, handlers, request and response objects and middleware exist in all of them; only the spelling changes.

Node.js and npm: Node.js is a runtime that lets JavaScript run outside the browser. It takes a JavaScript engine (V8, the same engine used in Chrome) and adds things a server needs, such as file system access and networking. Because Node uses an event loop with non-blocking input and output, one Node process can juggle many connections while it waits for the database or disk. npm is the package manager that comes with Node. You write a file called package.json that lists your project's name, scripts and dependencies, then run npm install to download them into a folder called node_modules. Express is one such package, a small, popular framework for building web servers in Node.

A minimal Express-style app: Here is the smallest useful server, written inline. First line: const express = require('express'). Second: const app = express(). Third: app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Bazar is open')). Fourth: app.listen(3000). Run it with node app.js and open http://localhost:3000 in your browser, and you see the text. Line three is the heart: it says when a GET request arrives for the path /, run this function. The function receives req, the request, and res, the response. localhost means your own computer, and 3000 is simply a free port number chosen for development.

Routes: A route is a pair of a method and a path joined to a handler function. app.get('/products', listProducts) handles reading the product list. app.post('/orders', createOrder) handles placing an order. The same path can have different handlers for different methods: GET /orders lists orders, POST /orders creates one. When no route matches, the framework sends 404 Not Found. The next lesson goes deeper into route parameters and how to organise routes; for now, just see a route as the address label on a kitchen counter: rice orders go here, fish orders go there.

The req object: Inside a handler, req tells you everything the client sent. req.method is GET or POST. req.path is the path. req.query holds the query string, so for /products?category=rice, req.query.category is 'rice'. req.headers holds headers like User-Agent or Authorization. req.body holds data sent in the body, for example the JSON of a new order, but only after a body parser has read it, which we will see in a moment. Remember that everything in req came from the outside world and can be faked, so it must be checked.

The res object: res is how you answer. res.status(201) sets the status code. res.set('Content-Type', 'text/html') sets a header. res.send('text') sends a body, and res.json(data) turns a JavaScript object into JSON, sets Content-Type to application/json and sends it. res.redirect('/login') sends a 3xx status with a Location header. A handler must finish by sending exactly one response; if it never responds, the browser waits until it times out, and if it tries to respond twice, Express reports an error because the headers were already sent.

Middleware: Middleware is a function that runs between receiving the request and the final handler, like checkpoints on the way to the kitchen. Each middleware gets req, res and a function called next. It can read or change req, end the request early by sending a response, or call next() to pass control to the next function in the chain. Example: a logger middleware prints the method, path and time, then calls next(). An auth middleware checks for a valid login; if there is none it sends 401, otherwise it calls next(). They run in the order you add them with app.use, so order matters: the logger should come first, and the auth check must come before the routes it protects.

Body parsing: The body of a POST arrives as raw bytes in a stream. The server must read it and convert it into something useful. For a JSON body, Express provides app.use(express.json()), a middleware that reads the body, parses the JSON and puts the result in req.body. For a classic HTML form with the default encoding, express.urlencoded() does the same for name=value pairs. File uploads with multipart/form-data need an extra package. If you forget the parser, req.body will be empty and your order handler will see nothing, a very common beginner bug.

Serving static files: A shop has many files that never change per user: CSS, front-end JavaScript, product images. Instead of writing a route for each, you point the framework at a folder: app.use(express.static('public')). Now a request for /css/style.css returns the file public/css/style.css. In production, Nginx or a CDN often serves these files instead.

Environment variables and configuration: Your app needs settings that differ between your laptop and the real server: the database address, the port, secret keys, the bKash or payment sandbox keys. These must never be written inside the code, because code goes to Git and can be seen by others. Instead they are kept in environment variables, values the operating system gives to the program when it starts. In Node you read them with process.env.PORT or process.env.DB_URL. During development many people keep them in a .env file that is listed in .gitignore so it never gets committed.

Logging: When something goes wrong on a server at 2 am, you cannot open DevTools on it. Logs are your eyes. A good back end writes a line for each request (time, method, path, status, how many milliseconds it took) and a detailed line for each error, including the stack trace. Example log line: 2025-03-14 21:05:12 GET /products 200 35ms. Never log passwords, card numbers or secret tokens.

Error handling: Things will fail: the database may be down, the input may be wrong, your code may have a bug. A back end must never crash on one bad request and take the whole shop offline. In Express you add a special error-handling middleware with four parameters, (err, req, res, next), placed after all routes. When a handler throws or passes an error to next(err), this middleware logs it and sends a clean response such as 500 with a short message like 'Something went wrong'. Do not send the raw error or stack trace to the user, because it can reveal file paths, library versions or SQL to an attacker. Wrong input from the client should get a 4xx, such as 400 Bad Request, not 500.

Real-life example 1, Bazar order flow: Nusrat in Mirpur adds 2 kg potatoes and 1 litre oil to her cart and taps Place order. The browser sends POST /orders with a JSON body. On the server, the logger middleware writes the request line. express.json() parses the body. The auth middleware confirms she is logged in. The createOrder handler checks each item exists, looks up the real prices from the database (2 x 40 = 80 taka plus 190 taka = 270 taka) instead of trusting any price from the browser, saves the order and replies 201 Created with the order number. If the database is down, the error middleware logs it and returns 500, and Nusrat sees a polite retry message instead of a frozen screen.

Real-life example 2, a public exam result site: On result day, hundreds of thousands of students in Bangladesh check their results at once. The result pages are dynamic, because each roll number gives a different answer, but the CSS, logo and scripts are static. A sensible setup serves static files from Nginx or a CDN, keeps the app code small and fast, caches results that do not change, and logs response times so the team can see slowness before the site falls over. When the server is overloaded you see 503 Service Unavailable, which is the back end saying it cannot take more work right now.

Common mistakes: Trusting data from the browser, such as prices or user ids sent in the body. Forgetting the body parser and then wondering why req.body is empty. Putting middleware in the wrong order, so a protected route runs before the auth check. Hardcoding passwords and API keys in code. Sending a stack trace to users. Writing a handler that forgets to send a response in one branch, so the request hangs. And blocking the Node event loop with a long CPU-heavy loop, which freezes every other user, not just one.

What exams ask: Client side versus server side, static versus dynamic pages, the server request lifecycle, middleware and why its order matters, web server versus application server, and a tiny route that returns JSON.

Recap: The back end is the trusted kitchen of a web app. It listens on a port, turns raw HTTP into req, routes it to a handler, runs middleware like logging, parsing and auth along the way, talks to the database, and answers with res: a status, headers and a body. Static files come straight from disk; dynamic responses are built per request. Settings live in environment variables, problems are recorded in logs, and one error handler turns crashes into clean 500 responses. Next we will organise routes properly and meet MVC.
key_points: The back end runs on a server the site controls; it holds shared data, trusted rules and memory over time.
Static responses send stored files as they are; dynamic responses are built per request, often from a database.
Request lifecycle: listen, accept, parse, route, run handler (and middleware), build response, send.
A web server like Nginx handles connections, HTTPS and static files; the application server runs your business logic.
In an Express-style app a route joins a method and path to a handler that receives req and res.
Middleware runs in order and either responds or calls next(); body parsers, loggers and auth checks are middleware.
Secrets and settings go in environment variables, never in code committed to Git.
A final error handler logs the error and sends a clean 500 without leaking stack traces.
lessons.tip: Whatever language your class uses, draw the same picture: request comes in, middleware chain, route handler, database, response out. If you can draw that box diagram from memory, you understand every back-end framework.
lessons.task: On paper, design the routes for a tiny Bazar back end: list products, show one product, place an order, list my orders. For each write the method, path, which middleware should run first (logger, body parser, auth) and the status code of a successful reply.

quiz.q: Why must the final price of an order be calculated on the server?
options: Because anything coming from the browser can be changed by the user
Because servers are always faster than phones
quiz.explain: The user controls their own browser and can edit requests, so trusted rules like prices must run on the server.

quiz.q: What does a middleware function do when it wants the request to continue?
quiz.explain: Middleware either sends a response itself or calls next() to pass control to the next function in the chain.

quiz.q: In an Express-style app, req.body is empty for a JSON POST. The most likely cause is:
options: No body-parsing middleware such as express.json() was added
quiz.explain: The body arrives as raw bytes; a parser middleware must read it and fill req.body.

quiz.q: Which job is a web server like Nginx typically better at than your application code?
options: Serving static files and handling many connections and HTTPS
Deciding which products a user may buy
quiz.explain: Nginx is optimised for the network side; business logic belongs in the application.

quiz.q: Where should a database password for the production server be kept?
options: In a comment at the top of app.js
In an environment variable read by the app at start-up
quiz.explain: Environment variables keep secrets out of the code and out of version control.

lessons.title: Routing, MVC and Templates: Organising a Web App
lessons.content:
Imagine a big government office in Dhaka where every visitor walks straight into one room and shouts their request. Passport, land records, tax, all in one room, handled by one tired clerk. It would be chaos. A good office has a reception desk that reads your token and sends you to the right counter, each counter has its own files, and the forms you receive are printed from a standard template. A well-built web app is organised the same way: routing is the reception desk, MVC splits the work into clear counters, and templates print the pages. In the last lesson we built a tiny server. Now we learn how to keep it tidy when it grows to hundreds of routes. Why organisation matters: A first project often lives in one file of 2,000 lines where SQL, HTML and business rules are mixed together. It works until a second person joins, or until you need to change the price rule and find it copied in seven places. The cost of software is mostly the cost of changing it later. So web frameworks give us patterns that tell every file what its job is. Once you know the pattern, you can open any project built on it and guess where things live. Routing recap: A route maps a method plus a path to a handler. GET /products shows the list, POST /orders creates an order. The router is the part of the framework that looks at each incoming request and picks the matching route. If nothing matches, it falls through to a 404 handler. So far our paths were fixed text. Real apps also need paths that carry data. Route parameters: Suppose Bazar has 500 products. You do not write 500 routes. You write one: app.get('/products/:id', showProduct). The colon marks a parameter. A request for /products/42 matches, and inside the handler req.params.id is '42'. Note it is a string, so you convert it to a number before using it and check that it really is one. A route can have several parameters, for example /shops/:shopId/products/:productId. Parameters identify which thing you want, and they make clean, readable URLs that people can bookmark and share. Query strings: The part after the question mark carries optional settings, not identity. /products?category=fish&sort=price&page=2 still means the products collection, just filtered, sorted and on page 2. In the handler these appear as req.query.category, req.query.sort and req.query.page, again as strings. A simple rule of thumb: if removing it would point to a different resource, use a path parameter; if it only changes how the same resource is shown, use a query string. So /products/42 for one product, but /products?category=fish for a filtered list. Route order: Most routers check routes in the order they were added and take the first match. That creates a classic bug. If you add /products/:id before /products/new, then a request for /products/new matches the first route with id equal to 'new', and your handler tries to find a product called new. The fix is to put specific fixed routes before general parameter routes. The same rule applies to the 404 handler: it must come last, after every real route, or it will swallow everything. Grouping routes: As the app grows you split routes by area. All product routes go in one file, order routes in another, user routes in a third. Express calls such a group a router: you create one with express.Router(), add routes to it, and mount it with app.use('/products', productRouter). Now inside that file, router.get('/:id') means /products/:id. Grouping also lets you attach middleware to a whole area, for example an admin check on every route under /admin. What MVC is: MVC stands for Model, View, Controller. It is a way of splitting an application into three kinds of code with separate jobs. The pattern is older than the web; it came from desktop user interfaces in the late 1970s, and web frameworks adapted it. The idea is simple: data and rules in one place, presentation in another, and a coordinator in between. The Model: The model represents the data and the rules about it. For Bazar, a Product model knows that a product has a name, a price in taka and a stock count, that price can never be negative, and how to load and save products in the database. An Order model knows how to calculate a total and that an order cannot contain zero items. The model does not know anything about HTML or HTTP. You could use the same model from a web page, a mobile API or a script that runs at night. The View: The view decides how data is shown. On a server-rendered site the view is usually an HTML template; in an API it might simply be the JSON format of the response. The view should contain as little logic as possible: show the product name, loop over the items, format the price. It should never run SQL or decide whether a user may buy something. The Controller: The controller is the coordinator. It receives the request from the router, reads the inputs (params, query, body), asks the models to do the work, picks a view and sends the response. A good controller is thin: it glues things together but does not hold business rules itself. If you find price calculations inside a controller, they probably belong in the model. Tracing one request through MVC: Rahim opens /products/42. Step 1: the router matches GET /products/:id and calls ProductController.show. Step 2: the controller reads req.params.id, converts it to the number 42 and asks the Product model for product 42. Step 3: the model runs a database query and returns an object: name 'Miniket rice 5 kg', price 380, stock 12. Step 4: if the model returns nothing, the controller sends 404. Step 5: otherwise the controller passes the product to the view product.html. Step 6: the view fills in the template and produces HTML. Step 7: the controller sends it with status 200. Each step has exactly one owner, so when the price shows wrongly you know to look in the model or the view, not everywhere. Server-side rendering with templates: A template is an HTML file with holes in it. A template engine fills the holes with data and produces a final HTML page on the server. In a generic syntax, the template might say:

{{ product.name }}

Price: {{ product.price }} taka

, and then a loop, for each review in reviews, print the review text. Different engines spell it differently, for example EJS, Handlebars and Pug in Node, Blade in Laravel, Jinja in Flask, Django templates, Thymeleaf in Spring, Razor in ASP.NET, but they all do the same job. Because the page arrives as finished HTML, it shows quickly and search engines can read it easily. Escaping in templates: When a template prints data, most engines escape it by default, turning characters like < and > into safe entities so that a product review containing script tags is shown as text, not run as code. Most engines also offer a raw or unescaped print for trusted HTML. Use that only for content you fully control. This is your first line of defence against cross-site scripting, which the security lesson covers in depth. Layouts and partials: Every page of Bazar has the same header with the logo and cart icon and the same footer with the address and hotline. Copying them into 40 templates means 40 edits when the hotline changes. A layout is a master template with a slot where each page's own content goes. A partial is a small reusable piece, such as a product card, included wherever it is needed. This is the DRY principle, do not repeat yourself, applied to HTML. Separation of concerns: This is the deeper idea behind all of the above. Each part of the program should handle one concern and know as little as possible about the others. Routes know URLs, controllers know the flow, models know data and rules, views know presentation. The benefit is that changes stay local. Redesign the product page and you touch only the view. Move from MySQL to PostgreSQL and mostly the model layer changes. Add a mobile app and you write new JSON views while the models stay the same. Full-stack frameworks: Express is minimal; it gives you routing and middleware and leaves the rest to you. Bigger frameworks give you a complete structure out of the box: a router, a controller system, an ORM for models, a template engine, form validation and security helpers. Laravel (PHP), Django (Python), Ruby on Rails (Ruby), Spring (Java) and ASP.NET Core (C#) are well-known examples. Django describes its own structure as MTV, model, template, view, where its view plays roughly the role of a controller; the idea is the same, only the names shift. Rails made popular the motto convention over configuration: if you follow the standard folder and naming rules, the framework wires things up without extra setup. Real-life example 1, a university notice board: Your department site has routes like /notices, /notices/:id and /teachers/:slug. A Notice model knows a notice has a title, date and PDF link, and that notices are listed newest first. The controller for /notices reads ?page=2 from the query string and asks the model for 10 notices. The view template loops over them using a shared layout with the university logo. When the department wants a new design, only templates change; the notice data is untouched. Real-life example 2, a cricket score site: During a Bangladesh match, /matches/:id shows the live scorecard. The model pulls the latest balls from the database and calculates the run rate, for example 156 runs in 24 overs gives 6.5 runs per over. The same model feeds two views: an HTML page for the website and a JSON response at /api/matches/:id for the mobile app. That reuse only works because the run rate rule lives in the model, not in either view. Common mistakes: Putting a general parameter route before a specific one. Forgetting that route parameters and query values are strings. Writing SQL inside templates, or HTML strings inside models. Fat controllers that contain every business rule. Using unescaped output for user content. And using query strings for identity, like /product?id=42 everywhere, which works but makes URLs less clean than /products/42. What exams ask: Explain MVC with a diagram and trace a request through it. Distinguish route parameters from query strings with examples. Explain why route order matters. Explain what a template engine does and what layouts and partials are. Define separation of concerns and give its benefits. Recap: The router is the reception desk that matches method and path, using parameters for identity and query strings for options, checked in order. MVC splits the app into models for data and rules, views for presentation and thin controllers to coordinate. Templates render HTML on the server, escape data by default, and share layouts and partials. All of it serves one goal, separation of concerns, so the app stays easy to change as it grows. Next we design the URLs of a clean REST API.
key_points: Route parameters like /products/:id identify a resource; query strings like ?sort=price only change how it is shown.
Params and query values arrive as strings and must be converted and checked.
Routers usually take the first match, so specific routes go before parameter routes and the 404 handler goes last.
MVC: the Model holds data and rules, the View presents, the Controller coordinates the request.
Keep controllers thin and put business rules in models.
Template engines fill HTML templates with data on the server and escape output by default.
Layouts and partials apply DRY to HTML.
Separation of concerns keeps changes local; full-stack frameworks like Laravel, Django, Rails, Spring and ASP.NET Core build on it.
lessons.tip: Take any feature you know, such as viewing one order, and say out loud: router, controller, model, view, response. If you can name what each step does for that feature, you have truly understood MVC, not just memorised the letters.
lessons.task: Write the route list for a small library website: list books, show one book, search books by author, borrow a book, list my loans. Mark which data goes in route parameters and which in query strings, and say which model, controller action and view each route uses.

quiz.q: For a URL like /products/42, inside the handler req.params.id is:
quiz.explain: Route parameters arrive as strings and must be converted before numeric use.

quiz.q: Routes /products/:id and /products/new are added in that order. What happens to GET /products/new?
options: It always shows the new-product form
It matches /products/:id with id equal to 'new'
quiz.explain: The router takes the first match, so specific routes must be added before parameter routes.

quiz.q: In MVC, where should the rule 'price can never be negative' live?
quiz.explain: The model owns data and its rules; views only present and controllers only coordinate.

quiz.q: Which URL best fits a filtered list of fish products sorted by price?
quiz.explain: It is still the products collection; filtering and sorting are options, so they go in the query string.

quiz.q: What is a partial in a template system?
options: A database table split into two
A small reusable template piece, such as a product card, included in many pages
quiz.explain: Partials and layouts let you write shared HTML once and reuse it.

lessons.title: REST API Design: Clean URLs, Methods and Status Codes
lessons.content:
Think of the post office. Every house in Bangladesh has an address, and there are only a few kinds of things you can do with the post: send a letter, collect a letter, return one. Because the rules are shared by everyone, a postman from Sylhet can deliver in Khulna without special training. A REST API brings the same idea to software. Every piece of data gets an address, a URL, and you use the same small set of HTTP methods to act on it. Because everyone follows the same rules, a mobile app, a website and a partner's system can all talk to the Bazar server without long meetings about how.

What an API is: API stands for Application Programming Interface. It is a contract that says how one program can ask another program to do something. A web API is an API that works over HTTP: the client sends an HTTP request, the server replies, usually with JSON instead of an HTML page. When the Bazar mobile app shows products, it is not loading a web page; it calls something like GET /api/products and draws the JSON it gets back in its own screens.

What REST is: REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It was described by Roy Fielding in his PhD dissertation in 2000 as an architectural style, a set of constraints, not a library or a protocol. The main constraints are: client and server are separate; each request is stateless and carries everything needed to understand it; responses say whether they can be cached; there is a uniform interface for working with resources; and the system can be layered, with proxies and caches in between. An API that follows these rules reasonably well is called RESTful. In daily practice, when people say REST API, they mostly mean resources named by URLs, standard HTTP methods, standard status codes and JSON bodies.

Resources and representations: A resource is any thing your API exposes: a product, an order, a customer, a review. The server stores it in its own way, maybe as rows in three database tables. What the client receives is a representation of it, for example this JSON: { 'id': 42, 'name': 'Hilsa 1 kg', 'price': 1200, 'stock': 8 } (real JSON uses double quotes; we show single quotes here only for readability). The client changes the resource by sending a representation back. That is where the name comes from: state is transferred through representations.

Nouns, not verbs: In REST the URL names the thing, and the HTTP method says the action. So instead of /getProducts, /createOrder and /deleteReview/7, you write /products, /orders and /reviews/7, and let GET, POST and DELETE carry the verb. Use plural nouns for collections, lowercase letters and hyphens for multi-word names, like /delivery-slots. This keeps the API small and predictable: once a developer learns the pattern for products, they can guess the pattern for orders.

Collections and items: A collection URL like /products stands for the whole set. An item URL like /products/42 stands for one member. Relationships can be shown by nesting one level: /orders/1001/items lists the items inside order 1001, and /customers/7/orders lists the orders of customer 7. Do not nest too deep; /customers/7/orders/1001/items/3/reviews is hard to read and hard to maintain. If an item has its own id, it can usually be reached directly too, like /orders/1001.

Methods mapped to CRUD: CRUD means Create, Read, Update, Delete, the four basic things you do with data. In REST: GET /products reads the list; GET /products/42 reads one; POST /products creates a new product in the collection, and the server chooses its id; PUT /products/42 replaces product 42 with the full representation you send; PATCH /products/42 changes only the fields you send, for example just the price; DELETE /products/42 removes it. With six method and URL pairs you have a complete product API.

Safe and idempotent methods: A method is safe if it does not change anything on the server: GET and HEAD are safe, so browsers, crawlers and caches can call them freely. A method is idempotent if doing it once or many times leaves the server in the same state. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: setting the price of product 42 to 1,150 three times still leaves it at 1,150, and deleting an already deleted product does not delete anything more. POST is not idempotent: sending POST /orders three times may create three orders. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent. This matters on a weak mobile connection in a village: if a PUT times out, the app can safely retry, but a retried POST could charge a customer twice.

Idempotency keys: Because orders and payments must be created with POST, many payment APIs let the client send a unique key in a header, often called Idempotency-Key. The server remembers the key and, if the same key arrives again, returns the first result instead of creating a second order. This is a widely used design pattern, not part of HTTP itself.

Status codes for APIs: A good API uses status codes precisely, because client code decides what to do based on them. 200 OK for a successful GET, PUT or PATCH that returns a body. 201 Created after POST creates something, usually with a Location header pointing to the new item, like /orders/1001. 204 No Content for success with no body, common after DELETE. 400 Bad Request when the request itself is malformed, such as broken JSON. 401 Unauthorized when the client is not authenticated, meaning it did not prove who it is; despite the name, it is about authentication. 403 Forbidden when the client is known but not allowed. 404 Not Found when the resource does not exist. 409 Conflict when the request clashes with the current state, for example registering an email that already exists. 422 Unprocessable Content (older documents say Unprocessable Entity) when the JSON is well-formed but the values fail validation, such as a quantity of -2; some APIs simply use 400 here. 500 Internal Server Error when the server failed.

Worked example: Let us design three calls for Bazar. Placing an order: POST /api/orders with body { items: [ { productId: 42, qty: 2 } ] } returns 201 Created, Location: /api/orders/1001, and the new order JSON with total 2,400 taka. Asking for an order that does not exist: GET /api/orders/99999 returns 404 with an error body. Cancelling an order you own: DELETE /api/orders/1001 returns 204 No Content. Trying to cancel someone else's order returns 403. Each answer tells the app exactly what happened without parsing any text.

Consistent JSON errors: A bare 400 is not enough; the developer needs to know what was wrong. Pick one error shape and use it everywhere, for example { error: { code: 'OUT_OF_STOCK', message: 'Only 3 left of Hilsa 1 kg', field: 'items[0].qty' } }. The code is for programs, the message is for humans. There is also an IETF standard for this, problem details for HTTP APIs, which uses the media type application/problem+json. Whatever you choose, never put stack traces or SQL in error bodies.

Statelessness in practice: Each request must carry everything the server needs: who the user is, usually as a token in the Authorization header, and all parameters. The server does not remember that the previous request was page 1, so the client asks for page 2 explicitly. This is what lets you run five copies of the API behind a load balancer: any copy can answer any request. The sessions and tokens lesson explains how identity travels with each request.

Filtering, sorting and pagination: A collection of 50,000 products cannot be sent in one response. Use query parameters: GET /products?category=fish&min_price=500&sort=-price returns fish over 500 taka, highest price first (a leading minus for descending is a common convention). For paging, the simple style is offset based: ?page=3&limit=20 skips 40 items and returns the next 20. It is easy to understand but can skip or repeat items if new rows are added while the user scrolls, and very large offsets get slow. The cursor style returns a marker with each page, like next_cursor, and the client sends ?cursor=abc to get the next page; it stays stable and fast on big, changing lists such as a news feed. Either way, return some paging information, such as the total count or the next link.

Versioning: Once a mobile app is installed on thousands of phones, you cannot force everyone to update the same day. If you rename a field from price to unit_price, old apps break. So breaking changes go into a new version. The most common style puts the version in the path: /api/v1/products and /api/v2/products. Others use a header. Adding a new optional field is usually not breaking, so you can do that without a new version; removing or renaming one is breaking.

Documenting with OpenAPI: An API is only as good as its documentation. The OpenAPI Specification, formerly known as Swagger, is a standard way to describe an API in a YAML or JSON file: every path, method, parameter, request body, response and status code. Tools can then generate interactive documentation pages where you can try calls, client code in many languages, and tests. Many teams write the OpenAPI file first and build the code to match it.

GraphQL in one paragraph: GraphQL, created at Facebook and released publicly in 2015, is an alternative style. There is usually a single endpoint, and the client sends a query that lists exactly the fields it wants, even across related objects, such as an order with its items and each item's product name, in one round trip. This avoids getting too much data (over-fetching) or making many calls (under-fetching). The cost is more complexity on the server, and HTTP caching is harder because most queries are POSTs to one URL. REST remains the most common choice for public and simple APIs.

Real-life example 1, a ride-sharing app in Dhaka: The rider app calls POST /rides with pickup and drop-off points and receives 201 with the ride id. It then polls or listens for GET /rides/555 to see status change from searching to accepted to on_trip. Cancelling is DELETE /rides/555 or PATCH /rides/555 with status cancelled, depending on whether the company keeps cancelled rides as records, which most do, so PATCH fits better. A 409 comes back if the rider tries to cancel a trip that has already ended.

Real-life example 2, mobile recharge from a shop app: The app sends POST /recharges with phone number, operator and amount 50 taka, plus an Idempotency-Key. The network is weak and the request times out, so the app retries with the same key. The server sees the key, finds the first recharge already succeeded, and returns that same result. The customer is charged once, not twice.

Common mistakes: Verbs in URLs. Using GET to change data, which crawlers and prefetching can trigger by accident. Returning 200 for every response with an error message inside. Mixing up 401 and 403. Breaking old clients by renaming fields without a new version. Returning whole tables with no pagination. Inconsistent naming, like /Products in one place and /product_list in another.

What exams ask: Define REST and its constraints. Design endpoints for a given system with methods and status codes. Explain safe versus idempotent methods with examples. Compare PUT and PATCH, 401 and 403, offset and cursor pagination, and REST and GraphQL.

Recap: A REST API names resources with noun URLs, uses HTTP methods as verbs, returns precise status codes and consistent JSON, and keeps each request stateless. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, so retries need care. Collections need filtering, sorting and pagination, breaking changes need a new version, and an OpenAPI document tells everyone the rules. Next we connect these endpoints to a real database.
key_points: REST is an architectural style (Fielding, 2000): stateless client-server, cacheable responses, uniform interface, layered system.
URLs name resources with plural nouns; HTTP methods carry the action.
CRUD mapping: POST creates, GET reads, PUT replaces, PATCH partly updates, DELETE removes.
GET and HEAD are safe; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, so idempotency keys protect payments.
Key codes: 200, 201 with Location, 204, 400, 401 (not authenticated), 403 (not allowed), 404, 409, 422, 500.
Use one consistent JSON error shape with a machine code and a human message.
Collections need filtering, sorting and pagination (offset or cursor); breaking changes go in a new version like /v2.
OpenAPI documents an API; GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint.
lessons.tip: Before writing any API code, write the endpoint table on paper: method, URL, request body, success code, error codes. Ten minutes of this saves days of renaming later, because changing a public API is far harder than changing private code.
lessons.task: Design a REST API for a hall canteen token system: menu items, tokens bought by students, and cancelling a token. For each endpoint write the method, URL, an example JSON body, the success status code and at least one error status code with its reason.

quiz.q: Which URL follows REST naming best for deleting review 7?
quiz.explain: The URL names the resource with a noun, and the DELETE method carries the action.
