Some designers remove it with outline: none because it looks 'ugly'; that makes the site unusable by keyboard. If you restyle it, use :focus-visible to show a strong custom focus ring. Focus order should follow the visual order, which happens naturally if the HTML source order matches the layout. When a modal dialog opens, move focus into it, keep focus inside while it is open, and return focus to the button that opened it when it closes. Semantic HTML first: The single most effective accessibility technique is using the right HTML element. A button element is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced as 'button'. A nav is announced as navigation. A table with th headers lets the screen reader say which column a cell belongs to. A list with ul and li tells the user how many items there are. Every div you use instead of the proper element is work you must redo by hand, and you will probably miss something. ARIA: WAI-ARIA, Accessible Rich Internet Applications, is a set of HTML attributes that add accessibility information when HTML alone cannot express it. role tells what something is, such as role='dialog' or role='tablist'. Properties and states describe it: aria-label gives a name to an icon-only button, like a cart icon:
key_points: Accessibility (a11y) lets people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive disabilities, and everyone in temporary limits, use the web.
WCAG from the W3C has levels A, AA (usual target) and AAA, built on POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
Give meaningful alt text; use alt='' for decorative images; never leave alt missing.
Use logical headings, landmarks, a skip link, lang on html, and a label for every input.
AA contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text; never use colour alone to carry meaning.
Everything must work with a keyboard, with a visible focus indicator; use real buttons and links, not clickable divs.
First rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML; use role, aria-label, aria-expanded and aria-live only where HTML cannot express it.
Test with keyboard only, Lighthouse or axe, and a screen reader such as NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack.
lessons.tip: Spend five minutes navigating your own project with only the Tab key and your eyes closed for the last minute. You will find more accessibility bugs this way than by reading any checklist.
lessons.task: Pick any website you use often. Using only the keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space), try to reach the search box, search for something and open a result. Write down every place where you got stuck or could not see where focus was. Then run Lighthouse's accessibility audit and compare its findings with yours.

quiz.q: Which WCAG level is the usual target in laws and company policies?
quiz.explain: AA is the common target; A is the minimum and AAA is the highest, not required for whole sites.

quiz.q: What is the correct alt text for a purely decorative background swirl image?
quiz.explain: An empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image; leaving it out may make them read the file name.

quiz.q: What minimum contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal-size text?
quiz.explain: AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; 21:1 is black on white, the maximum.

quiz.q:
Why is
Add
a poor button?
options: It is not keyboard-focusable and is not announced as a button
quiz.explain: A native button gets focus, Enter and Space handling and the button role automatically; a div gets none of these.

quiz.q: What does the first rule of ARIA say?
options: ARIA replaces the need for keyboard support
Prefer a native HTML element or attribute when one already provides the meaning and behaviour
quiz.explain: Native elements bring built-in semantics and behaviour; ARIA only changes what assistive tech is told and should fill real gaps.

lessons.title: SPAs, Front-End Frameworks and SEO: React, Vue, Angular, SSR and Being Found on Google
lessons.content:
Imagine two ways of reading a newspaper. In the first, every time you want the sports page, a delivery boy runs to the press and brings you a whole new newspaper. In the second, you have one newspaper in your hands and simply flip to the sports page; only the pages you need change. Classic websites work like the first way: every click loads a brand new page from the server. Single-page applications work like the second: the page loads once, and JavaScript swaps parts of it as you move around. This lesson explains both styles, the frameworks that make SPAs practical, and how to make sure search engines can still find and understand your pages. Multi-page applications: In a multi-page application, or MPA, each URL maps to a page that the server builds and sends as complete HTML. Click 'Vegetables' on Bazar and the browser requests /vegetables, receives a full new HTML document, throws away the old page and draws the new one. This is simple, works without JavaScript, is naturally friendly to search engines, and each page starts fresh. The downsides: every navigation reloads the header, menu and scripts, the screen blinks, and anything kept only in the page, such as the scroll position or a half-typed search, is lost. Single-page applications: In an SPA, the server sends one HTML shell, usually almost empty, plus a JavaScript bundle. The JavaScript builds the interface in the browser. When you click 'Vegetables', no new page is requested; the app fetches just the data, for example GET /api/products?category=vegetables returning JSON, and redraws only the product list. Navigation feels instant and app-like, like Gmail, Facebook or Google Maps. The costs: a bigger JavaScript download before anything useful appears, more work on slow phones, more complexity, and extra effort for SEO and accessibility. Client-side routing: An SPA still needs real URLs so that users can bookmark, share and use the back button. The browser's History API makes this possible. When the user clicks a link, the router calls history.pushState(data, '', '/vegetables'), which changes the address bar without loading a page, and then renders the matching view. When the user presses Back, the browser fires a popstate event, and the router renders the previous view. A route table maps patterns to views, such as /products/:id to a product detail component. One catch: if a user opens /vegetables directly, the server must send the same HTML shell for that path instead of a 404, so the hosting must be configured with a fallback. Components: Modern front-end frameworks build interfaces from components: small, reusable pieces that combine markup, style and behaviour. Bazar's page might be App containing Header, SearchBar, ProductList and CartSummary, and ProductList contains many ProductCard components. Each component is like a custom HTML tag you invented. Writing ProductCard once and reusing it 200 times keeps the code consistent: fix a bug in one place and it is fixed everywhere. Props and state: Data flows into a component as props, short for properties, like arguments to a function. ProductCard receives props such as name='Potato', price=40 and unit='kg'. A component's own changing data is called state, such as whether a dropdown is open or how many items are in the cart. The core idea of these frameworks is that the UI is a function of state: UI = f(state). You do not write step-by-step DOM commands like 'find the span and change its text'. You change the state, for example cartCount = cartCount + 1, and the framework updates the screen to match. Declarative UI and the virtual DOM: Telling the computer what the result should look like, instead of every step to get there, is called declarative programming. Manually updating the real DOM in many places is error-prone and can be slow if done carelessly. React's approach is the virtual DOM: when state changes, React builds a new lightweight description of the UI in JavaScript objects, compares it with the previous description (this comparison is called diffing or reconciliation), and then applies only the minimal real DOM changes needed. If only the cart count changed from 2 to 3, only that text node is updated. Other frameworks reach the same goal in different ways, for example by tracking exactly which data each part of the page depends on. React: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, created at Facebook (now Meta) and released as open source in 2013. Components are usually JavaScript functions that return JSX, an HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript, for example function ProductCard(props) { return
{props.name}: {props.price} taka
; }. State is managed with hooks such as useState. React itself focuses on the view; routing, data fetching and other parts come from separate libraries or from meta-frameworks built on top of it. It has a very large ecosystem and job market, and React Native reuses its ideas for mobile apps. Vue and Angular: Vue, created by Evan You and first released in 2014, is a progressive framework: you can add it to one part of an existing page or build a whole SPA. It uses HTML-based templates with special attributes such as v-if and v-for, and a reactivity system that automatically tracks which data each template uses. Many beginners find it gentle to learn. Angular, from Google, is a complete, opinionated framework written in TypeScript, with built-in routing, forms, HTTP client and dependency injection. It suits large teams that want one standard way of doing everything. The older AngularJS (version 1) is a different, now-retired framework, so do not confuse the two. Svelte is another approach that does most of its work at build time, compiling components into small JavaScript code. Choosing a framework: There is no single best one. The concepts transfer: components, props, state, one-way data flow, routing and talking to an API. A student who truly understands these in one framework can learn another in weeks. Pick based on the team's skills, the project's size, and the job market you are targeting, and remember that a simple content site may not need any SPA framework at all. Server-side rendering (SSR): A pure client-rendered SPA first shows an empty shell until JavaScript downloads and runs, which hurts slow phones and can hurt SEO. With server-side rendering, the server runs the same components and sends fully formed HTML for the requested URL, so the user sees content immediately. Then the JavaScript loads and hydrates the page. Hydration: Hydration means the client-side framework takes over the HTML that the server already rendered, attaching event listeners and state so the page becomes interactive, without rebuilding everything from scratch. Before hydration finishes, the page is visible but buttons may not respond yet. Reducing how much JavaScript needs hydrating is an active area of framework design. Static site generation (SSG): If a page is the same for everyone, like Bazar's 'About us' or a blog post, it can be rendered to HTML once at build time and served as a plain file from a CDN. This is very fast and cheap. Many sites mix strategies: SSG for marketing pages, SSR for product pages that change often, and client rendering for the logged-in dashboard. Meta-frameworks: Frameworks built on top of a UI library bring routing, SSR, SSG, data loading and bundling together. Examples include Next.js and Remix for React, Nuxt for Vue, and SvelteKit for Svelte. Angular also has its own server-rendering support. These tools change quickly, so learn the concepts and read the current official documentation for details. Progressive Web Apps (PWA): A PWA is a website that can behave more like an installed app. It needs HTTPS, a web app manifest (a JSON file with the name, icons, colours and start URL, so the browser can offer 'Add to Home screen'), and usually a service worker: a script that runs in the background, sits between the page and the network, and can cache files so the app opens offline or on bad connections. A Bazar PWA could show the last viewed product list even when the user's mobile data drops. Native mobile apps are covered in the Mobile Application Development course. SEO basics, how search works: Search engine optimization means helping search engines find, understand and rank your pages. Search engines do three things. Crawling: bots such as Googlebot follow links and download pages. Indexing: they process the content and store it in a giant index, like the index at the back of a book. Ranking: when someone searches 'online bazar Dhaka', they pick and order results by relevance and quality, using many signals, including how well the content matches the query, links from other sites, mobile-friendliness and page experience. Nobody outside the search company knows the exact formula, so be wary of anyone promising guaranteed first place. On-page SEO: Each page should have a unique, descriptive title element, such as 'Fresh Vegetables Delivered in Dhaka | Bazar', which usually becomes the clickable headline in results. Add a meta description, a short summary that search engines often show under the title; it is not a direct ranking factor, but a good one attracts clicks. Use one clear h1 and logical headings, semantic HTML, alt text for images, and descriptive link text instead of 'click here'. Write useful content for people first; keyword stuffing does not work and can be penalised. Technical SEO: Use clean, readable URLs, like /products/miniket-rice rather than /p?id=8812&x=3. A sitemap.xml file lists the URLs you want indexed, and you can submit it in tools such as Google Search Console. A robots.txt file at the site root tells well-behaved crawlers which paths not to crawl, such as /admin; it is a request, not security, and it does not hide pages from attackers. If the same content appears at several URLs, add a canonical link to say which one is the main one. Fast, mobile-friendly, HTTPS pages also help. SEO and SPAs: Google can run JavaScript and index client-rendered pages, but rendering may happen later than crawling, and other search engines and social media preview bots may not run JavaScript at all. If your product page shows content only after JavaScript fetches it, some bots may see an empty shell, and a shared link on Facebook may show no title or image. That is a major reason to use SSR or SSG for public pages, and to make every view reachable through a real URL with real links. Real-life example 1, Bazar's architecture: Public pages such as the home page, categories and product pages are server-rendered or statically generated, so they load fast and are fully visible to search engines and link previews. The cart and checkout are interactive components hydrated on top. The 'My orders' dashboard, which is private and not meant to be indexed, is a client-rendered SPA section. robots.txt disallows /account, and sitemap.xml lists all product URLs. Real-life example 2, a Bangladeshi news portal: A news site lives on search and social traffic. Each article must have its own URL, a clear title, a meta description, an image for link previews and fast server-rendered HTML. A purely client-rendered news site would risk showing blank previews when readers share stories on Facebook and could be indexed more slowly. On the other hand, the site's live cricket scoreboard widget can be a small client-side component that updates every few seconds. Common mistakes: Building an SPA for a simple content site that would be faster as plain HTML. Breaking the back button or using links without real URLs. Forgetting the server fallback, so refreshing /vegetables gives 404. Shipping a huge JavaScript bundle to show text. Same title on every page. Believing robots.txt protects private pages. Using div click handlers instead of real links, which hurts both SEO and accessibility. What exams ask: Compare MPA and SPA with advantages and disadvantages. Explain client-side routing and the History API. Define component, props and state. Explain the virtual DOM and why it helps. Compare React, Vue and Angular at a concept level. Define SSR, SSG and hydration. What is a PWA? Explain crawling, indexing and ranking, and the purpose of title, meta description, sitemap.xml and robots.txt. Recap: MPAs reload full pages from the server; SPAs load once and update parts with JavaScript, using the History API for real URLs. Frameworks build UIs from components with props and state, where the UI follows the state. React, Vue and Angular differ in style, but the concepts transfer. SSR, SSG and hydration combine fast first views with rich interaction. PWAs add installability and offline support. SEO means being crawlable, indexable and genuinely useful, with good titles, semantic HTML, clean URLs and server-rendered public pages.
key_points: MPA: server sends a full new page per click; SPA: one HTML shell, JavaScript fetches JSON and redraws parts.
Client-side routing uses the History API (pushState, popstate); the server needs a fallback for deep links.
Frameworks build UIs from reusable components; props flow in, state changes inside, UI = f(state).
React uses JSX and a virtual DOM diff; Vue uses templates and reactivity; Angular is a full TypeScript framework.
SSR sends ready HTML, SSG builds HTML at build time, hydration makes server HTML interactive.
A PWA needs HTTPS, a web app manifest and usually a service worker for caching and offline use.
SEO: crawling, indexing, ranking; use unique titles, meta descriptions, headings, clean URLs, sitemap.xml and canonical links.
robots.txt is a polite request to crawlers, not security; public SPA pages benefit from SSR or SSG for bots and link previews.
lessons.tip: Learn one framework deeply rather than three shallowly. If you can explain components, props, state and routing in React, picking up Vue or Angular is mostly learning new syntax.
lessons.task: Open any SPA you use, like Gmail or YouTube, and watch the address bar and the Network tab while clicking around: do you see full HTML pages or JSON requests? Then visit any site's /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml (for example a big news site) and write down three rules or URLs you find.

quiz.q: In a single-page application, what usually happens when you click to another section?
options: The server sends a complete new HTML page
JavaScript fetches data, often JSON, and redraws part of the page
Nothing; SPAs have only one view
quiz.explain: An SPA loads once; later navigation fetches just the data and updates only what changed.

quiz.q: Which browser API lets an SPA change the URL without loading a new page?
quiz.explain: history.pushState changes the address bar, and the popstate event handles the back button.

quiz.q: What is hydration?
options: Client-side code attaching events and state to HTML the server already rendered
quiz.explain: After SSR, the framework hydrates the HTML to make it interactive without rebuilding it.

quiz.q: What does robots.txt do?
options: Asks well-behaved crawlers not to crawl certain paths
quiz.explain: It is a polite instruction to crawlers, not a security measure; private pages need real access control.

quiz.q: Which file helps a browser offer 'Add to Home screen' for a PWA?
quiz.explain: The manifest gives the app's name, icons, colours and start URL; a service worker adds offline caching.

lessons.title: Deployment, Version Control and Course Wrap-Up: From Laptop to the Live Web
lessons.content:
Imagine you have cooked a perfect plate of biryani in your own kitchen. It tastes great, but nobody can buy it yet. To sell it, you need a shop with an address, a stove that works every day, a way to bring new recipes in without poisoning customers, and someone checking that the kitchen stays clean. A web app on your laptop is the same: it works at localhost:3000, but nobody in Sylhet or Khulna can use it. Deployment is everything needed to move it from your machine to a server on the Internet, keep it running safely, and update it again and again without breaking it.

What deployment means: Deployment is the process of putting a version of your application on servers where real users can reach it. It includes building the code, copying it to the server, configuring it with the right settings and secrets, running database changes, starting it, putting it behind a domain name with HTTPS, and watching it afterwards. Doing all this by hand once is fine for learning; doing it by hand every day leads to mistakes. Professional teams automate it.

Version control recap: Before code can be deployed safely, it must be tracked. Git, covered in depth in the Software Engineering course, records every change as a commit, lets each developer work on a branch, and merges branches back together. Teams host repositories on services like GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. A common web workflow is: create a branch such as feature/cart-discount, commit small changes with clear messages, push the branch, open a pull request, let teammates review the code and let automated tests run, then merge into the main branch. Main is kept in a state that could be deployed at any moment.

What to keep out of Git: Some files must never be committed. node_modules and other installed dependencies can be recreated from package.json and the lock file. Build output such as a dist folder is generated. Most importantly, .env files with passwords and API keys must stay out; list them all in .gitignore. A sample file such as .env.example, with variable names but no real values, tells teammates what settings are needed.

Environments: Most teams run at least three copies of the app. Development is each programmer's own laptop, with test data and debug tools. Staging is a server that copies production as closely as possible, where the team and testers check a release before users see it. Production is the live site that real customers use. Each environment has its own database and its own settings, given through environment variables like DATABASE_URL, NODE_ENV=production and PAYMENT_API_KEY. The same code runs everywhere; only the configuration changes. This idea, keeping config in the environment and not in code, is one of the principles of the well-known Twelve-Factor App guidelines.

The build step: Front-end code is usually not served exactly as written. A build tool bundles and minifies JavaScript and CSS, compiles TypeScript to JavaScript, optimizes images and adds content hashes to file names for caching. Running a command like npm run build produces a folder of ready files. The back end may also be compiled, as with Java or Go, or simply have its dependencies installed with npm ci, which installs exactly the versions recorded in the lock file so that the server matches what was tested.

Continuous integration (CI): CI means every push or pull request automatically triggers a pipeline on a server, such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins. A typical pipeline for Bazar: check out the code, install dependencies, run a linter to catch style problems and simple bugs, run unit and integration tests, and build the app. If any step fails, the pull request is marked red and cannot be merged. CI catches problems within minutes, while the change is still fresh in the developer's mind.

Continuous delivery and deployment (CD): Continuous delivery means every change that passes CI is automatically prepared and can be released with one click, usually after being deployed to staging. Continuous deployment goes one step further: every change that passes all checks goes to production automatically, with no human click. Many teams deploy small changes several times a day this way. Small, frequent releases are less risky than one huge release every three months, because if something breaks, you know exactly which small change caused it.

Hosting types: Where does the app actually run? Shared hosting puts many websites on one server managed by the provider; it is cheap and fine for a simple PHP or WordPress site but gives little control. A VPS, virtual private server, gives you your own virtual machine with root access; you install and maintain everything, including security updates. Cloud platforms such as AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud offer virtual machines plus hundreds of managed services like databases, storage and load balancers, with pay-as-you-go pricing. Platform as a Service (PaaS) lets you push code and the platform handles servers, scaling and often HTTPS. Static hosting, such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages, serves pre-built HTML, CSS and JS files from a CDN, perfect for static sites and SPA front ends.

Choosing hosting: For a student portfolio, static hosting is often free and enough. For a small Bazar-like shop, a PaaS or a modest VPS with a managed database is common. As traffic grows, teams move to cloud setups with several servers behind a load balancer. Also think about where your users are: hosting closer to Bangladesh, or using a CDN with nearby edge locations, reduces latency. Always check what the provider manages and what remains your responsibility, especially backups and security updates.

Domains and DNS: Users should type bazar.example.com, not an IP address. You rent a domain name from a registrar, for example a .com, or a .com.bd through the authority that manages the .bd domain. Then you add DNS records (DNS itself is taught in Computer Networks). An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, such as bazar.example.com to 203.0.113.10. An AAAA record maps to an IPv6 address. A CNAME record makes one name an alias of another, such as www.bazar.example.com pointing to bazar.example.com, or to a hosting platform's name. After a change, resolvers may keep old answers until the record's TTL expires, so lowering the TTL before a planned move makes switching faster.

HTTPS certificates: To serve HTTPS, the server needs a TLS certificate issued by a certificate authority that browsers trust, proving that you control the domain. Let's Encrypt is a non-profit certificate authority that issues free, automated certificates. A tool such as Certbot proves domain control, installs the certificate, and renews it automatically; Let's Encrypt certificates have short lifetimes, typically 90 days, which is why automatic renewal matters. Many PaaS, static hosts and CDNs handle certificates for you entirely.

Reverse proxy: On a VPS, your Node or Python app usually listens on an internal port such as 3000. In front of it sits a reverse proxy, often Nginx (Apache and Caddy are alternatives). The reverse proxy listens on ports 80 and 443, handles TLS, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, serves static files and compressed responses quickly, and forwards dynamic requests to the app on port 3000. It can also balance requests across several app instances. The app process itself is kept alive and restarted on crash by a process manager such as systemd or PM2.

Containers: 'It works on my machine' is a classic problem: different library versions on the laptop and the server. A container packages the app together with its runtime and dependencies into an image that runs the same everywhere. Docker is the most widely known tool. A short Dockerfile describes the steps: start from a Node base image, copy package files, install dependencies, copy the code, and set the start command. Containers share the host operating system's kernel, so they are lighter and start faster than full virtual machines. Large systems run many containers with an orchestrator such as Kubernetes, which you can explore later.

Database migrations during deploys: When a new version adds a column, such as discount_percent on products, the database schema must change too. Migrations are versioned scripts that make these changes in order and are stored in Git with the code. The deploy pipeline runs pending migrations before or during the release. Careful teams make changes backward compatible, for example adding a nullable column first, so the old and new code can both run during the switch. And always have backups, tested by actually restoring them, before changing production data.

Release strategies and rollback: Things will sometimes go wrong, so plan the way back. A rollback means returning to the previous working version quickly. In a blue-green deployment, two identical production environments exist; the new version goes to the idle one, and traffic is switched over only when it is verified, so switching back is instant. In a canary release, the new version first serves a small percentage of users, and is expanded only if errors stay low. Feature flags let you ship code switched off and turn it on later for some or all users.

Logs and monitoring: After deployment, you need eyes on the system. Logs record what happened: each request, errors with stack traces, and important events like 'order 1042 paid'. Do not log passwords, tokens or full card numbers. Monitoring tracks numbers over time: response time, error rate, CPU and memory, and database load. Uptime checkers ping your site every minute and alert you if it is down. Error tracking tools collect front-end and back-end exceptions with details. Alerts should reach a person by email, chat or phone, ideally before customers start complaining on Facebook.

Real-life example 1, deploying Bazar step by step: A developer merges a pull request adding cart discounts. GitHub Actions runs: install, lint, 120 tests pass, build. The pipeline builds a Docker image tagged with the commit hash and deploys it to staging, runs migrations there, and the tester checks the cart flow. With one approval, the same image goes to production: migrations run, new containers start, Nginx sends traffic to them once health checks pass, and old containers stop. Monitoring shows error rate stays near zero. If not, the team redeploys the previous image within minutes.

Real-life example 2, Eid traffic and a university result site: A shop expects five times the usual visitors during an Eid sale. The team load-tests staging beforehand, adds more app instances behind the load balancer, makes sure static files and product images are on a CDN, and freezes risky deployments during the sale. A university result portal faces a similar spike on result day; caching the result pages and scaling horizontally keeps it from showing 503 errors when thousands of students refresh at once.

Common mistakes: Committing .env files or keys to GitHub. Deploying straight from a laptop with untested changes. Having no staging or no backups. Editing files directly on the production server so Git no longer matches what runs. Forgetting HTTPS renewal. Running the app as the root user. Leaving debug mode on. Releasing on a Thursday night before a holiday with nobody watching the alerts.

Course recap: Over these lessons you followed a web app from idea to live site. You saw how a browser and server talk with HTTP; built pages with semantic HTML and forms; styled them with the box model, Flexbox, Grid and responsive design; made them interactive with JavaScript, the DOM, events and asynchronous fetch calls with JSON. On the server you routed requests, used MVC, designed REST APIs and connected to a database safely. You added sessions or tokens, hashed passwords, defended against XSS, SQL injection and CSRF, and made the site fast, accessible and findable. Finally, you learned how teams ship it with Git, CI/CD and proper hosting.

What to learn next: Build one complete project end to end, such as a small shop, a blood donor finder for your district, or a tuition marketplace, and deploy it with a real domain and HTTPS. Then go deeper in one direction: a front-end framework like React or Vue; a back-end framework like Express, Django, Laravel or Spring; TypeScript; testing; cloud and DevOps with Docker; or web security. Read official documentation such as MDN Web Docs, keep your code on GitHub, and contribute to open source. The web rewards people who build, ship and keep learning.
key_points: Deployment moves a tested build to servers, configures secrets and databases, adds a domain and HTTPS, and keeps watching it.
Use Git branches and pull requests; keep node_modules, build output and .env files out of the repository.
Run separate development, staging and production environments; the same code, different configuration via environment variables.
CI runs lint, tests and build on every push; continuous delivery makes releases one click, continuous deployment releases automatically.
Hosting options: shared, VPS, cloud, PaaS and static hosting, each trading control for convenience.
DNS A, AAAA and CNAME records point a domain to the server; Let's Encrypt provides free, automatically renewed certificates.
Nginx as a reverse proxy handles TLS and static files and forwards to the app; Docker containers package the app with its dependencies.
Plan migrations, backups, rollback, blue-green or canary releases, and use logs, monitoring and alerts after every deploy.
lessons.tip: Deploy something tiny in your first week, even a one-page portfolio on free static hosting. Seeing your own URL work on a friend's phone teaches more about DNS, HTTPS and caching than any chapter.
lessons.task: On paper, draw the path of a request to a deployed Bazar: user's phone, DNS lookup, CDN, Nginx reverse proxy, app container, database. Next to each box write one thing that can go wrong and how you would detect it (for example, an expired certificate: browser warning, uptime alert). Bonus: list the steps a CI pipeline for your own project should run.

quiz.q: Which environment is meant to copy production closely so a release can be checked before users see it?
quiz.explain: Staging mirrors production settings and data shape, so problems appear there before reaching real users.

quiz.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: Delivery keeps every passing change ready to release with a click; deployment releases it to production automatically
Delivery is for front end only
quiz.explain: Both run CI; continuous deployment removes the final human approval step.

quiz.q: Which DNS record makes www.bazar.example.com an alias of another name?
quiz.explain: A CNAME points one name to another name; A and AAAA point to IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

quiz.q: What does a reverse proxy like Nginx usually do in front of a Node app?
options: Handles TLS on ports 80/443, serves static files and forwards dynamic requests to the app
quiz.explain: The app listens on an internal port; Nginx faces the Internet, terminates HTTPS and passes requests along.

quiz.q: Why is a Docker container useful for deployment?
options: It makes code run without an operating system
It packages the app with its runtime and dependencies so it runs the same everywhere
quiz.explain: The same image runs on the laptop, CI, staging and production, avoiding 'works on my machine' problems.
